AS-0259.D: Encourage her to avoid using social media: removing a trigger without treating the anxiety, and often rejected by adolescents; not the main management.

AS-0269.A: Chronic lung disease: well controlled childhood asthma does not usually progress to chronic lung disease; this would only frighten the mother without basis.
AS-0269.C: Lifelong asthma: only a minority remain asthmatic as adults; this would be the prognosis only for severe, atopic disease with strong family history.
AS-0269.D: No correlation: there is a correlation, since severe or atopic childhood asthma increases the chance of persistence or relapse in adulthood.

AS-0271.A: Reassurance is only for pseudostrabismus with a normal, symmetric red reflex and corneal light reflex; an absent red reflex is never normal and may be a malignancy.

AS-0272.B: Removal and irrigation suit a superficial, loose foreign body or a chemical splash; pulling out a lodged metal object can worsen a penetrating injury and cause extrusion of ocular contents.
AS-0272.C: Antibiotics with clinic follow up fit a simple corneal abrasion after a superficial foreign body has been removed, not an object still embedded in the eye.
AS-0272.D: A pressure patch is avoided in suspected penetrating injury because pressure on the globe can expel contents; a rigid shield is used only as a bridge to referral, not as the management.

AS-0274.A: Observe with serial Hb: acceptable only for a stable infant with a benign swelling (caput or cephalohematoma) and normal Hb; observing a hypotensive neonate with Hb 7.5 risks death from ongoing bleeding.
AS-0274.C: Vitamin K: treats vitamin K deficiency bleeding, which prolongs the PT; here PT and PTT are normal, so the bleeding is traumatic and vitamin K will not correct shock or anemia.

AS-0282.A: Antipsychotics do not treat the cognitive deficit and raise mortality in elderly patients with dementia; they are reserved for severe psychosis or agitation that endangers the patient or others.
AS-0282.B: His withdrawal reflects apathy from dementia, not a depressive episode; an antidepressant is right when there are core depressive features (low mood, guilt) or pseudodementia, not progressive amnestic decline with atrophy.

AS-0285.A: CBT for insomnia is first line for chronic insomnia disorder (difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep on most nights for about 3 months despite adequate opportunity); here the problem is a self-imposed irregular schedule, so simple sleep hygiene comes first.

AS-0286.A: Organic acidemia: presents with poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, metabolic acidosis and ketosis in a sick neonate, not hypoglycemia in a well fed macrosomic infant of a diabetic mother.
AS-0286.C: Adrenal insufficiency: suggested by hypoglycemia with salt wasting (low Na, high K), ambiguous genitalia in a girl (CAH) or shock; nothing here points to it.
AS-0286.D: Glucagon deficiency: a very rare isolated cause; maternal diabetes and macrosomia point clearly to excess fetal insulin, not lack of counter-regulatory hormone.

AS-0289.A: Abdominal MRI: also an accepted staging study (no radiation, good for spinal extension) and preferred at some centers, but CT is the classic exam answer and shows calcification better.
AS-0289.C: Biopsy: tissue diagnosis comes only after imaging has defined the mass and its organ of origin; a suspected Wilms tumor is usually not biopsied upfront at all, because biopsy can spill tumor and upstage it.

AS-0293.A: CPAP with 100% oxygen: CPAP is a valid first support in a spontaneously breathing preterm, but routine 100% oxygen is wrong because preterm infants need oxygen titrated to target saturations to avoid hyperoxia injury such as retinopathy of prematurity.

AS-0294.A: CBC: may show anemia from chronic blood loss, but it is nonspecific and cannot confirm an ulcer.
AS-0294.B: Abdominal ultrasound: useful for gallstones, pancreatic or hepatic disease, but it cannot see the gastric or duodenal mucosa.
AS-0294.D: H. pylori stool antigen only: detects infection and is mainly used to confirm eradication after treatment; it cannot show an ulcer, and in children diagnosis should be by endoscopy with biopsy rather than a noninvasive test alone.

AS-0296.A: Will worsen with time: the noise may peak in the first months but laryngomalacia does not progressively worsen; it improves as the airway matures.
AS-0296.B: Needs surgical correction: supraglottoplasty is reserved for severe disease with failure to thrive, apnea, cyanosis or feeding difficulty; this infant is thriving.
AS-0296.C: Normal developmental sounds: the noise comes from a structural airway disorder (laryngomalacia), even though it is benign; calling it normal skips the diagnosis and the expected course.

AS-0298.A: Mask oxygen: fits mild distress with adequate effort; it does not support ventilation or provide pressure in severe distress.
AS-0298.C: Low-flow oxygen: suitable only for mild hypoxemia without significant distress; it is inadequate for a neonate in respiratory failure.

AS-0299.B: Prematurity schedule (corrected age): corrected age is used for growth and developmental assessment, not vaccine timing; there is no separate delayed schedule for preterm infants.
AS-0299.C: Immunize for 6 months: giving the 6-month vaccines now would be too early and skips the 2 and 4 month doses; the schedule follows actual age.

AS-0314.A: Conjunctivitis gives diffuse redness with discharge, grittiness or itch, usually bilateral; here there are no infection signs and the redness is a solid spot.
AS-0314.B: Scleritis causes severe, boring pain (often waking the patient), tenderness and a deep violaceous hue, and can threaten vision; this patient has no pain.
AS-0314.C: Episcleritis gives sectoral pinkish redness of dilated vessels with mild discomfort; it is engorged vessels, not a flat sheet of blood obscuring the sclera.

AS-0324.B: Admit for observation 24 hours: observation alone suits a child with minor head injury, normal mental status and only intermediate features (brief vomiting, headache, no LOC). A post-traumatic seizure with drowsiness needs imaging first; observation follows a normal CT.

AS-0326.A: High flow O2 and IV fluids: an escalation step for severe disease (marked work of breathing, persistent hypoxia on low flow, apnea, or inability to feed). Not the starting point for a typical case.

AS-0327.B: Throat culture: the back-up test when the rapid antigen test is NEGATIVE in a child with a suggestive picture. A positive rapid test is specific enough to treat without culture.
AS-0327.C: Reassurance: appropriate for viral pharyngitis (mild hyperemia, negative rapid test). Confirmed GAS needs antibiotics to prevent rheumatic fever and suppurative complications.
AS-0327.D: This option was blank in the recall and carries no content.

AS-0329.A: MMR.DTP.OPV: incomplete; it leaves out varicella, which is also given at school entry.
AS-0329.B: MMR.HBV.DTP.HAV: hepatitis B is completed in infancy and hepatitis A at 18 and 24 months, so neither belongs at school entry; varicella and OPV are missing.
AS-0329.D: MMR.varicella.OPV.PCV: PCV is an infant series vaccine (2, 4, 6, 12 months) and is not routine in a healthy 6-year-old; DTP is missing.

AS-0330.B: Suckling: the sucking reflex is triggered by something placed INSIDE the mouth or touching the palate, producing rhythmic sucking; stroking the cheek causes rooting, not sucking.

AS-0331.A: CT is not used to assess infant ocular alignment; imaging is reserved for abnormal findings such as leukocoria, proptosis or neurological signs.
AS-0331.B: Ophthalmology referral is right for a constant deviation at any age, a deviation persisting beyond about 4 to 6 months, an abnormal red reflex or an asymmetric corneal light reflex.

AS-0341.B: Desmopressin is for older children when behavioural measures and the alarm fail, or for short-term needs such as sleepovers; it is not the first step at 6.
AS-0341.C: Toilet training addresses daytime continence, which is usually already achieved; nighttime dryness depends on bladder maturation and ADH rhythm, not training.
AS-0341.D: The enuresis alarm is the most effective active treatment once a motivated older child and family want treatment after behavioural measures; it is not the first step here.

AS-0342.B: Psychosocial development delay: would need clear social red flags (no interest in peers, no pretend play, poor eye contact, loss of skills). "Plays alone" by itself, with intact comprehension, is not enough.
AS-0342.C: Gross motor delay: no gross motor finding is given (walking, running, stairs, tricycle); pouring water and drawing are fine motor tasks.
AS-0342.D: This option was not recalled ("Forget") and carries no content.

AS-0345.B: Give them pamphlet and arrange follow up: written material alone is passive and does not check understanding or skill; it supplements but does not replace face-to-face teaching.
AS-0345.C: Refer him to somewhere (not recalled): referral may help if specialist or psychosocial issues exist, but the first step in a health-promotion question is to educate the family yourself.

AS-0346.B: Give them pamphlet and arrange follow up: written material alone is passive and does not check understanding or skill; it supplements but does not replace face-to-face teaching.
AS-0346.C: Refer him to somewhere (not recalled): referral may help if specialist or psychosocial issues exist, but the first step in a health-promotion question is to educate the family yourself.

AS-0348B.A: Rooting reflex: a mouth response, turning toward a touch on the cheek or corner of the mouth; it involves no leg movement.

AS-0348C.B: By 4 months: the typical disappearance age of the rooting and Galant (trunk incurvation) reflexes, not stepping.
AS-0348C.C: By 6 months: the disappearance age of the Moro and palmar grasp reflexes.

AS-0351.C: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-0352.B: Short stature in Noonan can later be treated with growth hormone, but the priority now is the cardiac lesion and confirming the syndrome; endocrine referral first fits isolated short stature without dysmorphism or heart disease.
AS-0352.C: Gastroenterology referral fits failure to thrive with GI symptoms (malabsorption, chronic diarrhea); here the failure to thrive is part of a syndromic picture with a heart lesion.

AS-0356.A: Ocular toxocariasis gives a granuloma with vitreous inflammation in an older child with puppy contact; calcification is not its typical feature.
AS-0356.C: Coats disease (usually a young boy, unilateral) gives telangiectatic vessels with yellow subretinal exudate and exudative detachment, typically without calcification.
AS-0356.D: Congenital rubella causes cataract (absent red reflex) with microcephaly, PDA and deafness, not a calcified retinal mass.

AS-0358.A: Sertraline treats comorbid depression, which is not described; it does not slow cognitive decline.
AS-0358.C: Rivastigmine is another cholinesterase inhibitor with the same mechanism as donepezil; two drugs of the same class are never combined. Switching to it is an option when donepezil is not tolerated, not when the disease has progressed.
AS-0358.D: Stopping donepezil removes a drug that still offers benefit; memantine is added, not substituted, in moderate to severe disease. Switching to memantine alone fits intolerance or contraindication to cholinesterase inhibitors.

AS-0360.A: Amiodarone is reserved for refractory SVT under cardiology guidance after adenosine and cardioversion are considered; it is not a first line drug in children.
AS-0360.B: Adenosine is the usual drug for stable SVT once vagal maneuvers (ice to face, Valsalva) fail; the key here skips it, which only fits a child who is unstable or adenosine refractory.
AS-0360.D: Beta blockers are used for long term prevention of recurrent SVT, not for acute termination of an ongoing episode.

AS-0362.B: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.
AS-0362.C: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.
AS-0362.D: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-0363.A: Simethicone is widely used but trials show no benefit over placebo, so it is not the recommended treatment.
AS-0363.C: Antibiotics would only fit an infection with fever, poor feeding or toxic appearance; colic is not infectious.
AS-0363.D: Abdominal ultrasound is for red flags such as bilious vomiting, abdominal mass, distension or bloody stools (for example intussusception); a thriving infant with colic needs no imaging.

AS-0366.A: Rotavirus causes watery, non bloody diarrhea with vomiting and fever in infants and young children; it is the classic cause of dehydrating watery diarrhea.
AS-0366.B: Norovirus causes acute vomiting and watery diarrhea, typically in outbreaks (schools, cruise ships); no blood or mucus.
AS-0366.C: This option was not recalled; other causes of bloody mucoid diarrhea a student should consider are Shigella (especially with high fever or seizures), Salmonella, EHEC (bloody diarrhea then HUS) and amebiasis.

AS-0368.A: A risk of about 1 to 2% applies only to simple febrile seizures; stated as a fixed figure for all febrile seizures it ignores the higher risk with complex seizures, so it is weaker than B.
AS-0368.C: A parental history of febrile seizures raises the chance of the child having febrile seizures and recurrences, not epilepsy. It is a family history of EPILEPSY that increases the epilepsy risk.
AS-0368.D: Antipyretics make the child comfortable but have not been shown to prevent febrile convulsions or their recurrence.

AS-0374.A: Hemophilia A is X linked recessive: it affects boys and is classic for post circumcision bleeding, but the mother is usually an asymptomatic carrier; choose it when only male relatives (brothers, maternal uncles) bleed.
AS-0374.C: DIC is acquired, occurring in a sick neonate (sepsis, asphyxia) with diffuse bleeding; a family history makes no sense for it.
AS-0374.D: Inherited platelet disorders (for example Glanzmann, Bernard-Soulier) are rare and usually autosomal recessive; they need platelet count and function tests, and are less likely than vWD with this pattern.

AS-0377.A: Follow up alone is never enough for hemorrhoids that are actively bleeding and causing anemia.
AS-0377.B: Conservative treatment (fiber, fluids, stool softeners, sitz baths) is right for external hemorrhoids and uncomplicated grade I to II internal hemorrhoids without anemia.
AS-0377.C: Rubber band ligation is the office procedure for grade I to III internal hemorrhoids that fail conservative care; it is the usual next step for bleeding grade II piles without significant anemia.

AS-0378.A: Compression (direct pressure) is the first move only when there is active external hemorrhage from the wound; the stem describes no bleeding.
AS-0378.B: Analgesia and fluids are supportive and are part of resuscitation, but they are the answer only when the stem shows shock; they do not address the infection risk that defines open fracture care.
AS-0378.D: Surgical debridement and stabilization is the definitive step, done urgently in theatre after antibiotics; it becomes the answer when antibiotics are already given or the question asks for the next or definitive step.

AS-0379.A: A compressive dressing is right when the wound is actively bleeding (direct pressure is the first step for external hemorrhage); the stem mentions no bleeding, so the open fracture priority is antibiotics.
AS-0379.B: Analgesia and fluids support the patient and are given when there is pain or shock, but they are not the specific initial treatment of an open fracture.
AS-0379.D: Surgical debridement and stabilization is the definitive step after antibiotics; it is chosen when the question asks for the next step once antibiotics are running.

AS-0381.A: Continuing sports with only annual ECGs leaves an untreated, high risk patient exposed to exertion triggered arrhythmia; it fits only a normal screening ECG.
AS-0381.C: Pacemaker is not first line; it is considered for bradycardia or pause dependent torsades, and an ICD (not a pacemaker) is for survivors of cardiac arrest or recurrent events despite beta blockers.
AS-0381.D: Unrestricted sport would be correct only after the abnormal ECG and family history are explained and excluded; a long QT with family sudden death is not cleared.

AS-0382.A: Continuing sports with only annual ECG monitoring ignores a high risk diagnosis; this fits only a normal screening ECG.
AS-0382.C: Pacemaker is not first line in long QT; an ICD is reserved for aborted cardiac arrest or recurrent events despite beta blockers.
AS-0382.D: Limiting to low exertion sport addresses the trigger but gives no beta blocker, which is the cornerstone of therapy; the combined option is better.

AS-0383.B: Postponing clinic follow-up and weighing weekly at home is unnecessary and removes routine surveillance; weekly weights fit a baby with faltering growth.
AS-0383.C: Growth hormone evaluation is for falling height velocity or crossing length percentiles downward, often with low bone age; proportionate tracking on the 25th percentile is normal.
AS-0383.D: Extra calories are for failure to thrive (weight crossing percentiles downward); forcing calories in a normally growing infant risks overfeeding.

AS-0384.A: Growth hormone assessment is for true growth failure: height below the normal range or a falling height velocity (crossing percentiles downward). Steady tracking at the 25th percentile is not growth failure.
AS-0384.C: Increasing calories is for inadequate intake or weight faltering (weight crossing percentiles downward). Here feeding is good and weight and height are proportionate and stable.
AS-0384.D: Small size is never a reason to delay immunization; vaccines are given on schedule. Delay applies only to true contraindications or precautions (e.g., moderate to severe acute illness).

AS-0385.B: Day-to-day weight fluctuation is normal, but it does not address the real problem: a 9-month-old with no complementary feeding. Reassurance alone fits a well-fed infant tracking steadily on a percentile.
AS-0385.C: Adding protein alone is too narrow; the deficit at this age is overall energy (and iron) from missing complementary foods. A protein-specific change would fit only a documented protein deficiency, which is not suggested here.

AS-0386.A: Diuretics and other heart failure drugs control symptoms until surgery but do not correct the defect; medical treatment alone fits a small, asymptomatic, or spontaneously closing defect (e.g., small muscular VSD).
AS-0386.B: Higher-calorie feeds support weight gain in a child with heart failure, but they are adjunctive and do not treat the shunt.
AS-0386.D: Waiting until age 2 risks irreversible pulmonary hypertension (Eisenmenger physiology); catheterization is not the definitive treatment of an AVSD and is used only selectively to assess pulmonary vascular resistance.

AS-0387.A: Amoxicillin is for acute otitis media (fever, otalgia, bulging red TM); antibiotics give no lasting benefit in OME, and here there is no fever or pain.
AS-0387.C: Grommets are for OME persisting ≥3 months with documented hearing loss or speech, learning or behavioural impact, or structural TM changes; it is too early here.

AS-0388.B: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-0388B.A: Mastoidectomy is for cholesteatoma, coalescent mastoiditis or chronic suppurative disease, not uncomplicated effusion.
AS-0388B.B: Adenoidectomy alone does not restore hearing immediately; guidelines allow it (with or without tubes) from about age 4 or with nasal obstruction or repeat surgery, but tubes remain the standard first operation for hearing loss from OME.
AS-0388B.C: Myringotomy alone drains fluid but the incision heals within days and the effusion reaccumulates, so it is not recommended without a tube.

AS-0389.A: Decongestants and antihistamines have no proven benefit in OME and are not recommended.
AS-0389.B: Amoxicillin is for acute otitis media (fever, otalgia, bulging TM); there are no signs of acute infection here.
AS-0389.D: Tympanostomy tubes come later, for OME persisting ≥3 months with documented hearing loss; hearing must be measured first.

AS-0390.B: Surgical nerve exploration/repair is considered only if function does not recover after about 3 to 6 months, not as the next step in a newborn.
AS-0390.C: Calcium supplements treat neonatal hypocalcemia (e.g., infant of a diabetic mother), which causes jitteriness or seizures, not a weak one-sided Moro.
AS-0390.D: Dextrose treats neonatal hypoglycemia, common in macrosomic infants of diabetic mothers, but that produces jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy or seizures rather than a focal weak Moro.

AS-0391.C: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-0392.D: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-0393.A: Withholding fits only when immunity is accepted as proven (documented vaccination, laboratory evidence, or provider-verified disease); this key treats a mother's photo as not sufficient proof.
AS-0393.B: There is no reason to postpone to 2 years; live vaccines are delayed only after recent immunoglobulin/blood products, during moderate to severe illness, or with immunosuppression, none of which is present.
AS-0393.D: Immunoglobulin is for post-exposure prophylaxis in high-risk susceptible people (immunocompromised, pregnant, certain newborns); this is a healthy child, and IG given with the live vaccine would reduce its effectiveness.

AS-0394.B: MMR is the post-exposure option (within 72 hours) for exposed people aged 6 months or older; at 5 months it is not given because maternal antibodies interfere and it is not licensed at this age.
AS-0394.C: Maternal antibodies may have waned by 5 months and cannot be relied on; young infants exposed to measles get severe disease and must receive prophylaxis.
AS-0394.D: There is no specific antiviral for measles prophylaxis; vitamin A is given to children who have measles (to reduce severity), not to prevent infection in an asymptomatic contact.

AS-0395.A: Pneumonia needs infection risk factors (maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis) or signs of sepsis, and the X-ray would show consolidation or infiltrates rather than fissural fluid; this baby is afebrile (36.6 °C) and no risk factors are given.
AS-0395.B: Meconium aspiration needs meconium-stained liquor, typically in a post-term or distressed baby, with patchy infiltrates and hyperinflation on X-ray; none of that is described.
AS-0395.C: RDS is a disease of preterm infants with surfactant deficiency, showing a diffuse ground-glass (reticulogranular) pattern with air bronchograms and worsening distress; this is a term baby with fissural fluid.

AS-0400.B: Urine culture is for suspected UTI (fever, dysuria, foul urine, pyuria or nitrites on urinalysis) and is not a first test; UTI does not explain weight loss and marked thirst.

AS-0401.B: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-0402.A: Mild dehydration: child is alert and thirsty with normal eyes, wet tongue, normal pulse and normal capillary refill; this child is lethargic and hypotensive.
AS-0402.B: Moderate dehydration: irritable, sunken eyes, dry tongue, slow skin pinch, but still alert with maintained blood pressure; lethargy plus hypotension takes this beyond moderate.
AS-0402.D: No dehydration: no signs at all; this child has seven episodes a day of losses with clear clinical dehydration.

AS-0403.A: Hemophilia A (factor VIII) prolongs the aPTT only with a normal PT; it presents with hemarthrosis or circumcision bleeding, not a prolonged PT.
AS-0403.B: Von Willebrand disease gives mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, gums, menorrhagia, dental extraction) with prolonged bleeding time and normal or mildly prolonged aPTT; the PT stays normal.

AS-0408.B: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-0410.B: Hearing test is right for an isolated speech or language delay with otherwise normal social interaction; it is part of the autism work-up, but it does not explain absent eye contact and repetitive toy lining.
AS-0410.C: Speech therapy referral treats a pure expressive language delay; here the core problem is social communication and repetitive behavior, which needs autism assessment first.

AS-0412.A: CT is not used to assess infant ocular alignment; imaging is reserved for abnormal findings such as leukocoria, proptosis or neurological signs.
AS-0412.B: Ophthalmology referral is right for a constant deviation at any age, a deviation persisting beyond about 4 to 6 months, an abnormal red reflex or an asymmetric corneal light reflex.

AS-0413.B: Referral is right when the corneal light reflex is displaced (temporally in the deviated eye in esotropia), the cover test shows movement, the deviation is constant, or the red reflex is abnormal.

AS-0416.A: Antibiotics are always given, but antibiotics alone are reserved for patients with no neurological deficit or who are unfit for surgery; with weakness and sphincter loss, delaying decompression risks permanent paralysis.
AS-0416.C: Image-guided needle aspiration is an option only in selected patients without deficit (or poor surgical candidates); it cannot decompress a cord or cauda equina already compromised.
AS-0416.D: Observation wastes the time window; any new or progressing deficit in epidural abscess needs urgent decompression.

AS-0417.A: Reassure is only acceptable for a healthy, vaccinated animal that can be observed for 10 days, or for exposures with no broken skin; a sick animal makes this a rabies risk.
AS-0417.B: Prophylactic antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate) are considered for cat bites because of Pasteurella, especially punctures or hand wounds, but they do nothing for the life-threatening rabies risk and the wound shows no infection.
AS-0417.C: Irrigation with soap and water is always done for every bite, but irrigation ONLY leaves the child without rabies post-exposure prophylaxis despite a suspicious animal.

AS-0418.A: Reassurance fits a healthy, observable, vaccinated pet or contact without broken skin; a sick animal makes it unsafe.
AS-0418.B: Vaccine alone is right for minor (category II) exposures such as nibbling or minor scratches without bleeding, or for a previously vaccinated person; a bite needs immunoglobulin as well, because vaccine antibodies take about a week to appear.
AS-0418.C: Immunoglobulin alone gives only short-lived passive protection; it is never given without the vaccine series.

AS-0420.B: Cardiac contusion usually presents with arrhythmias or ECG changes (and troponin rise); it does not explain raised neck veins with clear, equal lungs as well as tamponade does.
AS-0420.C: Massive hemothorax gives reduced air entry and dullness on one side, with <i>flat</i> neck veins from blood loss; here air entry is equal and veins are distended.
AS-0420.D: Tension pneumothorax gives absent breath sounds, hyperresonance and tracheal shift; a bilateral one would leave her in severe respiratory distress with silent chests, not talking comfortably with RR 18 and normal air entry on both sides.

AS-0421.B: Prophylactic antiepileptics are not recommended for simple febrile seizures, because the prognosis is excellent and drug side effects outweigh any benefit; antiepileptics fit epilepsy (2 or more unprovoked seizures).
AS-0421.C: Urgent CT brain is for focal deficits, head trauma, signs of raised ICP, or persistently altered consciousness; a quick recovery after a short generalized seizure does not need imaging.
AS-0421.D: EEG is not needed after a simple febrile seizure; it is used for unprovoked seizures or suspected epilepsy.

AS-0422.A: Reassurance is for typical vasovagal syncope (prodrome, upright posture, trigger) with a normal exam and ECG; exertional syncope with a murmur is never reassured.
AS-0422.B: Electrolytes help when vomiting, diarrhea, eating disorder or drugs suggest an arrhythmia from hypokalemia; nothing here points to that.
AS-0422.D: ECG is done early in every syncope and screens for long QT, WPW or LVH; it would be the answer if the question asked for the initial or next test, but it cannot define the outflow lesion causing the murmur.

AS-0423.A: Rifampicin monotherapy treats latent TB (usually for 4 months); using one drug for active disease breeds resistance.
AS-0423.B: Isoniazid plus rifampicin for 3 months is a latent TB regimen for a positive test with a normal chest X-ray and no symptoms; this child has symptoms and consolidation.

AS-0427.B: No carbs eating removes a major energy source when CF patients need extra calories; carbohydrate does not cause the pain, and even CF-related diabetes is managed with insulin rather than carbohydrate restriction.
AS-0427.C: Multivitamins alone (fat-soluble A, D, E, K) are needed in CF, but without enzymes the fat and protein, and the vitamins themselves, are still malabsorbed.
AS-0427.D: Decreasing fat worsens the energy deficit; CF diets are deliberately high fat (around 35 to 40% of calories) with enzyme cover, unlike other malabsorption states.

AS-0430.B: Ceftriaxone: covers typical bacterial pneumonia, sepsis and meningitis, but has no reliable activity against Bordetella pertussis. Right when the picture is high fever with lobar consolidation or neutrophilia.
AS-0430.C: Nebulized salbutamol: for wheeze in asthma or a trial in bronchiolitis; it does not relieve pertussis paroxysms. Here there is no wheeze, just paroxysmal cough with lymphocytosis.
AS-0430.D: Corticosteroid: not recommended in pertussis; steroids are the answer for croup (barking cough, stridor) or asthma exacerbations, not for whooping cough.

AS-0437.B: Use of pacifier: pacifier use is a recognized RISK factor for recurrent otitis media, so it should be reduced, not encouraged.
AS-0437.C: Daily prophylactic antibiotics: no longer recommended for recurrent otitis media because of resistance and limited benefit; frequent recurrences are referred to ENT to consider tympanostomy tubes.

AS-0442.A: Direct Coombs test: confirms immune hemolysis (autoimmune hemolytic anemia, hemolytic disease of the newborn); it is negative in sickle cell disease and does not explain dactylitis.
AS-0442.C: Osmotic fragility test: the initial test for hereditary spherocytosis (spherocytes on smear, jaundice, splenomegaly, family history); it does not detect HbS.
AS-0442.D: LDH: a nonspecific marker of hemolysis that will be raised in many hemolytic anemias; it supports hemolysis but cannot confirm the cause.

AS-0444.A: Chromosomal analysis: right when there are dysmorphic features or multiple structural anomalies suggesting a syndrome; it does not explain hepatitis, hepatosplenomegaly and cytopenias.
AS-0444.C: Abdominal ultrasound: may document organomegaly but adds nothing to the cause; the distension is already explained by hepatosplenomegaly.
AS-0444.D: CT abdomen: unnecessary radiation in a neonate and not diagnostic of the underlying infection.

AS-0448.A: Blood gas: right for an acutely dehydrated or shocked child with suspected acidosis; this child has normal vital signs and a chronic course.
AS-0448.B: CBC: may show anemia but is nonspecific and will not identify the cause of chronic diarrhea and faltering weight.
AS-0448.D: Genetic test: HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing is mainly used to rule celiac disease OUT; it is not the first test, and other genetic tests (for example for cystic fibrosis) need a different clinical picture such as recurrent chest infections.

AS-0453.B: Conservative management (ultrasound surveillance) is for small asymptomatic polyps: 6 to 9 mm without risk factors, or ≤5 mm with a risk factor. A 4 cm symptomatic lesion must be removed.

AS-0454.B: A 6 to 9 mm polyp cannot simply be ignored; at minimum it needs ultrasound surveillance for growth. No follow-up is acceptable only for very small polyps without risk factors.
AS-0454.C: Liver function tests do not guide polyp management; the decision rests on polyp size, malignancy risk factors, growth and symptoms. The ducts are already normal on ultrasound.
AS-0454.D: Not the keyed answer here, although it is what size-based guidance recommends for a 6 to 9 mm polyp with no risk factors: repeat ultrasound to detect growth.

AS-0459.B: Non-organic failure to thrive: right when growth faltering comes from inadequate intake or psychosocial factors (neglect, poor feeding technique) in a child WITHOUT symptoms of disease; here vomiting and feeding irritability are disease features.
AS-0459.C: Chromosomal abnormality: usually gives symmetric growth failure (weight, length and often head circumference all low) with dysmorphism or developmental delay, which is not described.
AS-0459.D: Normal variation in growth: right when a child tracks steadily along a low percentile with proportional parameters (familial short stature, constitutional delay); weight below the 3rd percentile with symptoms is never normal variation.

AS-0460.A: Incentive spirometry: used to re-expand collapsed alveoli in post-operative atelectasis in cooperative older patients; it does not splint a collapsing trachea and a 2-year-old cannot perform it.
AS-0460.B: High-flow nasal cannula: gives only modest, unreliable distending pressure and is delivered through the nose, which a tracheostomy bypasses; it cannot hold a 90% collapse open.
AS-0460.D: Negative pressure ventilation: lowers intrathoracic pressure to draw air in and gives no positive end-expiratory pressure, so it does nothing to prevent expiratory collapse of the trachea.

AS-0461.A: Incentive spirometry: used to re-expand collapsed alveoli in post-operative atelectasis in cooperative older patients; it does not splint a collapsing trachea and a 2-year-old cannot perform it.
AS-0461.B: High-flow nasal cannula: gives only modest, unreliable distending pressure through the nose, which a tracheostomy bypasses; not enough for a 90% collapse.
AS-0461.C: Non-invasive ventilation: delivered by mask or nasal interface, so it makes little sense once a tracheostomy is in place; it would be the choice for milder disease when avoiding a tracheostomy.

AS-0462.A: Administer oxygen and order a chest X-ray: delays airway clearance in a cyanotic child; X-ray and bronchoscopy are for a stable child with suspected aspiration who is still moving air.
AS-0462.B: Give nebulized adrenaline: treats mucosal swelling in croup (barking cough, stridor after a viral prodrome); it will not move a foreign body.
AS-0462.C: Encourage a strong cough: right only when the cough is EFFECTIVE (loud, able to cry or speak); a weak cough with cyanosis means coughing has failed.

AS-0463.A: Fever: frequent but nonspecific (viral URTI, otitis, UTI) and may be absent in young infants or atypical pneumonia.
AS-0463.B: Shortness of breath: a subjective symptom that is hard to assess in a toddler and also occurs with asthma or bronchiolitis.
AS-0463.C: Cough: very common in URTI, asthma and bronchitis, so it is sensitive for respiratory illness in general but not a good discriminator for pneumonia.

AS-0464.A: Vague, nonspecific option; general education matters, but it is not a recognised specific preventive measure the way trigger avoidance is.
AS-0464.C: Good spacer technique improves drug delivery and is checked when asthma is uncontrolled despite treatment; it optimises therapy rather than removing the cause of attacks.
AS-0464.D: Peak flow monitoring helps detect worsening early and guide an action plan, and is less reliable in a 6-year-old; it monitors rather than prevents exacerbations.

AS-0465.B: A leukotriene receptor antagonist is a later-step maintenance add-on and has no role in treating an acute severe attack.
AS-0465.C: Inhaled steroid is the maintenance controller he should be taking regularly; it is the answer for chronic control, not for the acute severe exacerbation in the ED.
AS-0465.D: Removing the cats is important for long-term prevention, but it does nothing for the severe attack happening now.

AS-0466.A: Low-dose corticosteroid is a controller step; he is probably already on a twice-daily inhaler, and drug changes fail while the trigger and non-adherence persist.
AS-0466.B: A leukotriene receptor antagonist is a step-up add-on, used only after adherence, technique and triggers have been addressed.
AS-0466.C: Inhaled steroid is the standard controller, but he likely already has one; adding it does not address the cats, which drive his attacks.

AS-0467.A: Rituximab is a second-line or refractory option in severe lupus, not the standard first agent added for neuropsychiatric SLE.
AS-0467.C: Hydroxychloroquine is background therapy for almost all SLE patients and alone suits mild skin and joint disease; it is not enough for active CNS lupus.
AS-0467.D: Mycophenolate is the preferred induction agent for lupus nephritis; here creatinine and urine are normal, and the threatened organ is the brain.

AS-0468.B: ED referral is right if the patient is unstable, has peritonitis, worsening pain or abnormal findings; this patient is stable with mild pain, so an immediate ED transfer is not the most appropriate first step.
AS-0468.C: Blood tests (Hb, LFT) may support but cannot localize or exclude an organ injury; a normal Hb a week later does not rule out a hematoma, so imaging is the decisive step.

AS-0469.A: Immediate surgery is for a ruptured or symptomatic (tender, painful) aneurysm; elective repair is for diameter above the threshold or rapid growth. A 4.5 cm asymptomatic AAA meets none of these.

AS-0469B.B: EVAR is a method of repair, used once repair is indicated (≥5.5 cm, growth >1 cm/year, symptoms or rupture) and anatomy is suitable; not indicated at 4.5 cm.
AS-0469B.C: Open surgical repair has the same indications as EVAR (often chosen in younger, fit patients or unsuitable anatomy); below threshold its operative risk outweighs rupture risk.

AS-0470.B: Carotid stenting is an alternative to endarterectomy for significant symptomatic stenosis (≥50%, mainly 70 to 99%) in patients at high surgical risk; at 48% there is no indication for revascularization.
AS-0470.C: Endarterectomy benefits symptomatic patients with 70 to 99% stenosis (and selected 50 to 69%), ideally soon after the event; below 50% it gives no benefit and adds operative stroke risk.

AS-0506.B: Renal duplex looks at renal artery and vein flow (renal artery stenosis or thrombosis, transplant kidney). Nothing here points to a primary renovascular event.
AS-0506.C: Abdominal US can show a collection or hydronephrosis, but views are poor on day 2 after a laparotomy with gas, dressings and a stoma; it is the choice when a stable patient needs a quick bedside look for a collection.
AS-0506.D: CT with contrast is the test for a stable patient with suspected abscess or leak (e.g. spiking fever after Hartmann). Here the kidneys are already failing to make urine, and IV contrast adds nephrotoxic risk.

AS-0507.B: CT abdomen is the step after the wound is opened, or first-line if there are signs of a deep or intra-abdominal collection (spiking fever, ileus, tenderness away from the wound). The findings here are confined to the wound.

AS-0507.D: Antibiotics alone cannot clear pus trapped under a closed wound. They are added when there is spreading cellulitis or systemic sepsis, not used instead of opening the wound.

AS-0508.A: Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin plus steroid is empirical cover for pneumococcus and meningococcus in younger adults; it misses Listeria entirely, and dexamethasone is not beneficial in Listeria meningitis.
AS-0508.B: Ceftriaxone plus ampicillin plus vancomycin is the correct empirical regimen for meningitis in patients over 50 before the organism is known; here the Gram stain already shows Listeria, so targeted ampicillin is the answer.
AS-0508.C: Same three drugs as option B in a different order: right as empirical therapy in an older adult with unknown organism, but not once Gram positive, catalase positive bacilli are reported.

AS-0509.B: Fluid restriction does nothing for malnutrition; it is used for fluid overload states such as heart failure, SIADH or advanced kidney disease.
AS-0509.C: TPN is for a non-functioning gut (obstruction, ileus, high-output fistula, short bowel). A functioning gut should be used, and TPN in a malnourished patient adds line sepsis and refeeding risk.
AS-0509.D: NG feeding is for a patient who cannot or will not take enough by mouth (coma, unsafe swallow, failed oral supplements). This patient can still eat, so oral supplementation comes first.

AS-0509B.A: Limiting soft tissue damage matters (splinting does this too) but it is not life-threatening; it ranks after hemorrhage control.
AS-0509B.C: Preserving joint movement and function is the goal of definitive fixation and rehabilitation, not the first priority.
AS-0509B.D: Analgesia is given early and is important, but untreated hidden blood loss can kill; pain control comes after circulation is secured.

AS-0510.B: Fine-needle aspiration is not a first step for a small, recent, benign feeling node. Tissue sampling (usually excisional biopsy in children) is right for a node that persists or grows after observation, is hard or fixed, supraclavicular, or comes with fever, weight loss or night sweats.
AS-0510.C: Antibiotics treat acute bacterial lymphadenitis: a tender, warm, red, rapidly enlarging node, often with fever. This node is painless and non tender, so there is no infection to treat.

AS-0511.A: Herniotomy (sac ligation alone) is the operation for children, whose problem is a patent processus vaginalis with a normal posterior wall. Adults need the posterior wall reinforced.
AS-0511.C: Herniorrhaphy (suture or tissue repair without mesh) has a higher recurrence rate than mesh; it is kept for contaminated fields such as a strangulated hernia with bowel resection.
AS-0511.D: Watchful waiting suits an older or high-risk man with a small, minimally symptomatic hernia. A large inguinoscrotal hernia in a young labourer who wants it treated should be repaired.

AS-0527.A: Colonoscopy is done after resuscitation and bowel preparation, usually in a stable patient. It is the main test in a stable lower GI bleed, but not the first step in a tachycardic patient.
AS-0527.C: A plain abdominal CT does not locate active bleeding. When imaging is needed for active lower GI bleeding, CT angiography is used, and only after resuscitation has started.

AS-0528.A: The option text was not recalled, so it cannot be assessed; the compiler notes that urgent colonoscopy was NOT among this recall's options. Colonoscopy would in any case suit a stable patient after bowel prep, not one who is pale and tachycardic.
AS-0528.B: IV fluid and blood is the INITIAL step and is always started first, but it supports the patient rather than finding or stopping the bleed. It is the answer when the question asks "initial" or "first".

AS-0531.C: A PPI alone heals the ulcer but leaves H. pylori in place, so the ulcer recurs; PPI alone is the answer for an NSAID ulcer (see the paired card), while here PPI is just one part of the eradication regimen.

AS-0531B.C: CT abdomen does not evaluate mucosal disease or H. pylori; it is used for suspected complications, masses or non dyspeptic causes, not uncomplicated dyspepsia.

AS-0532.A: A healthy diet is general advice; diet does not cause or prevent peptic ulcer, so it does not prevent recurrence.

AS-0533.A: A healthy diet is reasonable general advice but does not cause or prevent peptic ulcer, so it does not reduce recurrence.

AS-0534.A: A healthy diet is generic advice; diet does not cause or heal peptic ulcers and does nothing to prevent recurrence after a perforation.
AS-0534.B: Avoiding NSAIDs is sensible and is the key step when the stem stresses NSAID use, but the stem gives no NSAID history; the recall keys eradication of the commonest cause, <i>H. pylori</i>.

AS-0578.B: Admit and start IV amoxicillin: wrong setting (no admission needed) and it lacks atypical cover.
AS-0578.C: Outpatient azithromycin alone: monotherapy is for previously healthy outpatients without comorbidities (and only where macrolide resistance is low); diabetes requires combination therapy.

AS-0578B.D: One source keyed meropenem, but it is for hospital acquired pneumonia or Pseudomonas or resistant gram negative risk (recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics, prior Pseudomonas, structural lung disease); none is present, so it is unnecessarily broad for this CAP.

AS-0579.A: Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is the correct regimen for a patient who needs admission (ward CAP), but with CURB-65 of 0 this stable man does not need to be admitted.
AS-0579.B: Admission is not indicated at CURB-65 0, and IV amoxicillin alone gives no atypical cover.
AS-0579.C: Azithromycin monotherapy is reserved for healthy outpatients without comorbidities; diabetes (and smoking) calls for beta-lactam based therapy instead.

AS-0580.B: Infliximab (anti-TNF) is for fistulizing or perianal disease, severe or high-risk disease, or steroid refractory/dependent cases, not the routine first option for uncomplicated luminal Crohn's.
AS-0580.C: Methotrexate is a steroid-sparing maintenance agent; it is slow in onset and not used to induce remission first.
AS-0580.D: This is a placeholder from the recaller, not a treatment option.
