AS-0581.B: Partial exchange transfusion with saline is for symptomatic polycythemia (hyperviscosity signs) or very high hematocrits; plethora alone is a sign of polycythemia, not a hyperviscosity symptom.
AS-0581.C: Phototherapy treats hyperbilirubinemia; polycythemia raises the jaundice risk, but there is no jaundice here and it does not lower the hematocrit.

AS-0582.A: Smoking is the strongest single risk factor for PAD in active smokers, but he quit 15 years ago, which the recall uses to make it a historical rather than current driver. It would be the answer if he were still smoking.
AS-0582.C: Reduced walking distance is not normal ageing; exertional limb symptoms with multiple vascular risk factors need assessment for PAD (ankle-brachial index).

AS-0583.B: tTG-IgA (with total IgA) is the right first test when there are celiac symptoms (diarrhea, distension, failure to thrive), or as screening of an at-risk relative once older (about 2 to 3 years); this toddler is well and young, so testing can wait.
AS-0583.C: Starting a gluten free diet without serology and biopsy is wrong: it is unnecessary in a healthy child and causes false negative results if testing is later needed.

AS-0584.A: Reassurance misses a high-risk child; normal growth does not exclude celiac disease, which can be silent in relatives.
AS-0584.C: Starting a gluten-free diet before testing is wrong: gluten withdrawal makes serology and biopsy falsely negative, and diet is only started after the diagnosis is confirmed.

AS-0585.A: Paracentesis is for ascites (diagnostic or therapeutic), not for mechanical bowel obstruction with peritonism.
AS-0585.B: Gastrografin is a water soluble contrast study used in uncomplicated adhesive SBO to predict and help resolution; it is contraindicated once there are signs of peritonitis or strangulation.
AS-0585.D: NGT, analgesia and bowel rest is the correct first approach for uncomplicated SBO (soft abdomen, no peritonism); rigidity and recurrent episodes take this patient beyond conservative care.

AS-0586.B: Exploratory laparotomy with patch repair is the definitive treatment, but taking an under resuscitated, peritonitic patient straight to theatre is unsafe; it is the answer when the question asks for definitive or most appropriate management.

AS-0587.A: Atypical lymphocytes are the smear finding of infectious mononucleosis (EBV), not HUS.
AS-0587.B: Eosinophilia suggests parasitic infection, allergy or drug reaction; it is not a feature of HUS.

AS-0588.B: Aspirin is avoided in children because of Reye syndrome risk; it is reserved for specific indications such as Kawasaki disease.
AS-0588.C: Synovial aspiration is the step for a single hot joint with fever or systemic toxicity where septic arthritis must be excluded; here two joints (oligoarticular) 2 weeks after an enteric infection, without fever, fits reactive arthritis.
AS-0588.D: IV antibiotics treat septic arthritis (usually one joint, febrile, toxic child), after aspiration and cultures; reactive arthritis is sterile.

AS-0589.A: Oral ibuprofen treats reactive arthritis or transient synovitis, but only after septic arthritis is excluded in a monoarticular hot joint.
AS-0589.B: Aspirin is avoided in children (Reye syndrome) and does not address the need to exclude infection.
AS-0589.D: IV antibiotics are started for suspected septic arthritis, ideally after aspiration and cultures are taken; the diagnostic step comes first here.

AS-0590.B: pH (or pH impedance) monitoring quantifies reflux and links it to symptoms such as cough or apnea; it confirms GERD but does not show the anatomy needed before surgery.
AS-0590.C: Endoscopy with biopsy assesses esophagitis, strictures or eosinophilic esophagitis; it is invasive and not the first study here.
AS-0590.D: A PPI trial is for uncomplicated symptoms in older children; in infants it is not a diagnostic test, and with aspiration pneumonias and failure to thrive objective evaluation is needed.

AS-0591.A: High-intensity statin is for clinical ASCVD, LDL ≥4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL), or high-risk diabetics; a normotensive non-diabetic with LDL 3.47 does not meet these.

AS-0592.B: Lifestyle alone with a 3-month recheck suits a low-risk person with mildly raised LDL (like a young normotensive non-smoker); with HTN plus heavy smoking, delaying statin is not appropriate.
AS-0592.C: Aspirin is not routine for primary prevention because bleeding risk offsets the benefit, and withholding a statin removes the key preventive drug.

AS-0593.B: Azithromycin (a macrolide) does not cover E. coli and other Gram negative uropathogens and has no role in UTI.
AS-0593.C: Cefepime is a broad spectrum antipseudomonal agent for hospital-acquired or resistant infections; a mild community UTI does not need it.
AS-0593.D: IV ceftriaxone is for infants under about 2 months, toxic appearance, vomiting or inability to take oral medication; none applies here.

AS-0594.B: Oral azithromycin: a macrolide with poor activity against E. coli and other Gram-negative uropathogens; it is used for atypical respiratory infections, not UTI.
AS-0594.C: IV cefepime: a broad-spectrum antipseudomonal agent kept for complicated, hospital-acquired or resistant infections; far too broad and needlessly IV for a mild community UTI.
AS-0594.D: IV ceftriaxone: right if the infant were under about 2 months, toxic looking, vomiting or unable to take oral fluids; this baby is alert and feeding.

AS-0594C.B: Metronidazole: covers anaerobes and protozoa (C. difficile, Giardia, bacterial vaginosis), not the Gram-negative organisms that cause UTI; constipation is not an infection to treat.
AS-0594C.D: No treatment: right only for asymptomatic bacteriuria in a healthy child; a symptomatic UTI must be treated to relieve symptoms and prevent pyelonephritis and renal scarring.

AS-0595.A: Barium swallow assesses structure and motility in dysphagia (strictures, rings, achalasia); it does not confirm acid reflux.
AS-0595.B: Endoscopy is for alarm features (anemia, dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding, older age) or refractory symptoms; none is given here (compare the Hb 110 version, where endoscopy is the answer).
AS-0595.C: Manometry diagnoses motility disorders (achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm with dysphagia) and is done before fundoplication, not to diagnose reflux.

AS-0596.A: Barium swallow is for dysphagia work-up or when endoscopy is contraindicated or unavailable; it cannot biopsy or reliably show a bleeding lesion.
AS-0596.C: Manometry is for motility disorders (achalasia, esophageal spasm) or before fundoplication, not for anemia with reflux symptoms.
AS-0596.D: pH monitoring confirms reflux when there are NO alarm features or when endoscopy is normal (the Hb-not-mentioned version); anemia needs direct visualization first.

AS-0602.B: Von Willebrand disease: usually autosomal dominant, affects both sexes and passes through either parent. It typically causes mild mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, gums, menorrhagia) and rarely severe neonatal circumcision bleeding; it fits best with mucosal bleeding and a parent of either sex affected.
AS-0602.C: DIC: secondary to a severe illness (sepsis, asphyxia, shock) in a sick neonate who bleeds from many sites; it is not inherited and would not explain a family history.
AS-0602.D: Platelet disorder: causes petechiae and mucosal bleeding, and most inherited platelet function disorders are autosomal; it fits best with petechiae or a low platelet count, not an X-linked history with circumcision bleeding.

AS-0603.A: Hypospadias is associated with cryptorchidism too, but it is the association asked when the question focuses on sexual development or DSD; as a general associated finding the patent processus (hernia) is commoner.
AS-0603.C: Pyloric stenosis is a first born male infant problem with projectile non bilious vomiting at around 6 weeks; it has no link to testicular descent.
AS-0603.D: Congenital heart disease is not a typical association of isolated cryptorchidism; it suggests a syndrome (e.g. Noonan, Down) only when other features are given.

AS-0604.B: Inguinal hernia is the most common associated finding overall (patent processus vaginalis), but it is a structural defect, not a disorder of sexual development.
AS-0604.C: Pyloric stenosis causes projectile non bilious vomiting in a young infant and is unrelated to genital development.
AS-0604.D: Congenital heart disease is not linked to sexual development and is only expected when a syndrome is described.

AS-0605.A: Immediate drug therapy is for BP ≥160/100, target organ damage, or high cardiovascular risk; 138/88 without these starts with lifestyle change.
AS-0605.C: Home or ambulatory monitoring is right to CONFIRM a single raised office reading (especially near 140/90); here readings are already raised and lifestyle advice is indicated regardless.

AS-0606.B: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.
AS-0606.C: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.
AS-0606.D: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-0607.A: IV tPA is limited to 4.5 hours from onset (or last known well); at 12 hours it adds bleeding risk without proven benefit.
AS-0607.B: Observation (supportive care, antiplatelet) fits when there is no vessel to open or the tissue is already fully infarcted with no salvageable brain; here an occluded large vessel with a mild-to-moderate core still has tissue to save.
AS-0607.D: Bridging tPA plus thrombectomy is used when the patient arrives within 4.5 hours; at 12 hours only thrombectomy is given.

AS-0608.A: Transverse myelitis also gives a sensory level, UMN signs and bladder involvement, but it typically affects younger patients, often after infection or with MS/NMO, and MRI shows no compressive lesion.
AS-0608.B: GBS is an ascending polyneuropathy with areflexia and no sensory level; brisk reflexes exclude it.
AS-0608.C: Cauda equina is a lower motor neuron root lesion below L1: reduced or absent reflexes, saddle anesthesia and back pain, not hyperreflexia with a T10 level.

AS-0609.A: Felon is an abscess of the closed pulp space of the fingertip, with a tense, throbbing, very painful pad, usually after a puncture wound; here the problem is at the nail fold.
AS-0609.C: Onychomycosis is a chronic fungal infection of the nail plate (thickened, discoloured, brittle nail) without acute swelling; here the nail is intact and the onset is acute.
AS-0609.D: Cellulitis is diffuse spreading redness of skin and subcutis, often with fever; the localised periungual swelling after a hangnail is more specifically paronychia.

AS-0610.A: Azathioprine is a slow acting steroid sparing agent used for maintenance of remission; it takes weeks to work and has no role in rescuing an acute severe flare.
AS-0610.C: Oral prednisone is used for moderate flares in an outpatient who is not toxic; a very sick patient with severe bloody diarrhea needs IV steroids.

AS-0611.B: BiPAP needs an alert, cooperative patient who can protect the airway; it is best for hypercapnic COPD exacerbations with moderate acidosis. An agitated patient with pH 7.1 and severe hypoxemic pneumonia is a contraindication and delaying intubation worsens outcome.

AS-0618.A: Arterial ulcers are painful, punched out ulcers on the toes or pressure points with absent pulses and ischaemic skin; they are not linked to burn scars.
AS-0618.B: Cushing ulcer is a stress peptic ulcer of the stomach or duodenum after head injury or raised intracranial pressure; it is not a skin lesion.
AS-0618.D: Neuropathic ulcers occur on pressure points of an insensate foot (diabetes, leprosy) and are painless but punched out with callus; they do not arise in burn scars.

AS-0619.A: Amiodarone: a second-line antiarrhythmic for refractory SVT in a stable child, usually with expert advice; it is slow to act and can worsen hypotension.
AS-0619.B: Vagal maneuvers: the first step in a <i>stable</i> child with SVT (ice to the face in infants, Valsalva in older children); they waste time in a child with altered consciousness and hypotension.
AS-0619.C: Adenosine: the drug of choice for stable SVT after vagal maneuvers fail; in an unstable child it may be tried only if IV access is already in place and it causes no delay, but cardioversion is the standard answer when consciousness is impaired.

AS-0624.B: Needle aspiration only empties the cyst temporarily; the epithelial tract remains, so it recurs and can become infected. Aspiration is not definitive treatment.
AS-0624.C: Reassurance is wrong because thyroglossal cysts do not regress, tend to get infected, and rarely harbour carcinoma; they should be excised.

AS-0628.A: Bilateral knee X-rays: not needed to confirm OA, and X-ray changes correlate poorly with symptoms. Right when the stem asks for baseline imaging or there are atypical features (choose standing films).
AS-0628.B: MRI of the right knee: reserved for suspected internal derangement (meniscal or ligament injury with locking or giving way) or an unclear diagnosis.
AS-0628.D: Arthroscopy for the right knee: invasive and has no role in diagnosing OA; used only for selected mechanical problems.

AS-0634.B: Fasting to promote ketone production: the opposite of correct; these children cannot oxidize fat to make ketones, so fasting is the trigger for hypoglycemia and crisis.
AS-0634.C: High-fat diet: increases the load on the defective pathway; long-chain defects are managed with a low long-chain fat diet, often supplemented with MCT.
AS-0634.D: Protein restriction: the mainstay for urea cycle disorders and organic acidemias (hyperammonemia), not for fatty acid oxidation defects.

AS-0639.A: Start oral corticosteroids and hospitalize: hospitalization is for severe or life-threatening attacks (SpO2 below 92%, too breathless to talk, poor response to bronchodilators). Systemic steroids are part of exacerbation care, but this child needs bronchodilator and reassessment first, not admission.
AS-0639.B: Add salmeterol and hospitalize: salmeterol is a long-acting controller with slow onset, not a reliever, and is never used alone in asthma; admission is not indicated for a mild attack.
AS-0639.C: Add ipratropium: added to repeated salbutamol in severe or life-threatening exacerbations or poor response to SABA, not as the first step in a mild attack.

AS-0641.B: Prophylactic low-dose antibiotics: URTIs are viral, so antibiotics give no benefit and promote resistance; prophylaxis has a role in selected conditions (e.g. asplenia, rheumatic fever, some recurrent UTI) but not in normal childhood colds.
AS-0641.C: Tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy: considered for frequent, documented recurrent tonsillitis or obstructive sleep apnea from adenotonsillar hypertrophy, not for simple colds in a 6-month-old.

AS-0642.B: Empiric IV antibiotics are an adjunct (for surrounding cellulitis, systemic signs or immunocompromise), not a substitute for opening and debriding an infected wound with a collection.
AS-0642.C: A wound swab is taken when the wound is opened, but observing an established infection in a diabetic delays source control and risks deep or necrotizing spread.
AS-0642.D: Reassurance fits a seroma (painless swelling without redness or fever); here the wound is red and tender, which is infection.

AS-0643.B: Postpone vaccination until recovery: right only for a moderate or severe acute illness (child looks unwell or toxic); a mild URTI in a slightly ill child does not justify delay.
AS-0643.C: Give MMR without the rubella component: there is no valid reason to drop a component; the combined vaccine is given, and true contraindications (severe allergy, e.g. to neomycin or gelatin, pregnancy, significant immunosuppression) apply to the whole live vaccine.
AS-0643.D: The second dose should be given at 4 years: does not answer what to do today; in the Saudi schedule the 18-month visit is itself an MMR dose, with another at school entry.

AS-0649.A: HbA1c every 6 months: HbA1c underestimates glycemia in CF (increased red cell turnover) and is not sensitive enough to screen; it is used to monitor once diabetes is diagnosed, not to screen.
AS-0649.B: Fasting blood glucose annually: early CFRD causes post-meal hyperglycemia with normal fasting glucose, so FBG misses many cases.
AS-0649.C: No need to screen until 18 or older: screening starts in childhood (by age 10) because CFRD is common in adolescents and worsens lung function and nutrition.

AS-0650.A: Sertraline treats depression or anxiety, not psychotic symptoms; it is right if the dominant problem is low mood.
AS-0650.C: Amitriptyline is a tricyclic with strong anticholinergic effects that worsen confusion and can provoke hallucinations in dementia, and it opposes donepezil; it is used for neuropathic pain or depression in younger patients.
AS-0650.D: Donepezil has improved his cognition and cholinesterase inhibitors can reduce hallucinations in Lewy body disease, so stopping it removes benefit; it is stopped for intolerance.

AS-0651.B: IV normal saline with admission is for severe dehydration (lethargy, poor perfusion), persistent vomiting with inability to take oral fluids, or failure of ORS; this infant is well.
AS-0651.C: Stool culture is reserved for bloody or mucoid diarrhea, high fever or toxicity, outbreaks, or immunocompromise; it does not change management of simple watery diarrhea.
AS-0651.D: Drugs (antidiarrheals, antiemetics, antibiotics) are not used routinely in infant watery diarrhea; antibiotics need a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial cause, and antimotility agents are unsafe in young children.

AS-0651B.B: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-0652.A: IV antibiotics and chest X-ray do not address the immediate problems (secretions, distress, dehydration); chest X-ray is not routine in bronchiolitis, and antibiotics are added when bacterial pneumonia is suspected (high fever, toxic look, focal consolidation) after the child is stabilized.

AS-0653.B: Carotid stenting is an alternative to endarterectomy for significant symptomatic stenosis in patients at high surgical risk; it is not indicated for 48%.
AS-0653.C: Carotid thrombectomy is not a standard treatment for carotid stenosis; mechanical thrombectomy is for an acute large-vessel intracranial occlusion in a current stroke.
AS-0653.D: Endarterectomy is right for symptomatic stenosis of 70 to 99% (and selected 50 to 69%), ideally within 2 weeks of the TIA; 48% is below the threshold.

AS-0656.B: The word 'compensated' does not fit a pH this high, and neither disorder is compensating the other. Strictly, a PCO2 well below the expected value would mean a second, respiratory alkalosis, but exam keys read a normal PCO2 as no compensation.
AS-0656.C: Respiratory alkalosis is the primary problem only when PCO2 is low and HCO3 falls to compensate; here HCO3 is high and PCO2 is not low.
AS-0656.D: Respiratory compensation would show a clearly raised PCO2 near the expected value; a PCO2 of 44 is too close to normal to call compensation.

AS-0657.A: Uncompensated means PCO2 stays normal; respiratory compensation develops within hours, so by day 5 some rise in PCO2 is expected.
AS-0657.B: Respiratory acidosis needs hypoventilation as the primary problem (for example COPD or sedation), with low pH; NG loss gives a high pH from a metabolic cause.
AS-0657.C: A combined metabolic and respiratory alkalosis would need a low PCO2 from a second cause such as pain, sepsis or anxiety driving hyperventilation; nothing here suggests that.

AS-0658.A: VCUG alone shows reflux and urethral anatomy but misses hydronephrosis, renal size and structural anomalies that ultrasound detects; in recurrent UTI both are needed.
AS-0658.B: Renal ultrasound alone is the work-up after a first febrile UTI; with recurrent infections it cannot exclude reflux, so VCUG must be added.
AS-0658.D: KUB ultrasound is essentially the same structural scan as renal ultrasound and does not assess reflux, so it is incomplete for recurrent UTI.

AS-0658B.A: DMSA scan detects renal scarring; it is done months after the acute infection in atypical or recurrent UTI, not as the initial study.
AS-0658B.C: CT abdomen gives radiation and adds nothing for routine pediatric UTI evaluation; it is kept for complications such as suspected abscess when ultrasound is inconclusive.
AS-0658B.D: MCUG (VCUG) is invasive and needs catheterization; it is indicated after an abnormal ultrasound or recurrent febrile UTI, not first line.

AS-0659.A: Omenn syndrome is a SCID variant of early infancy with erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and eosinophilia; here the nodes are absent and the child is 4.
AS-0659.B: This option was not recalled; any other immunodeficiency would need features this stem lacks (eczema and low platelets for Wiskott-Aldrich, normal or high IgM for hyper-IgM, later onset for CVID).
AS-0659.D: SCID presents in the first months with failure to thrive and opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, candida, severe viral) and is usually fatal early without transplant; a 4-year-old with mainly bacterial and Giardia infections fits a B cell defect.

AS-0659B.A: SCID requires profoundly low or absent T cells (combined defect) with opportunistic infections; normal T-cell counts exclude it.

AS-0660.A: Complete resolution is not the expected outcome of maintenance therapy; its goals are symptom suppression and relapse prevention, and most patients keep some residual symptoms.
AS-0660.B: 5% understates outcomes; roughly a third do well, so remission is far more common than this.
AS-0660.C: 70% with satisfactory quality of life overstates outcomes; only about a third do well in the long term, and the rest have relapses or chronic impairment.

AS-0662.A: A thyroid scan is used when TSH is low, to look for a hot autonomous nodule; with a normal TSH it does not replace cytology.
AS-0662.C: Total thyroidectomy is for confirmed malignancy (Bethesda 6) or other clear indications; operating without a cytological diagnosis is premature. Persistently nondiagnostic results on repeat FNA may then lead to diagnostic surgery.

AS-0672.A: Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity (pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, coma); there is no opioid exposure and sweating is not an opioid feature.
AS-0672.B: Glucagon is the antidote for beta blocker (or calcium channel blocker) overdose and treats hypoglycemia; it has no role in NMS.
AS-0672.C: Meropenem is for severe bacterial sepsis; the confusion and sweating here follow the haloperidol dose increase and are drug induced, not infection, although sepsis should be excluded.

AS-0675.A: Laparotomy is for intraperitoneal bleeding (for example positive FAST with instability); opening the abdomen does not control retroperitoneal pelvic bleeding and can release tamponade.
AS-0675.C: Crystalloid and observation suit a stable patient without active bleeding; a hypotensive patient with active extravasation needs blood, and large volumes of crystalloid worsen coagulopathy.

AS-0677.A: Supportive care alone fits viral rhinosinusitis, which typically improves within about 10 days; symptoms persisting past 10 days indicate bacterial infection that warrants antibiotics.
AS-0677.C: Intranasal steroids are an adjunct (mainly in allergic or chronic rhinosinusitis) and do not replace antibiotics for acute bacterial sinusitis in a child.
AS-0677.D: Sinus X-ray is not recommended; uncomplicated sinusitis is a clinical diagnosis, and imaging (contrast CT) is reserved for suspected orbital or intracranial complications.

AS-0678.A: Myocardial contusion follows blunt trauma and presents with arrhythmias or a raised troponin, not muffled heart sounds after a stab wound.
AS-0678.B: Hemothorax causes hypotension with decreased breath sounds and dullness on one side, and the neck veins are usually flat from blood loss.
AS-0678.C: Tension pneumothorax also gives hypotension and raised JVP, but with absent breath sounds, hyperresonance and tracheal shift; the lungs here are clear.

AS-0680.A: Zero PEEP lets alveoli collapse and reopen with each breath (atelectrauma) and worsens hypoxemia; removing PEEP does not prevent lung injury, and adequate PEEP is part of lung-protective ventilation.
AS-0680.B: Increasing tidal volume causes overdistension and volutrauma, the main mechanism of ventilator-induced lung injury.
AS-0680.C: Hyperventilation to wash out CO2 needs higher volumes or rates, increasing lung stress, and the hypocapnia causes alkalosis and cerebral vasoconstriction; it is not a protective strategy.

AS-0681.A: Membranous nephropathy causes nephrotic syndrome in adults (heavy proteinuria, edema, hypoalbuminemia), not post-infectious nephritic hematuria with hypertension.
AS-0681.B: IgA nephropathy gives hematuria within a few days of (or during) an upper respiratory infection; it would be right with a 1 to 2 day latency, not 3 weeks with a positive ASO.

AS-0682.A: Rectus abdominis is an abdominal wall muscle with no role in bladder storage or voiding.
AS-0682.C: Perianal muscles (external anal sphincter) relate to fecal continence and encopresis, not nocturnal bladder control.
AS-0682.D: Pelvic floor dysfunction is linked to dysfunctional voiding with daytime symptoms; the classic muscle target in enuresis is the detrusor.

AS-0684.A: BCG and Hep B alone cover only the birth doses and miss DTaP, polio and the measles dose he is old enough for; delaying them wastes a vaccination opportunity.
AS-0684.B: This leaves out DTaP and polio, the core primary series; giving PCV while omitting DTaP and polio does not prioritize the essential missed vaccines.
AS-0684.C: This is close to the routine 9-month visit for a fully vaccinated child (measles + MCV4) plus DTaP and OPV, but it omits BCG and Hep B, which an unvaccinated child still needs.

AS-0685.A: Factor VIII deficiency also gives an isolated prolonged aPTT with hemarthrosis, but normal plasma supplies the missing factor, so the aPTT corrects on mixing. Right when the mixing study corrects.
AS-0685.B: Bernard Soulier syndrome is a platelet adhesion defect (GpIb) with large platelets, often low counts and mucocutaneous bleeding; PT and aPTT are normal and joint bleeds are not typical.
AS-0685.C: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia causes petechiae and intracranial bleeding with a LOW platelet count; coagulation times are normal. Here platelets are normal.

AS-0686.A: Lactate supports ischemia but is nonspecific and may be normal early; a normal lactate does not exclude mesenteric ischemia.
AS-0686.B: Plain X-ray is usually normal early and only shows late signs (pneumatosis, free air); it is the first test for obstruction or perforation.
AS-0686.C: Ultrasound is limited by bowel gas and cannot reliably assess the mesenteric vessels in an acute abdomen; it is the first test for biliary pain.

AS-0687.A: Abdominal X ray may show a single bubble (distended stomach) but cannot measure the pylorus or confirm the diagnosis; it is not the test of choice.
AS-0687.B: Upper endoscopy is invasive, needs anesthesia and is not used to diagnose pyloric stenosis; it is for mucosal disease such as esophagitis or ulcers.

AS-0689.B: CT angiography is the confirmatory (most appropriate) test for planning revascularization, not the initial bedside test; with paralysis, imaging is skipped altogether.
AS-0689.C: ABI is the first test for chronic peripheral arterial disease (claudication), not for an acute ischemic limb, where Doppler signals guide urgency.

AS-0694C.A: Protein is needed for growth in a child with cirrhosis; restriction was older teaching reserved for hepatic encephalopathy, which is not described here.
AS-0694C.B: Carbohydrates are the main energy source and are encouraged to meet the high calorie needs of cirrhosis; they are not avoided.
AS-0694C.D: Minerals and vitamins (especially fat soluble A, D, E, K) are supplemented in chronic liver disease, not avoided.

AS-0695.B: Monthly immunoglobulin replacement only covers the antibody defect and is a supportive bridge until transplant; it does not restore T cell immunity. It is the long term treatment for pure antibody defects such as X linked agammaglobulinemia.

AS-0698.A: Systemic therapy is reserved for advanced HCC (vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread); conventional chemotherapy has little role in localized disease.
AS-0698.B: Radiotherapy is not the standard primary treatment of a resectable HCC; it is used selectively when other locoregional options are not possible.
AS-0698.C: Palliative care alone is for end-stage disease (poor performance status or decompensated cirrhosis); this tumour is localized and treatable.

AS-0702.A: Positive serology alone is not the definitive test here; no stem detail (such as very high tTG levels confirmed on a second sample) supports skipping the biopsy.
AS-0702.C: HLA DQ2/DQ8 typing has a high negative predictive value and is used to rule celiac disease OUT in unclear cases; a positive result does not confirm it.
AS-0702.D: Repeating serology in 6 months delays diagnosis; repeat serology is used to monitor adherence once the child is on a gluten free diet.

AS-0703.A: Oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone is the long term maintenance regimen once the baby is stable; it is too slow and unreliable in an acute crisis.
AS-0703.C: Sodium bicarbonate and insulin only shift potassium temporarily, do not treat the cortisol and aldosterone deficiency, and insulin would worsen the hypoglycemia.

AS-0704.A: Coagulation profile is normal in ITP, so it does not confirm the diagnosis; it helps when a clotting disorder or DIC is suspected.
AS-0704.B: Bone marrow aspirate is reserved for atypical features (another cytopenia, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, bone pain, blasts) or failure to respond to treatment, where leukemia or aplasia must be excluded.

AS-0704B.B: Blood film: a quick supportive step that may show blasts, but it cannot confirm or classify leukemia and may be blast free (aleukemic); it would be the answer if the question asked for the initial test.

AS-0705.B: Intubation and mechanical ventilation are for respiratory failure (apnea, severe distress or hypoxia despite oxygen or CPAP); the stem gives no such severity.
AS-0705.C: Immediate surfactant is not given before RDS is established and the baby is assessed; it is typically given via an endotracheal tube to a baby with confirmed RDS needing support.
AS-0705.D: Empirical antibiotics are right when there are sepsis risk factors (maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, GBS); none are given here, and the stem's emphasis is the diabetic mother.

AS-0707.A: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is chronic lung disease of prematurity (oxygen need at 36 weeks corrected age) with tachypnea, retractions and diffuse polyphonic wheeze; it does not explain a fixed monophasic central wheeze.
AS-0707.C: Congenital subglottic stenosis is present from birth and causes biphasic or inspiratory stridor and recurrent croup; an ACQUIRED stenosis after intubation is possible but still gives stridor, not expiratory wheeze.
AS-0707.D: Laryngomalacia causes INSPIRATORY stridor from early weeks, worse supine and better prone; it is not related to ventilation and does not cause expiratory wheeze.

AS-0710.A: Loss of interest (anhedonia) is a core symptom that helps diagnose depression, but it is not singled out as a suicide risk marker the way isolation is.
AS-0710.C: Changes in appetite and sleep are neurovegetative features of depression; they support the diagnosis but are not the most concerning risk feature.
AS-0710.D: Decreased concentration is a common depressive symptom affecting function but does not by itself signal high suicide risk.

AS-0711.A: Bipolar disorder has manic or hypomanic episodes lasting days to weeks not linked to the cycle; here symptoms recur only before menses.
AS-0711.B: Generalised anxiety disorder is excessive worry on most days for at least 6 months, not cyclic premenstrual symptoms.
AS-0711.C: Perimenopausal depression occurs near menopause (usually mid-40s or later) with irregular cycles and vasomotor symptoms; she is 27.

AS-0712.A: Postponing for a month is reserved for decompensated conditions (heart failure with volume overload, recent MI, uncontrolled thyroid disease, severe hypertension); these mild elevations do not justify cancelling an elective case.
AS-0712.C: A routine preoperative chest X-ray has no role without cardiorespiratory symptoms or signs; it does not address the abnormal BP and glucose.
AS-0712.D: Baseline bloods (renal function, electrolytes) may well be checked in a diabetic hypertensive, but they are routine work-up, not the action this question targets; the abnormal findings presented are BP and glucose, which need treating.

AS-0714.B: A high fiber diet is general advice, but extra fiber beyond normal age intake has little proven benefit and can increase bulk in an already overstretched rectum; it is not the key preventive step.
AS-0714.C: Long term laxatives (maintenance osmotic laxative such as PEG) are used after disimpaction to keep stools soft, but they are combined with, not a substitute for, toilet training in this recall.

AS-0715.A: Lupus nephritis needs features of SLE in the child (malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, cytopenias, positive ANA/anti-dsDNA); a family history alone is not evidence, and HSP already explains the renal findings.
AS-0715.B: JIA is a chronic arthritis (≥6 weeks) with morning stiffness and does not cause hematuria, proteinuria or abdominal pain; the ankle swelling here is the HSP arthritis/edema.
AS-0715.D: UTI gives dysuria, fever and pyuria; significant <i>proteinuria</i> with hematuria points to a glomerular process, not infection.

AS-0718.B: Oxygenation is part of resuscitation (and a GCS of 8 needs a secured airway), but oxygen does not remove the expanding hematoma compressing the brain.
AS-0718.C: Steroids give no benefit in traumatic brain injury and are associated with harm; they help vasogenic edema around tumors, not traumatic bleeds.
AS-0718.D: A shunt treats hydrocephalus (CSF diversion), not an acute extra-axial hematoma causing herniation.

AS-0718B.B: Waiting while the conscious level is falling lets an expanding arterial bleed progress to herniation. Intubation protects the airway but does not treat the lesion.
AS-0718B.C: MRI is slow and adds nothing once CT has shown the bleed; it is used for diffuse axonal injury or subtle lesions, not acute surgical hematomas.
AS-0718B.D: Observation suits a small hematoma in a child who is fully alert with no neurological deficit; this child is already drowsy.

AS-0719.B: Oxygen supports resuscitation but does nothing for a space-occupying hematoma; she is already maintaining a GCS of 14.
AS-0719.C: High-dose steroids are not used in head injury and are associated with worse outcomes; they suit tumor-related vasogenic edema.

AS-0720.B: IV mannitol temporarily lowers ICP while theatre is prepared; it does not remove the clot, so it is a bridge, not the management.
AS-0720.C: ICU observation suits a small hematoma without shift in a neurologically stable patient, not a comatose patient with midline shift.

AS-0721.B: Afternoon caffeine worsens sleep onset and maintenance; caffeine should be avoided later in the day.
AS-0721.C: A regular schedule and limiting screens are sleep hygiene, which is only one part of CBT-I and not enough alone for chronic insomnia; it is the answer when a behavioural cause is the whole problem without established chronic insomnia.
AS-0721.D: Sedative hypnotics are short-term adjuncts only, with tolerance, dependence and falls risk; they are not first line.

AS-0722.A: CBT for insomnia is first line for chronic insomnia disorder (difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep on most nights for about 3 months despite adequate opportunity); here the problem is a self-imposed irregular schedule, so simple sleep hygiene comes first.

AS-0723.A: Elimination diets are not recommended routinely; they are used only when a specific food allergy is proven or strongly suspected to trigger flares.
AS-0723.B: Systemic corticosteroids cause rebound flares and long-term adverse effects in children; they are avoided except for short courses in severe flares under specialist care.

AS-0725.B: Polysomnography is the diagnostic test for OSA, but before pediatric tonsillectomy it is reserved for children with comorbidities (obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial or neuromuscular disease, sickle cell disease) or when tonsil size does not match the reported symptoms.

AS-0734.A: Fruit juice (including cranberry) has weak evidence for preventing UTI in children and is not a recommended preventive strategy.
AS-0734.B: Long-term prophylaxis is not routine after one febrile UTI; it is reserved for selected children (e.g. high-grade VUR, frequent recurrences) given resistance and side effects.
AS-0734.C: Front to back perianal hygiene is reasonable advice, but when toilet training and constipation prevention is offered, it addresses the stronger risk factor (bladder and bowel dysfunction).

AS-0735.A: Increasing fruit juice (cranberry) has no solid evidence of preventing UTI in young children and is not recommended.
AS-0735.B: Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis is not routine after one UTI 6 months ago; it is kept for selected high-risk children (e.g. high-grade VUR or frequent recurrences) because of resistance and adverse effects.

AS-0736.A: Oral amoxicillin treats uncomplicated acute bacterial sinusitis; orbital involvement needs admission, IV antibiotics and imaging.
AS-0736.C: Reassurance is never appropriate with eye signs; orbital cellulitis can cause vision loss, cavernous sinus thrombosis or brain abscess.
AS-0736.D: ENT (and ophthalmology) input is needed, but the CT is what defines an abscess needing drainage and should not be delayed; referral alone is not the most appropriate step.

AS-0737.B: Withholding influenza vaccine for egg allergy is outdated; egg allergy (even beyond hives) does not contraindicate inactivated influenza vaccine.
AS-0737.C: Withholding MMR is wrong: egg allergy is not a contraindication to MMR. MMR is withheld for anaphylaxis to gelatin or neomycin, pregnancy or significant immunosuppression.
AS-0737.D: Deferring both leaves the child unprotected for no valid reason; the true absolute contraindication is anaphylaxis to a previous dose or to a vaccine component.

AS-0738.A: Sodium disturbance is not a characteristic metabolic problem of infants of diabetic mothers and is an uncommon cause of jitteriness.
AS-0738.B: Hypocalcemia does occur in infants of diabetic mothers and can cause jitteriness, but it is less common and usually later than hypoglycemia; check calcium if glucose is normal.
AS-0738.C: Hypomagnesemia also occurs (and accompanies hypocalcemia), but it is a secondary consideration after glucose and calcium.

AS-0739.A: Spastic CP is from upper motor neuron damage (periventricular white matter or cortex), classically with prematurity or HIE, not bilirubin injury of the basal ganglia.
AS-0739.C: Hypotonia can be seen early in bilirubin encephalopathy, but it is nonspecific and evolves; the characteristic chronic sequela is dyskinetic movement.
AS-0739.D: Ataxic CP results from cerebellar damage, not basal ganglia injury.

AS-0740.B: A sacral dimple with loss of anal tone is a red flag for spinal dysraphism or tethered cord (organic, neurogenic bowel), arguing against functional constipation and needing spinal imaging.
AS-0740.C: Normal intake with two stools a day is a normal bowel pattern and does not support constipation at all.

AS-0741.B: Laparotomy is for unstable blunt trauma with a positive FAST (intraperitoneal blood) or peritonitis. Pelvic bleeding is retroperitoneal and not controlled by opening the abdomen; laparotomy can make it worse.

AS-0742.A: An NG tube decompresses the stomach (ileus, obstruction, aspiration risk); it does nothing for hemorrhagic shock.
AS-0742.B: Laparotomy treats intraperitoneal bleeding. A pelvic hematoma is retroperitoneal, and opening the abdomen releases its tamponade.
AS-0742.C: Blood is given alongside the binder in a fluid non-responder, but transfusion only replaces losses; the step keyed here is controlling the source.

AS-0743.A: Massive transfusion will run in parallel in a patient this sick, but it replaces volume without controlling the open-book bleed; the binder is the specific first manoeuvre the question asks for.
AS-0743.B: CT is for hemodynamically stable patients; sending someone with a BP of 70/30 to the scanner is unsafe.
AS-0743.D: Abdominal exploration treats intraperitoneal bleeding (unstable + positive FAST). It does not control pelvic bleeding and releases the retroperitoneal tamponade.

AS-0744.B: Acyclovir treats herpes simplex/varicella infections; HSV hepatitis is a concern in neonates or the immunocompromised, not a school outbreak of jaundice.
AS-0744.C: Antibiotics have no role in viral hepatitis; they would fit bacterial infections such as ascending cholangitis or bacterial dysentery.

AS-0744B.A: Liver transplant is for acute liver failure (encephalopathy, severe coagulopathy); a well child with raised enzymes alone does not meet that threshold.
AS-0744B.C: Acyclovir is for herpes virus infections (e.g. neonatal or immunocompromised HSV hepatitis), not a daycare hepatitis A outbreak.
AS-0744B.D: Ribavirin ("Rabivirne") has no role in hepatitis A; there is no specific antiviral therapy for HAV.

AS-0749.A: Cefixime is unnecessary: antibiotics are for bacterial infection (e.g. bloody diarrhea with systemic features), not watery diarrhea with mild dehydration.
AS-0749.C: Anti-emetics are not routine; a single dose of ondansetron is kept for persistent vomiting that prevents oral rehydration, which is not described in this mildly dehydrated infant.
AS-0749.D: Both parts are unnecessary: no indication for anti-emetics, and cotrimoxazole is not indicated without confirmed bacterial infection.

AS-0750.B: Diphenhydramine only sedates; cholestatic itch is not histamine driven, so antihistamines do not treat the cause. It may be used as a night-time adjunct, not as the main treatment.
AS-0750.C: IV corticosteroids do not relieve established cholestatic itch and add infection risk; steroids are sometimes given early after a Kasai to promote bile flow, which is a different goal from treating pruritus.
AS-0750.D: Vitamin K corrects coagulopathy from fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption in cholestasis; it does nothing for itch. It is right when the question shows a prolonged PT/INR or bleeding.

AS-0758.B: Analgesia and IV fluids are supportive. Fluids alone, without source control, dilute clotting factors and do not stop the pelvic bleed.
AS-0758.C: Antibiotics are needed for open fractures, but they are not life-saving in the first minutes of hemorrhage.

AS-0762.B: Wilms tumour arises from the kidney itself, distorting the collecting system; it is usually a well child with a flank mass, hypertension or hematuria, not a paravertebral mass with cord compression.
AS-0762.C: Retinoblastoma is an eye tumour presenting with leukocoria or strabismus; it does not produce an abdominal paravertebral mass.
AS-0762.D: Hepatoblastoma arises in the liver (right upper quadrant mass, raised AFP) in infants and toddlers; it does not come from the sympathetic chain.

AS-0766.A: Stepping up corticosteroids treats poor control but leaves the trigger in place; environmental triggers, adherence and technique are addressed before escalating therapy.
AS-0766.B: Only addresses the mother's weekend shisha and ignores the father's daily cigarette smoking indoors, the larger exposure; it is a partial answer.
AS-0766.D: A face mask does not reliably protect a child from indoor smoke and is not a recommended prevention strategy; the exposure itself must be removed.

AS-0767.A: This restates what the father already does; smoking in another room does not prevent exposure, so it reinforces his misconception instead of correcting it.
AS-0767.B: Smoking outside reduces but does not eliminate exposure (residue on clothes and hands), and endorsing continued smoking misses the chance to counsel cessation.

AS-0768.A: Staph aureus is the most common surgical site infection organism overall, but it gives thick creamy-yellow pus, not green discharge.
AS-0768.B: Strep pyogenes causes spreading cellulitis and lymphangitis, often early, with thin serous discharge rather than green pus.
AS-0768.C: Clostridium perfringens causes gas gangrene: severe pain, crepitus, gas in the tissues and dark "dishwater" discharge after contaminated wounds, not green pus.

AS-0773.B: Herbal teas have no proven benefit for colic and may displace milk feeds in a young infant; they are not recommended.

AS-0774.A: Simethicone has no proven benefit over placebo for colic, despite the "passes gas" clue; medication is not recommended.
AS-0774.C: There is no fever or sign of infection; antibiotics have no role in colic.
AS-0774.D: Imaging is for red flags such as bilious vomiting, a mass, fever or poor growth (for example intussusception); a well infant with typical colic needs no investigation.

AS-0786.A: Coagulation factors (PT, aPTT) are normal in ITP; they are right when bleeding suggests a factor problem such as hemophilia (joint or deep bleeding, prolonged aPTT) or DIC.
AS-0786.B: Bone marrow examination is reserved for atypical features, such as abnormal Hb or WBC, blasts, organomegaly, bone pain or failure to respond, where leukemia or marrow failure must be excluded.
AS-0786.D: Antiplatelet antibody testing has poor sensitivity and specificity and is not used to diagnose ITP.

AS-0787.A: Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs are avoided in suspected dengue because they worsen bleeding risk with falling platelets; paracetamol is the antipyretic of choice.
AS-0787.B: The picture is viral and the child is stable; empiric antibiotics are indicated only for suspected bacterial sepsis or an unstable, toxic child.

AS-0789.A: Adenovirus (enteric types) causes childhood gastroenteritis, but there is no licensed vaccine for adenoviral gastroenteritis.
AS-0789.B: Astrovirus causes mild gastroenteritis in young children; no vaccine is licensed.
AS-0789.C: Norovirus is the leading cause of outbreak gastroenteritis across all ages, but no vaccine is licensed yet.

AS-0790.B: IGRA is an alternative screening test (useful when BCG makes a TST hard to interpret), not a confirmatory step after a clearly positive TST in a close contact; repeating testing only delays treatment.

AS-0794.B: Analgesia and fluids are supportive and are given alongside, but they do not address the open wound itself; fluids become the priority only if the patient is in shock.
AS-0794.C: Early IV antibiotics are essential in every open fracture and are started in the ED, but in this recall's logic they follow covering and controlling the wound; they would be the answer if the stem stressed that bleeding is controlled and asked about infection prevention.
AS-0794.D: Debridement and stabilization are the definitive treatment done in theatre after initial ED care (dressing, antibiotics, tetanus, splinting); they are not the initial step.

AS-0798.A: Cyclophosphamide is reserved for severe organ threatening lupus, classically neuropsychiatric lupus or severe nephritis; no such involvement is described.
AS-0798.C: MMF is the preferred immunosuppressant for lupus nephritis; it would be right if proteinuria, active sediment or rising creatinine were given, not as the next add on here.

AS-0798B.A: Azathioprine is a steroid sparing or maintenance agent (and the pregnancy compatible substitute for MMF), not the first drug in new mucocutaneous and joint lupus.
AS-0798B.C: Cyclophosphamide is for severe organ threatening disease, classically neuropsychiatric lupus; the stem explicitly says no CNS involvement.
AS-0798B.D: MMF is the choice for lupus nephritis; it would fit if proteinuria or active urinary sediment were present, but renal function is normal here.

AS-0799.A: CT shows calcification well but is avoided in suspected retinoblastoma because ionising radiation raises second cancer risk in RB1 carriers.
AS-0799.C: Ocular ultrasound (B scan) is the quick bedside test that demonstrates an intraocular mass with calcification; it is not the keyed answer here but is often used first.
AS-0799.D: Plain X ray has no role in evaluating an intraocular mass.

AS-0800.A: Urology referral is for red flags: daytime symptoms with recurrent UTI (renal US and VCUG), abnormal neurologic or spine findings, or a structural cause; none are described.
AS-0800.B: Behavioral therapy (alarm, reward charts) is used for persistent enuresis after about 5 to 6 years; at 4 years it is premature and can add stress.
AS-0800.D: This option was not recalled; whatever it was, active intervention or referral is not needed for monosymptomatic enuresis at this age.

AS-0801.B: Corticosteroids prevent RDS when given to the <i>mother</i> before preterm delivery; they are not the treatment for an infant already showing RDS.
AS-0801.C: Antibiotics are added when sepsis or congenital pneumonia is suspected (maternal fever, PROM, chorioamnionitis); they do not treat surfactant deficiency, which is the problem in an otherwise unremarkable preterm.
AS-0801.D: Chest tubes or bronchial intubation are for complications such as pneumothorax or for ventilation, not the specific management of RDS.

AS-0806.B: Omphalocele is a congenital midline defect present at birth, with bowel or liver covered by a membrane (amnion and peritoneum) and the cord inserting into the sac; it does not appear later as a skin covered bulge only on crying.

AS-0812.B: Doxycycline + rifampicin for 6 weeks is first line for adults and children 8 years or older; at 6 years doxycycline is avoided.
AS-0812.C: Ciprofloxacin alone is monotherapy (high relapse rate) and quinolones are not first line in brucellosis, especially in children.
AS-0812.D: Ceftriaxone has poor intracellular activity against Brucella and is not a standard regimen; single agent therapy also relapses.

AS-0816.A: Skipping the team briefing removes the checklist step that catches errors such as unchecked anticoagulation; briefing is never skipped.
AS-0816.B: Anesthetic dosing is titrated to the patient, never given "randomly"; underdosing risks awareness and hemodynamic instability.
AS-0816.D: Restarting anticoagulation right before surgery greatly raises bleeding risk; it is resumed after surgery once hemostasis is secure (with bridging decided case by case).

AS-0818.A: Rooting reflex: a mouth response, turning toward a touch on the cheek or corner of the mouth; it involves no leg movement.

AS-0818B.B: By 4 months is the disappearance age of the rooting and Galant (trunk incurvation) reflexes.
AS-0818B.C: By 6 months is when the Moro and palmar grasp reflexes disappear.

AS-0819.B: Plain reassurance ignores a real family history and gives no follow up plan; reassurance alone fits only when there is no risk factor and development is normal, and even then routine screening still happens at 18 to 24 months.

AS-0821.A: A blood glucose of 55 mg/dL is within the acceptable range for a newborn and says nothing about the lungs. Glucose would only matter here if it were clearly low and the baby had symptoms.
AS-0821.B: TTN typically resolves over 24 to 72 hours, so symptoms still present at 24 hours are expected and not a sign of deterioration. It is persistence well beyond about 72 hours that should prompt you to look for another diagnosis.

AS-0823.A: Routine care without extra monitoring is right for an appropriately grown, well term baby. An SGA baby is at risk, and hypoglycemia can be silent, so it needs targeted screening.
AS-0823.B: Immediate IV glucose is for confirmed hypoglycemia that is symptomatic, severe or not responding to feeds. Giving it to an asymptomatic baby with no glucose result skips monitoring and early feeding.

AS-0832.B: IV glucose (with protein stopped) is part of the initial stabilization because it halts catabolism. However, it does not remove the ammonia already present, and glucose is normal here. On its own it is not enough at this ammonia level.
AS-0832.C: Sodium benzoate is a nitrogen scavenger that is given alongside dialysis or used alone for milder hyperammonemia. Its effect is too slow to be the sole treatment for a markedly high level in an encephalopathic neonate.
AS-0832.D: Lactulose lowers gut ammonia production and is used for hepatic encephalopathy in adults. It has no role in the acute treatment of neonatal urea cycle disorders.

AS-0836.C: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-0838.B: Low-dose oral aspirin is the routine antiplatelet step once the fever settles after IVIG, continued until echo follow-up is clear. It does not treat persistent inflammation, so it is not the answer when the stem signals refractory disease or coronary involvement.

AS-0839.A: After a simple febrile seizure (generalized, under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours, in a neurologically normal child), the risk of epilepsy is only slightly above that of the general population. Parents should be reassured that it does not cause epilepsy.

AS-0847.B: Oral prednisone is kept for reactive arthritis that does not respond to NSAIDs, or for severe disease (intra-articular steroid is another option). It is not first line.
AS-0847.C: Synovial aspiration is essential when a hot joint has an effusion and septic arthritis must be excluded, especially an acute single joint with fever. Here there is no effusion and the history points to a post-infectious arthritis.
AS-0847.D: IV antibiotics are the treatment for septic arthritis after the joint has been aspirated. Reactive arthritis is sterile, so antibiotics do not treat the joint inflammation.

AS-0849.B: The stepping reflex is elicited by holding the infant upright with the soles touching a surface, which produces alternating walking movements. It involves the legs, not the mouth.

AS-0849B.A: Disappearance at 2 months is too early for rooting. Around 2 to 3 months is when the asymmetrical tonic neck reflex fades.
AS-0849B.C: Six months is when the Moro and palmar grasp reflexes disappear, not rooting.

AS-0852.B: Meconium aspiration is a disease of term or post term babies born through meconium stained liquor, with patchy infiltrates and hyperinflation on CXR; a preterm baby rarely passes meconium in utero.
AS-0852.C: Transient tachypnea of the newborn is due to delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid, typically in a term baby delivered by C-section, mild and self resolving, with fluid in the fissures on CXR. Prematurity points to RDS instead.
AS-0852.D: Congenital heart disease presents with cyanosis out of proportion to respiratory effort, murmur, abnormal pulses or a failed hyperoxia test; nothing in the stem points to a cardiac lesion, and prematurity is the classic RDS clue.

AS-0856.A: A pelvic binder is a pre-hospital/ED measure to close an unstable pelvic ring and reduce bleeding before definitive fixation; after surgical fixation it has no role.
AS-0856.B: Analgesia and fluids are routine supportive care for every post-op patient, but they are not the specific management goal the question targets; fluids are the answer in the resuscitation phase.
AS-0856.C: Antibiotics are perioperative prophylaxis (or for open fractures/infection); there is no sign of infection here to justify ongoing broad-spectrum cover.

AS-0859.C: Hydrocolloid is occlusive and suits low exudate, clean wounds; on a diabetic ulcer it may conceal infection and is generally avoided.
AS-0859.D: Transparent film absorbs nothing; it is for dry superficial wounds or IV sites, not an exudative plantar ulcer.

AS-0860.B: Steroids are the first step to reduce cord edema, but they have already failed here; escalating them does not decompress the cord.
AS-0860.C: Conservative care would be right only for a patient unfit for surgery or with very poor prognosis; with a progressing deficit it risks permanent paraplegia.

AS-0862.C: Surgical exploration is reserved for perforation (mediastinitis, peritonitis, free air, shock); here vital signs are stable and findings are mild local redness and tenderness.
AS-0862.D: Discharge is only for a fully asymptomatic child with no oral lesions; drooling and difficulty swallowing are warning signs of esophageal injury and need inpatient monitoring.

AS-0864.C: Observation delays removal and risks post obstructive pneumonia, bronchiectasis or complete obstruction; a positive history plus focal signs is an indication for bronchoscopy, not watchful waiting.
AS-0864.D: Flexible bronchoscopy is useful diagnostically when suspicion is low or findings are equivocal, but it is poor for retrieving organic material in a child; with clear evidence of a retained foreign body, rigid bronchoscopy is preferred because it is therapeutic.

AS-0870.A: Coagulation factor assays are for hemophilia or von Willebrand disease, which give deep bleeding or hemarthroses with a normal platelet count; this child's bleeding is petechial with low platelets.
AS-0870.C: EBV serology is relevant when there is fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes; it does not confirm the cause of anemia plus thrombocytopenia, and a malignancy must be excluded first.

AS-0874.B: Septic arthritis is acute (days), with fever, an ill child and severe pain or refusal to move the limb; 7 weeks of afebrile morning stiffness with negative blood culture does not fit.
AS-0874.C: Reactive arthritis is an asymmetric, mainly lower limb oligoarthritis that follows a GI or genitourinary infection, often with conjunctivitis or urethritis; the stem gives no preceding diarrhea or urethritis, and persistent arthritis beyond 6 weeks in a child points to JIA.
AS-0874.D: Hemophilia A causes acute hemarthrosis, often after minor trauma, in a boy with a bleeding history; it does not give weeks of inflammatory morning stiffness.

AS-0878.A: Immediate surgery in a newborn is unnecessary because spontaneous descent is common in early infancy; operating now exposes the baby to avoidable anaesthetic and surgical risk.
AS-0878.B: Waiting until after 2 years is too late; delayed orchidopexy worsens the risk of impaired fertility and makes malignancy harder to detect. Surgery should be done by about 18 months.

AS-0884.A: Sorafenib is systemic therapy for advanced HCC with vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread; here the veins are patent and the tumour is confined to the liver.
AS-0884.B: Transplant is for HCC within Milan criteria (single lesion ≤5 cm, or up to 3 lesions each ≤3 cm); a single 6 cm lesion is outside them.
AS-0884.C: Resection suits a single mass under 6 cm with well-preserved liver function; this lesion is 6 cm and the patient has ascites, low albumin, raised INR and thrombocytopenia, signs of portal hypertension and limited reserve.

AS-0885.A: Regular antipyretics (ibuprofen or paracetamol) during febrile illnesses make the child more comfortable but do not reduce the recurrence of febrile seizures.
AS-0885.B: Continuous antiepileptic drugs can reduce recurrences but their adverse effects outweigh the benefit in simple febrile seizures, and they do not prevent later epilepsy; they are not recommended.
AS-0885.C: EEG is not indicated after a simple febrile seizure in a neurologically normal child; it does not predict recurrence or later epilepsy. It is considered for atypical or complex features.

AS-0886.A: Fine needle aspiration gives only cells without tissue architecture, so it cannot reliably type and grade a sarcoma; it suits cystic or thyroid lesions and lymph nodes.
AS-0886.B: Excising a suspected sarcoma before diagnosis (the unplanned "whoops" excision) leaves inadequate margins and compromises the definitive resection; excisional biopsy suits only small, superficial lesions.
AS-0886.C: Open incisional biopsy contaminates tissue planes and risks haematoma and spillage; it is reserved for when core biopsy is nondiagnostic.

AS-0888.A: Needle thoracostomy treats tension pneumothorax (hypotension, raised JVP, tracheal shift, hyperresonance); none of those signs are described.
AS-0888.B: A chest tube drains a pneumothorax or haemothorax; flail chest alone does not need one unless an associated air or blood collection is found.
AS-0888.D: A three-sided occlusive dressing is for an open (sucking) chest wound; this is blunt trauma with an intact chest wall.

AS-0889.B: Oesophageal rupture can widen the mediastinum, but it follows forceful vomiting or endoscopy and shows pneumomediastinum, subcutaneous emphysema or pleural effusion; no such history is given.
AS-0889.C: GERD gives burning retrosternal discomfort related to meals and lying down, never sudden severe pain or a widened mediastinum.
AS-0889.D: Pancreatitis gives epigastric pain radiating to the back too, but after gallstones or alcohol, with vomiting and raised lipase; it does not widen the mediastinum.

AS-0892.B: A glycerin suppository suits meconium plug syndrome or simple functional constipation; using it here only gives temporary decompression and delays the diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease, which carries a risk of enterocolitis.

AS-0896.A: Simple reassurance ignores a real aneurysm that can grow and rupture; it needs scheduled imaging and risk factor control, not discharge.
AS-0896.B: Urgent surgery is for a symptomatic (tender, painful) or ruptured AAA; elective repair is for ≥5.5 cm in men (≥5 cm in women) or rapid growth. This one is asymptomatic and 4.5 cm.
AS-0896.D: Endarterectomy removes atherosclerotic plaque from a stenosed artery (e.g. carotid); it is not an aneurysm operation. AAA repair is open graft replacement or EVAR.

AS-0897.A: ABI is the first test for stable chronic PAD (claudication); in an acute presentation it does not localise the occlusion or guide urgent treatment.
AS-0897.C: MR angiography is slower, less available, and reserved for when iodinated contrast is contraindicated; not an initial test.
AS-0897.D: CT angiography is the confirmatory, gold standard test (the answer to "most appropriate" or "confirmatory" investigation), not the initial one.

AS-0898.A: There is no fever or infective picture; antibiotics alone would treat empyema or pneumonia but not drain blood compressing the lung.
AS-0898.B: Needle aspiration is used for a small primary spontaneous pneumothorax (and needle decompression for tension pneumothorax with hypotension and tracheal shift); a needle cannot effectively drain a traumatic haemothorax.
AS-0898.D: Thoracic surgery (thoracotomy or VATS) is for massive haemothorax (>1500 ml on tube insertion, or about 200 ml/hour for 2 to 4 hours), instability, or a retained clotted collection after a chest tube, not as the first step.

AS-0899.B: A glycerin suppository suits meconium plug syndrome or simple functional constipation; using it here only gives temporary decompression and delays the diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease, which carries a risk of enterocolitis.

AS-0900.A: Supportive treatment only: right for viral pharyngitis with a NEGATIVE rapid test and mild findings; a confirmed GAS infection must be treated to prevent rheumatic fever and suppurative complications.
AS-0900.B: Acyclovir for 7 days: treats herpes simplex (e.g. herpetic gingivostomatitis with gum involvement) or varicella; it has no activity against streptococci.

AS-0901.A: Hyperthermia: IUGR babies get HYPOthermia because of reduced subcutaneous fat and a large surface area relative to weight.
AS-0901.B: Hyperglycemia: IUGR babies get HYPOglycemia from low glycogen stores; neonatal hyperglycemia is more a problem of extremely preterm infants on IV dextrose.
AS-0901.D: Anemia: chronic fetal hypoxia raises erythropoietin, so IUGR babies get POLYCYTHEMIA (with hyperviscosity and jaundice), not anemia.

AS-0902.A: Neurogenic shock follows spinal cord injury: loss of sympathetic tone gives hypotension with a normal or slow heart rate and warm, dry peripheries, often with a neurological deficit. Tachycardia argues against it.

AS-0903.B: CT (CT urography) images the kidneys and ureters; the upper tract is already covered by the normal pyelogram, and CT misses small flat bladder lesions.
AS-0903.C: Ultrasound assesses kidneys, residual volume and prostate size but is insensitive for small bladder tumours; it does not replace cystoscopy.
AS-0903.D: Prostate biopsy is for a suspicious DRE or raised PSA; the prostate here is benign-feeling with "no suspicious features".

AS-0904.A: Cystoscopy looks at the bladder and urethra; it is the test for painless hematuria in an older patient (bladder cancer workup), not the first test when flank pain points to the kidney or ureter.
AS-0904.C: Plain X-ray KUB misses radiolucent (uric acid), small or overlying stones; it is used to follow known radiopaque stones, not to make the diagnosis.

AS-0906.A: 10 days of oral penicillin: this eradicates GAS from the throat in an acute pharyngitis (primary prevention, and also given once at ARF diagnosis); it does not protect against future infections and recurrences.
AS-0906.C: Strep vaccine: no group A streptococcal vaccine is available for clinical use, so it cannot be offered.
AS-0906.D: Flu vaccine: protects against influenza, not group A streptococcus; it has no role in preventing rheumatic fever recurrence.

AS-0910.A: Tubular adenoma is the most common adenoma but has the lowest malignant risk of the three adenoma types (ranks third).
AS-0910.C: Hyperplastic polyps are non-neoplastic and carry the lowest risk of all the options.
AS-0910.D: Tubulovillous adenoma has intermediate risk (ranks second), below a pure villous adenoma.

AS-0916.A: SLE: maternal anti-Ro/anti-La antibodies cross the placenta and damage the conduction system, causing congenital complete heart block (neonatal lupus), not myocardial hypertrophy.

AS-0919.B: Acute cholecystitis needs ultrasound signs of inflammation (thick gallbladder wall, pericholecystic fluid) plus fever and RUQ tenderness; here the wall is normal, there is no fluid and vitals are normal.
AS-0919.C: Obstructive jaundice would show yellow sclera, dark urine, pale stools and itching; the stem explicitly says sclera and skin are normal with no urine or stool change.
AS-0919.D: Small bowel obstruction presents with colicky pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation; this patient has no vomiting and no change in bowel habit, and ultrasound shows a biliary cause.

AS-0920.B: Von Willebrand disease: mucosal bleeding (gums, epistaxis, menorrhagia) with a prolonged bleeding time and often a prolonged PTT from low factor VIII; here both are normal.
AS-0920.C: Bernard-Soulier syndrome: platelet adhesion defect (GPIb) with giant platelets, low count and a prolonged bleeding time; bleeding time is normal here.
AS-0920.D: Hemophilia: X-linked factor VIII or IX deficiency with a prolonged PTT and joint bleeding; a normal PTT excludes it even though a brother is affected.

AS-0921.B: IV antibiotics treat infection; there is no fever, leukocytosis or gas in the collection, and antibiotics do not decompress a pseudocyst.
AS-0921.C: Antibiotics plus observation is wrong twice: no infection is present, and observation is only for small, asymptomatic or early collections, not an enlarging symptomatic one.
AS-0921.D: Surgical drainage (cystgastrostomy) is reserved for failure or unsuitability of endoscopic drainage; it is not first line and not "immediate".

AS-0922.A: Discouraging physical activity: the opposite of advice; regular exercise and a healthy weight lower the risk of hypertension.
AS-0922.B: Normal salt intake: does not protect; lifestyle advice for an at-risk child is to limit added salt, and diet alone does not replace BP monitoring.
AS-0922.C: Start antihypertensive: never indicated for a normotensive child; drugs are used only for confirmed hypertension (e.g. stage 2, symptomatic, or not controlled by lifestyle).

AS-0923.B: Discharging an equivocal RLQ pain risks missing early appendicitis that progresses to perforation; discharge with return advice fits only clearly non-surgical, resolving pain.
AS-0923.C: Analgesia should be given and does not mask appendicitis, but on its own it does not establish or exclude the diagnosis; it is part of care, not the strategy that prevents a miss.

AS-0927.A: Follow up: right for asymptomatic, mild to moderate aortic stenosis with good LV function; this child has symptoms and a significant gradient.
AS-0927.B: Start anticoagulant: plays no role in native valve stenosis in sinus rhythm; anticoagulation is for mechanical valves or atrial fibrillation.
AS-0927.D: Diuretics: may ease congestion in heart failure but do not relieve the fixed outflow obstruction; LV function is good and there is no heart failure here.

AS-0930.B: Prolonged antibiotics will worsen symptoms: antibiotics have no role in viral wheeze, so this is not the counselling point; the mother's question is about the course of the wheeze, which is expected to resolve.
AS-0930.C: Corticosteroids will cause diabetes: inhaled corticosteroids at usual doses do not cause diabetes; this is false reassurance in the wrong direction.
AS-0930.D: Inhaled salbutamol will prevent asthma: salbutamol is a reliever that treats bronchospasm; no inhaler, not even an inhaled steroid, changes the natural history or prevents asthma.

AS-0932.A: Meconium aspiration: needs meconium-stained amniotic fluid, usually in a post-term or distressed baby, with patchy infiltrates and hyperinflation on CXR; neither is given here.

AS-0936.A: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding prolongs the PT (and later aPTT) with a normal platelet count; it fits a home birth with no vitamin K prophylaxis or maternal antiepileptic use, not isolated thrombocytopenia.
AS-0936.C: Hemophilia A gives a prolonged aPTT with normal platelets and normal PT, classically in a boy bleeding after circumcision; here aPTT is normal.
AS-0936.D: A congenital platelet function defect causes bleeding with a normal or only mildly low count (normal in Glanzmann, mildly low with giant platelets in Bernard-Soulier); it does not explain a count of 18,000 or the maternal SLE link.

AS-0939.B: Steroids can be added in immune thrombocytopenia but act slowly and are not first line in a bleeding neonate; they would not stop bleeding now.
AS-0939.C: FFP replaces clotting factors; it is right when PT/aPTT are prolonged (DIC, factor deficiency), but here both are normal.
AS-0939.D: Vitamin K with PCC treats vitamin K deficiency bleeding, which prolongs the PT with normal platelets; here the PT is normal and the platelets are low.

AS-0942.B: Premature (surfactant deficient) lung causes respiratory distress syndrome in a preterm baby, with a ground glass (reticulogranular) CXR; TTN is typically a term cesarean baby.

AS-0947C.B: LFTs may be mildly deranged in brucellosis (liver involvement) but are nonspecific and cannot make the diagnosis.
AS-0947C.C: CBC may show mild cytopenias or relative lymphocytosis but is nonspecific; it is a supportive test, not a diagnostic one.
AS-0947C.D: FNA of a node is invasive and its cytology (e.g. granulomas) is nonspecific; it is right for a persistent localized node, e.g. suspected mycobacterial (M. bovis) lymphadenitis from raw milk or lymphoma, or when serology is negative.

AS-0947D.B: Doxycycline + rifampicin for 6 weeks is first line for adults and children 8 years or older; at 6 years doxycycline is avoided.
AS-0947D.C: Ciprofloxacin alone is monotherapy (high relapse rate) and quinolones are not first line in brucellosis, especially in children.
AS-0947D.D: Ceftriaxone has poor intracellular activity against Brucella and is not a standard regimen; single agent therapy also relapses.

AS-0948.A: Suicide risk is highest in older patients (and adolescents); 38 is not a high-risk age.
AS-0948.B: Women attempt suicide more often, but men complete suicide more often, so female sex is not the highest-risk factor.
AS-0948.D: Chronic or terminal illness raises suicide risk; its absence is not a risk factor.

AS-0957.A: CT enterography images the small bowel (Crohn disease, obscure small bowel bleeding) and cannot take tissue; it is not the test for a suspected colon cancer.
AS-0957.B: Barium enema is outdated, misses small lesions and cannot biopsy; it is used only when colonoscopy is impossible.
AS-0957.C: Sigmoidoscopy sees only the distal colon and would miss a right-sided cancer, which typically causes anemia; a positive occult blood test needs full colonoscopy.

AS-0958.B: Transabdominal ultrasound cannot resolve the layers of the stomach wall; at most it may show liver metastases or ascites.
AS-0958.C: A nuclear (bone) scan looks for skeletal metastases when symptoms suggest them; it says nothing about depth of invasion.
AS-0958.D: A contrast (Gastrografin) study outlines the lumen and mucosa or shows a leak, but cannot measure how deep the tumour penetrates the wall.

AS-0959.A: CT is the first staging scan for distant metastases and gross invasion of neighbouring organs, but it cannot separate the wall layers to define early T stage.
AS-0959.B: PET is best for detecting occult distant metastases (M stage); its spatial resolution is too low to judge depth of wall invasion.
AS-0959.C: MRI is not a routine staging tool for esophageal cancer and is less accurate than EUS for wall depth.

AS-0960.A: Static (non progressive) motor delay is common to every CP type and also to other static brain injuries; it supports CP in general but does not define the diplegic pattern seen here.
AS-0960.C: Prematurity is a risk factor for periventricular leukomalacia and diplegia, not a finding that establishes the diagnosis; many preterm babies never develop CP.
AS-0960.D: Periventricular white matter changes are the cause already given in the stem; imaging supports the etiology, but the CP subtype is diagnosed from the clinical tone pattern.

AS-0964.A: CBC would be right if the child had symptoms of leukemia (pallor, bruising, bone pain, fever, hepatosplenomegaly); an uncle with leukemia is not an indication in a well child.
AS-0964.B: CXR has no role here; it would be for a suspected chest infection or a mediastinal mass (e.g. T cell leukemia/lymphoma), and a self limiting URTI 2 weeks ago in a well child needs no imaging.
AS-0964.D: BRCA 1/2 testing is for families with breast, ovarian, prostate or pancreatic cancer; it is unrelated to retinoblastoma or leukemia.

AS-0966.B: A MAP of 45 is profound hypotension; the usual resuscitation target is a MAP of at least 65, so this value shows ongoing shock, not adequate fluid.
AS-0966.C: Urine output of 0.1 mL/kg/h is severe oliguria; adequate resuscitation is shown by at least 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults.
AS-0966.D: Lactate reflects tissue perfusion and anaerobic metabolism rather than intravascular volume, and a value of 2 sits at the upper limit of normal, so on this key's logic it does not confirm fluid status.

AS-0967.A: Urine output is the best burn endpoint, but the target is at least 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults (1 mL/kg/h in children); 0.1 mL/kg/h means under-resuscitation.
AS-0967.B: A MAP of 45 is severe hypotension and indicates inadequate resuscitation; the target is a MAP of at least 65.
AS-0967.C: CVP is invasive and a poor predictor of volume status in burns, where massive capillary leak and fluid shifts distort it; it is not used as the resuscitation endpoint.

AS-0970.B: Intussusception: typically an infant or toddler (about 6 months to 3 years) with episodic colicky crying, drawing up the legs, a sausage-shaped mass and red currant jelly stool; a 10-year-old with localized RLQ peritonism does not fit.
AS-0970.C: Meckel's diverticulum: classically presents in young children with painless rectal bleeding; Meckel's diverticulitis can mimic appendicitis but is far rarer, so it is not the diagnosis for this classic picture.

AS-0973.A: EBV PCR or serology suits infectious mononucleosis (fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes), which does not cause bone pain with anemia and marked thrombocytopenia.

AS-0974.B: Observation is acceptable only with normal mental status and exam, as in a child who vomited or had a headache but is fully alert; drowsiness after a seizure removes that option.
AS-0974.C: Electrolytes are for an unprovoked or febrile seizure without trauma; here the trigger is head injury, so intracranial injury must be excluded first.
AS-0974.D: Neurosurgery referral follows a CT showing a surgical lesion such as an epidural or subdural hematoma; without imaging there is nothing to refer yet.
