AS-0979.A: Reassurance and continuing the same drug is wrong once there is no improvement at 72 h; that defines failure of first line therapy.
AS-0979.B: ENT referral is for complications (orbital or intracranial), recurrent or chronic sinusitis, or failure of second line antibiotics; a single amoxicillin failure is handled by broadening the antibiotic.

AS-0980.A: Colonoscopy: an elective, preparation-requiring investigation, not the next step in acute severe abdominal pain; it is used for bleeding or suspected colorectal cancer once the acute picture is clarified.
AS-0980.B: Sigmoidoscopy: useful for suspected sigmoid volvulus (huge tympanic distension, coffee bean sign) or distal lesions, but should follow examination, not replace it.
AS-0980.C: US abdomen: reasonable imaging for biliary or pelvic causes, but the bedside examination (including DRE) is completed first; in a frail elderly patient with diffuse pain, CT is usually the more informative imaging.

AS-0984.B: There is no separate "prematurity" schedule; corrected age is used for growth and developmental assessment, not for vaccine timing.
AS-0984.C: Waiting until 6 months leaves a vulnerable preterm infant unprotected; the only common timing nuance is the hepatitis B birth dose in very low birth weight babies.

AS-0986.A: Extended bed rest: increases the risk of DVT/PE, pneumonia, pressure sores and deconditioning; it is the opposite of prevention.
AS-0986.B: High-dose corticosteroids: no preventive role after trauma surgery; they impair wound and fracture healing and raise infection risk.
AS-0986.D: Empirical antibiotics for 5 days: surgical prophylaxis is short (a single pre-incision dose, at most about 24 h for closed fractures); prolonged empirical courses promote resistance and C. difficile without benefit.

AS-0987.A: Multivitamins do not raise energy in a well-nourished child with normal growth; they fit a documented deficiency or restricted diet.
AS-0987.B: Her weight is normal, so extra calories would only promote overweight in a sedentary child; they fit undernutrition or faltering growth.
AS-0987.C: Endocrine referral needs red flags (growth failure, abnormal weight, goitre, other symptoms of hypothyroidism); none are present.

AS-0998.A: Fluid resuscitation: the patient is not hypotensive (HR 96, no shock); the problem is respiratory, and excess fluid worsens pulmonary contusion. Fluids would lead if he were in hemorrhagic shock.
AS-0998.C: Needle decompression: treats tension pneumothorax (hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal shift, raised JVP, hypotension), none of which is described.
AS-0998.D: Thoracostomy chest tube: for pneumothorax or hemothorax seen on examination or X-ray; the film here shows only rib fractures.

AS-1005.A: Blood film is the first screening test and may show blasts, but it cannot confirm leukemia (blasts can be absent in the periphery, especially with a normal WBC). It would be the answer only if the lead-in asked for the first screening test; here "initial" is tied to "confirm".
AS-1005.B: Virology (EBV, CMV) fits an infectious mononucleosis-like picture with tender nodes and short illness; 2 months of nodes plus bicytopenia needs marrow examination.

AS-1006.A: CT is avoided in retinoblastoma because radiation increases second malignancy risk in RB1 carriers, and it shows soft-tissue and optic nerve extension less well; CT is the first choice in stroke or trauma, not here.

AS-1013.A: Action: the first months (under about 6) of actively doing the new behaviour. He has passed that window and is now focused on keeping the change, not starting it.
AS-1013.C: Contemplation: aware of the problem and thinking about changing within the next months but not yet acting. He is already acting consistently.
AS-1013.D: Pre-contemplation: no intention to change and often denies the problem. He has had surgery and changed his lifestyle, so this clearly does not fit.

AS-1015.A: Bed rest: appropriate only for a stable, minor (e.g. pubic ramus) fracture; useless in a hypotensive patient.
AS-1015.B: Laparotomy: pelvic bleeding is retroperitoneal and is not controlled by laparotomy; laparotomy is for intra-abdominal bleeding with a positive FAST in an unstable patient.
AS-1015.C: IV fluids: a limited initial crystalloid bolus may be given while blood is prepared, but large-volume crystalloid dilutes clotting factors and worsens bleeding; ongoing shock from pelvic hemorrhage needs blood.

AS-1019.A: Poor response to analgesics is common in migraine and medication-overuse headache; on its own it is not an imaging indication.
AS-1019.B: Photosensitivity is a typical migraine feature (with phonophobia and nausea) and does not suggest a structural lesion.
AS-1019.D: Vomiting with headache attacks is common in migraine; it becomes a red flag only when it is early-morning or persistent vomiting with a worsening pattern.

AS-1020.A: Inhaled corticosteroids treat airway inflammation (asthma); tracheomalacia is a structural softening of cartilage and steroids do not stiffen it.
AS-1020.B: Home oxygen may support hypoxia but does not prevent the dynamic collapse or fix the failure to thrive; it fits stable chronic hypoxia, not severe malacia.
AS-1020.D: Beta-2 agonists relax airway smooth muscle and can make a floppy trachea collapse more; they are for bronchospasm, not malacia.

AS-1020B.A: Conservative observation is right for mild tracheomalacia with noisy breathing and normal growth; complications like recurrent pneumonia and failure to thrive mean waiting is no longer safe.

AS-1020C.A: Nebulized SABA: the wheeze is from dynamic collapse of a soft trachea, not bronchospasm, so bronchodilators do not help (they can even worsen collapse by relaxing airway smooth muscle). Right for asthma or reactive airway wheeze, which is polyphonic and responds to bronchodilators.
AS-1020C.B: Systemic steroids: there is no airway inflammation to treat. Right for an acute asthma exacerbation or croup, not a structural floppy airway.
AS-1020C.D: Tracheostomy: reserved for severe tracheomalacia with life threatening apnoeic spells, recurrent respiratory failure or failure to thrive. This infant is thriving with no distress.

AS-1039.B: Sign Out: done before the patient leaves the operating room; it covers the procedure name, instrument, sponge and needle counts, specimen labeling, equipment problems and recovery concerns.
AS-1039.C: Time Out: done before skin incision; the team introduces itself, reconfirms patient, site and procedure, antibiotic prophylaxis within the last 60 minutes, anticipated critical events and imaging. Allergy is checked earlier, before induction.
AS-1039.D: Postoperative: not a phase of the checklist, and too late; anesthetic drugs and antibiotics would already have been given.

AS-1045.A: Left lobectomy: an option for low-risk, unifocal differentiated cancer (roughly 1 to 4 cm) without risk factors, or for an indeterminate Bethesda IV nodule; the radiation history removes this option.
AS-1045.B: Left lobectomy with isthmusectomy: still a unilateral procedure, with the same limitation as lobectomy; it leaves the contralateral lobe at risk in a radiation-exposed gland.
AS-1045.C: Subtotal thyroidectomy: leaves residual thyroid tissue, which is inadequate oncologically and interferes with radioactive iodine; it is an old operation for benign goiter or Graves disease.

AS-1057.A: Adjust the alpha-blocker dose: alpha-blockers have a quick, largely dose-limited effect; after 2 years of persistent symptoms, a higher dose adds side effects (orthostatic hypotension) without meaningful benefit.
AS-1057.B: Suprapubic catheterization: used for acute retention when urethral catheterization fails or is contraindicated (e.g. urethral trauma or stricture); this patient is voiding, not in retention.
AS-1057.C: Clean intermittent catheterization: for neurogenic bladder or chronic retention in patients unfit for surgery; it is not the next step for symptomatic BPH failing medication.

AS-1059.A: Chemotherapy acts too slowly to relieve an acute compression; it is used only for very chemosensitive tumors alongside definitive local treatment.
AS-1059.B: Steroids are the first step to reduce cord edema, but they have already failed here; escalating them does not decompress the cord.
AS-1059.C: Conservative care would be right only for a patient unfit for surgery or with very poor prognosis; with a progressing deficit it risks permanent paraplegia.

AS-1062.A: CBC: may support infection but does not localize the source; the decisive next step is the targeted bedside examination of the surgical site.
AS-1062.B: Urine culture: UTI is the classic cause on days 2 to 3 (especially after catheterization); on day 4 the wound comes first.
AS-1062.D: Review medication: drug fever is a diagnosis of exclusion, considered later when no infectious source is found.

AS-1069.A: Necrotizing fasciitis shows pain out of proportion to findings, rapid spread, systemic toxicity, crepitus, bullae or skin necrosis; none are described here.
AS-1069.B: Folliculitis gives small pustules centred on hair follicles, not a diffuse warm swelling with lymphangitis.
AS-1069.D: Impetigo is a superficial epidermal infection with honey-coloured crusts, typically on the face of children.

AS-1072.A: Skin tag: a small, soft, skin-covered flap at the anal verge, often painless or linked to a fissure; it is not a mucosal, circumferential protrusion.
AS-1072.C: Haemorrhoid: prolapsed hemorrhoids appear as separate cushions with radial grooves between them, and classically present with painless bright red bleeding, not concentric circular folds.

AS-1082.B: MRI is the right test, but <i>outpatient</i> timing is wrong: suspected cord compression needs same-day imaging, because delay risks permanent paralysis and sphincter loss. Outpatient MRI suits chronic mechanical back pain without red flags.

AS-1117.A: Flail segment needs multiple rib fractures with paradoxical chest wall movement; it causes hypoxia and pain but does not shift the trachea or raise the JVP.
AS-1117.B: Cardiac tamponade also gives raised JVP and hypotension (Beck triad with muffled heart sounds), but breath sounds stay equal and the trachea stays central; it is typical of penetrating injury.
AS-1117.C: Pulmonary contusion causes hypoxia and crackles developing over hours, but no tracheal deviation, raised JVP or obstructive shock.

AS-1132.A: A corneal ulcer (infective keratitis) develops over days, often in contact lens wearers, and shows a white infiltrate or opacity with a staining defect; this is an immediate traumatic defect.
AS-1132.C: Subconjunctival hemorrhage is painless with a bright red patch and no fluorescein uptake.
AS-1132.D: Acute conjunctivitis gives redness with discharge and grittiness, usually without severe pain or a staining epithelial defect.

AS-1153.A: Intubation is indicated for GCS ≤8, inability to protect the airway, hypoxia or aspiration risk; here the GCS is reduced but above 8, so the airway is not the immediate problem.
AS-1153.C: Reassurance fits a minor head injury with normal GCS and no imaging findings; a child with vomiting, drowsiness and an intracranial bleed on CT cannot be reassured.
AS-1153.D: CT already made the diagnosis and is the test of choice for acute head trauma; MRI only delays treatment and is reserved for subacute or subtle injuries (for example diffuse axonal injury).

AS-1163.A: Iron deficiency also causes microcytosis, but the RBC count falls with it (Mentzer above 13), target cells are not prominent and splenomegaly is not expected; in a child it usually follows a poor diet such as excess cow's milk, with low ferritin.
AS-1163.B: Anemia of chronic disease needs an underlying chronic illness, is usually normocytic or mildly microcytic, has high ferritin and no splenomegaly or target cells.
AS-1163.C: Sideroblastic anemia shows ringed sideroblasts on marrow and high iron; it is rare in children and has no high RBC count or prominent target cells.

AS-1177.B: Conventional angiography is invasive arterial imaging used for intervention planning in established arterial disease; with intact pulses it is not an initial test.
AS-1177.C: ABI is the first test for suspected peripheral arterial disease (claudication, absent pulses, arterial ulcer); it does not detect DVT and is often falsely high in diabetics with calcified vessels.
AS-1177.D: CT with contrast (or CT angiography) suits acute limb ischemia or deep abscess or osteomyelitis planning; it is not the initial test for a warm tender calf and carries contrast risk in a diabetic.

AS-1182.B: Functional constipation is a disease of older infants and children (often around toilet training) with a normal meconium history and a rectum full of hard stool; a newborn who has not passed meconium in 48 hours must be assumed to have an organic cause.

AS-1186.A: Vitamin C supplements have not been shown to prevent colds or flu in the general population; at most they may modestly shorten symptom duration. It would only be right if the child had true scurvy (bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhage, poor diet).

AS-1187.A: CBC: useful when anemia or infection could explain fatigue, but nothing here points to it, and it does not explain slurred speech with cannabis use.
AS-1187.C: Pulmonary function test: would be relevant for chronic respiratory symptoms in a smoker, not for evaluating a mood and behaviour change.
AS-1187.D: Thyroid function test: part of the routine organic workup of new depression, but here the clear clue is substance use with slurred speech, so the drug screen comes first.

AS-1188.B: Medications cannot relieve a fixed valvular obstruction or change prognosis in AS; they are only supportive (e.g., heart failure treatment while awaiting intervention). A child with new exertional symptoms needs the obstruction relieved.
AS-1188.C: Reassurance with echo follow-up is appropriate only for mild or asymptomatic AS; new progressive exertional dyspnoea is a warning sign (risk of syncope and sudden death) and needs intervention.

AS-1190.A: Serial abdominal x-rays are not a screening tool; imaging is done only if there are signs of obstruction (bilious vomiting, distension). Duodenal atresia presents within hours with a double bubble rather than being found on routine films.
AS-1190.B: Pyloric stenosis presents at around 2 to 8 weeks with projectile non-bilious vomiting and is not a recognised Down syndrome screen; ultrasound is done only when symptoms suggest it.
AS-1190.D: The option says "necrotizing fasciitis" but means necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). Fecal calprotectin is not a newborn screen (levels are physiologically high in neonates), and NEC is a clinical and radiological diagnosis (feeding intolerance, bloody stool, pneumatosis), mainly in preterm infants.

AS-1200.B: Admission for observation is the plan after CT is negative or for low-to-intermediate risk head injury; it must not replace imaging when there is a seizure and drowsiness.
AS-1200.C: A short ER observation period suits minor head trauma with an isolated low-risk feature and normal mental status; it is unsafe when the child has seized and remains drowsy.
AS-1200.D: Discharge with head-injury instructions is only for low-risk minor head trauma with normal mental status and no seizure, vomiting or loss of consciousness.

AS-1202.B: IM ceftriaxone is a parenteral option for children who look toxic, are vomiting, cannot take oral medication, or are young infants; it is not needed for a well child with fever and dysuria.
AS-1202.C: IV ciprofloxacin is not first line in children (musculoskeletal adverse effects, resistance concerns) and is reserved for resistant or complicated infections; the IV route is also unnecessary here.

AS-1206.A: Avoiding punishment is one element of the behavioural approach, not a complete management plan on its own; the family centred package includes it.
AS-1206.B: Desmopressin comes after behavioural measures and the alarm in this ladder, and the intranasal form is no longer used for enuresis because of hyponatraemia and seizure risk (oral tablets or melts are used). It fits when rapid short term dryness is needed, such as a sleepover or camp.
AS-1206.C: The bed alarm with positive reinforcement is the second step in this ladder, used when behavioural measures fail in a motivated child and family.

AS-1215.B: More fluid is harmful here; overly rapid fluid replacement is linked to cerebral oedema, so the fluid rate should be reduced. Extra fluid fits shock or persistent hypovolaemia, not a falling conscious level with stable vitals.
AS-1215.C: Stopping insulin would let ketoacidosis rebound and does not treat raised intracranial pressure; insulin is continued, with dextrose added as glucose falls.
AS-1215.D: Dextrose is added to fluids when glucose falls to allow insulin to continue, but switching to dextrose fluids only does nothing for brain swelling. It would fit hypoglycaemia, which is excluded by the steadily declining but not low glucose.

AS-1219.A: Bronchiolitis (infant under about 2 years, viral prodrome, crackles and diffuse polyphonic wheeze) and bronchitis are acute infections, not a recurrent barky cough with a fixed monophasic wheeze.
AS-1219.C: Laryngomalacia is supraglottic, so it causes inspiratory stridor in early infancy that worsens supine and improves prone; the stem explicitly says no inspiratory stridor.
AS-1219.D: Asthma gives a polyphonic, diffuse expiratory wheeze that responds to bronchodilators, not a monophasic central wheeze with a brassy barky cough.

AS-1220.A: Feeding is normal and there is no vomiting, bloody stool or poor growth to suggest cow's milk protein allergy; routine formula changes are not recommended for colic.
AS-1220.B: Colic drops such as simethicone have no proven benefit, and anticholinergic drops are unsafe in young infants.
AS-1220.C: Respite may ease caregiver stress, but a baby sitter is not a treatment and does not teach the soothing and coping strategies that are the mainstay.

AS-1224.A: Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise, heart failure or acute severe symptoms; a stable child with chronic IDA corrects well with oral iron.
AS-1224.C: Bone marrow aspiration is invasive and not needed for typical nutritional IDA; it fits pancytopenia, blasts or suspected leukaemia or marrow failure.
AS-1224.D: Folate deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia; here the MCV is low, and multivitamins contain too little iron to treat established anaemia.

AS-1268B.B: Virology screening: right when a viral illness such as infectious mononucleosis is suspected; it does not confirm or exclude leukaemia.

AS-1327.A: Observation is only acceptable for intermittent deviation in early infancy (roughly the first 4 months); waiting until 24 months with a constant squint risks amblyopia and a missed tumour or cataract.

AS-1329.B: There is no required waiting interval after a local reaction; delaying 2 months leaves the infant unprotected and off schedule for no benefit.
AS-1329.C: Only a moderate or severe acute illness justifies postponing a vaccine; a mild URTI with low grade temperature does not, so waiting for it to resolve is a missed opportunity.
AS-1329.D: Dropping the pertussis component (DT) is reserved for true pertussis contraindications such as encephalopathy within 7 days of a previous dose; a local swelling is not one of them.

AS-1330.A: Waking a young child for a 3 AM meal treats the symptom, not the cause, and is impractical; the fix is to lower the excess basal insulin.
AS-1330.C: Rapid acting insulin before meals causes lows in the hours after meals; it would be reduced if the hypoglycemia were postprandial, not nocturnal.
AS-1330.D: Feeding extra carbohydrate to cover too much insulin leads to weight gain and erratic control; it does not correct the overdosed basal insulin.

AS-1331.A: The jaundice here is hemolytic (unconjugated) and the organomegaly is from extramedullary hematopoiesis, so LFTs do not identify the cause; they matter later for iron overload liver damage.
AS-1331.C: TSH is part of the work up of unexplained short stature (hypothyroid child: short, overweight, delayed bone age), but this child has a clear hemolytic picture that explains the growth failure.
AS-1331.D: Pituitary (growth hormone) testing fits a short child with low IGF-1, delayed bone age and otherwise normal exam, not one with pallor, jaundice and skeletal marrow expansion.

AS-1338.B: Caries is caused by free sugars and how often they are eaten, not carbohydrate in general; a blanket 'eat less carb' message is too narrow and misses the fruit and vegetable deficit.
AS-1338.C: Fluoride is a useful adjunct to strengthen enamel, but it does not remove the cause; the main counselling point when diet is clearly the problem is dietary change.

AS-1339.A: Observation fits caput succedaneum (soft, crosses sutures, maximal at birth and shrinking) or cephalohematoma (limited by sutures, stable baby); a growing swelling with pallor, lethargy and low Hb is life threatening.
AS-1339.B: IV antibiotics would be for sepsis or an infected cephalohematoma (fever, erythema); here the picture is acute blood loss, not infection.
AS-1339.C: The option text was not recalled; whatever it was (e.g. vitamin K or plasma), it cannot outrank volume and blood replacement in a shocked, anemic baby with normal coagulation.

AS-1341.A: 'Complication of pneumonia' is too vague to be the answer; the gas pins down the specific complication, which is failure of gas exchange.
AS-1341.B: ARDS needs bilateral opacities on imaging and a low PaO2/FiO2 ratio with PEEP, and early ARDS usually gives hypoxemia with low or normal CO2; neither imaging nor these criteria are provided here, while the marked CO2 retention fits respiratory failure.
AS-1341.D: A parapneumonic effusion would be suggested by dullness, reduced breath sounds and a fluid level on X-ray; it does not by itself explain a PCO2 of 70 with acidosis.

AS-1342.B: Meconium aspiration affects term or post term babies born through meconium stained liquor and causes persistent respiratory distress, not intermittent self limiting spells in a 28 week infant.
AS-1342.C: Airway malformations give obstructive symptoms (stridor, distress, feeding difficulty) that do not resolve with simple stimulation.

AS-1352.C: Ultrasound: lung ultrasound is a research or point of care tool, not the standard imaging for bronchiolitis; ultrasound is first line for things like intussusception or pyloric stenosis.
AS-1352.D: CT: high radiation and not indicated; reserved for complications or suspected structural lung disease, not a routine viral bronchiolitis.

AS-1354.A: Graves disease: low TSH with high T4, but the gland is non tender, ESR is normal, and there may be eye signs or diffuse uptake; it does not follow a URTI with neck pain.
AS-1354.C: Hashimoto thyroiditis: painless goiter with high TSH (hypothyroidism) and positive anti TPO antibodies; inflammatory markers are not raised.
AS-1354.D: Euthyroid sick syndrome: abnormal TFTs (low T3 first, sometimes low T4 and TSH) in a child who is acutely, seriously ill, such as in ICU; it causes no neck tenderness or raised ESR.

AS-1355.A: Antibiotics alone treat cellulitis (redness, warmth, no fluctuance); for an abscess they are only an adjunct after drainage when there is systemic illness, extensive surrounding cellulitis or immunosuppression.
AS-1355.C: A CBC does not change management of a localized abscess; it may help in a systemically unwell patient, but drainage is still needed.

AS-1367.B: Observation is acceptable only for small, asymptomatic lymphatic malformations; a 10 cm mass needs treatment.
AS-1367.C: Chemotherapy treats malignant neck masses such as lymphoma, which would give lymphoid cells on FNA rather than clear lymphatic fluid.
AS-1367.D: Radiotherapy has no role in a benign lymphatic malformation in a child and carries growth and malignancy risks.

AS-1373.A: Diaphragmatic hernia: bowel loops in the chest with mediastinal shift, a scaphoid abdomen and absent breath sounds on one side, often known antenatally; it gives severe distress from birth, not a CS related wet lung.

AS-1376.A: Neutrophils, high protein, low glucose: bacterial meningitis; it would be the answer with a toxic child, purpura, turbid CSF or organisms on Gram stain.
AS-1376.C: Normal leukocytes: makes meningitis unlikely; a child with neck stiffness, photophobia and altered consciousness is expected to have pleocytosis (a normal count with meningism suggests meningismus or very early disease).
AS-1376.D: Lymphocytes, high protein, low glucose: tuberculous (or fungal) meningitis, with a subacute course over weeks, TB exposure and cranial nerve palsies.

AS-1377.A: Neuropathic ulcers sit on pressure points of the sole (metatarsal heads, heel) in a warm foot with palpable pulses and loss of sensation, not on the lateral leg.
AS-1377.C: Malignancy (Marjolin ulcer) is suspected in a long-standing non-healing ulcer with rolled or everted edges; nothing here suggests it.
AS-1377.D: Arterial ulcers have absent pulses, a cold limb and a deep, punched-out, necrotic (black) base; the cold limb is missing here, but the absent pulse and black base point this way.

AS-1378.A: Diabetes mainly causes neuropathic ulcers over plantar pressure points (metatarsal heads, heel) and contributes to arterial disease; it is not the main driver of a medial gaiter ulcer.
AS-1378.B: Atherosclerosis causes arterial ulcers on distal pressure or trauma sites (toes, heel, lateral malleolus) with absent pulses and pain, usually in older smokers.

AS-1379.A: Neuropathic ulcers occur over plantar pressure points with loss of sensation, not on the lateral leg.
AS-1379.C: Malignant change (Marjolin ulcer) is considered in a long-standing non-healing ulcer with rolled edges or rapid growth; epithelialisation argues against it.
AS-1379.D: Arterial ulcers require absent or reduced pulses and a cold limb; here the pulses are intact and the leg is warm.

AS-1385.A: Colonoscopy is not needed for a typical midline fissure; it is indicated for atypical (lateral or multiple) fissures suggesting Crohn disease, or for red flags like age-related cancer risk.
AS-1385.C: Lateral internal sphincterotomy is for chronic fissures (over 6 weeks, sentinel tag) that fail medical therapy, not the initial step.
AS-1385.D: Antibiotics treat perianal abscess or infection (fever, fluctuant swelling, discharge), which is not present here.

AS-1474.A: Abdominal ultrasound: done to confirm the gallstone cause and assess the CBD, but it is an investigation, not the initial management; the diagnosis is already made on pain plus enzymes.

AS-1476.B: High-calorie formula treats inadequate calorie intake when the family feeds correctly, or when increased needs exist (e.g. cardiac disease); it does not fix the cause here (wrong preparation, poverty), and concentrated feeds in a newborn need supervision.
AS-1476.C: Teaching correct formula preparation is right when a stable infant with mild weight faltering has a simple preparation error and a family able to follow advice with close outpatient follow-up; the key here treats this newborn as needing admission first.

AS-1477.A: Supplemental oxygen with noninvasive positive pressure suits mild to moderate distress with adequate oxygenation; in severe MAS it is insufficient, and positive pressure without control can worsen air trapping and air leak (pneumothorax).

AS-1511.C: Conventional angiogram: invasive; now used mainly when an endovascular intervention is planned in the same sitting, not as the first diagnostic test.
AS-1511.D: MR angiogram: slower and less available in an acute setting; an alternative when CT contrast is contraindicated.

AS-1512.B: Above knee amputation: only for irreversible ischemia (fixed mottling, rigid paralysis) or a non-salvageable limb; at 4 hours this limb is still salvageable.
AS-1512.C: Catheter-directed thrombolysis: right for in situ thrombosis on atherosclerotic disease (acute on chronic ischemia) in a limb not yet severely threatened; it acts too slowly when motor function is already altered.
AS-1512.D: Heparinization and observation: heparin is the first step in all acute limb ischemia, but alone it does not restore flow to a threatened limb.

AS-1513.A: CT angiogram: the most appropriate investigation for acute limb ischemia when the limb is not threatened (no motor or sensory loss); here it would only delay revascularisation.
AS-1513.B: Vascular ultrasound: the initial imaging in a stable, viable limb; not when motor function is already altered.
AS-1513.C: Conventional angiogram: invasive and time-consuming; it may be done on the table during the procedure but must not delay surgery.

AS-1514.B: Femoral thrombectomy: the operation for a cardiac embolus (e.g. AF) lodged in a healthy artery; with no embolic source and diffusely diseased vessels it is not first choice.
AS-1514.C: Above knee amputation: only for irreversible ischemia or a non-salvageable limb; nothing here suggests that.
AS-1514.D: Heparinization and observation: heparin is the first step but on its own does not reopen an acutely occluded artery.

AS-1520.B: Keeping the baby NPO is a reasonable supportive measure in a tachypnoeic neonate to reduce aspiration risk, but it does nothing for the low saturation and is not the next step.
AS-1520.C: Surfactant is for surfactant-deficient RDS in a preterm infant (and sometimes for severe meconium aspiration after intubation); it is not first-line for a term or post-term baby who has only just been started on support.
AS-1520.D: Magnesium sulfate is a maternal drug for preeclampsia/eclampsia and fetal neuroprotection; it has no role as the next step in a hypoxic newborn.

AS-1526.B: Percutaneous biopsy: not used to work up a suspected gallbladder malignancy because it risks seeding the tract and a negative result does not exclude cancer; resection is diagnostic and therapeutic.
AS-1526.C: Cholecystostomy tube: a temporary drain for acute (often acalculous) cholecystitis in a patient too sick for surgery; it does not treat the cancer risk.
AS-1526.D: Observation: may be discussed only for an asymptomatic patient unfit for surgery; this patient has symptoms.

AS-1527.A: Oral antibiotics at home suit an older, well-looking child who tolerates oral intake; this young, lethargic, vomiting infant may not absorb oral drugs and is at risk of sepsis, so outpatient oral treatment is unsafe.

AS-1528.A: BP and HR would matter if you suspected systemic adrenaline or anaesthetic toxicity (palpitations, tachycardia, agitation, perioral tingling); the complaint here is local pain and numbness in the operated hand.
AS-1528.B: Doppler US is a second step once examination shows signs of ischemia or is equivocal; imaging never comes before a bedside vascular exam.

AS-1530.A: Angiodysplasia causes painless GI bleeding, typically in the elderly (often with aortic stenosis or CKD), but it does not produce varices or splenomegaly.
AS-1530.B: An arteriovenous shunt into the portal system (e.g. after trauma or liver biopsy) raises pressure in the whole portal system; nothing in this history suggests it, and pancreatitis points to splenic vein thrombosis instead.
AS-1530.D: Splenic artery aneurysm can complicate pancreatitis and may rupture with sudden hemorrhage, but it is an arterial lesion and does not create varices.

AS-1536.A: TTN is a term (usually CS) baby with mild, self-resolving tachypnoea and perihilar streaks with fluid in the fissures on X-ray; patchy infiltrates with air leak in a post-term baby admitted to NICU point to meconium aspiration instead.

AS-1536B.A: TTN is the classic term CS baby with mild, self-limiting tachypnoea and fluid in the fissures; here maternal diabetes, which delays lung maturity, is the clue the key uses to choose RDS over TTN.
AS-1536B.C: Tracheoesophageal fistula presents with frothy secretions, choking and cyanosis with feeds and failure to pass a nasogastric tube (coiled on X-ray), not with distress plus hyperinflation at birth.

AS-1538.B: Reassure the parents: right for mild laryngomalacia with normal growth and no apnea, which resolves by 1 to 2 years. Failure to thrive and apnea rule out simple reassurance here.
AS-1538.C: Start bronchodilators: laryngomalacia is a structural floppiness of the supraglottic larynx, not bronchospasm, so bronchodilators do nothing. They suit wheeze from asthma, not inspiratory stridor.
AS-1538.D: Order a chest X-ray: does not show the larynx or confirm laryngomalacia. Diagnosis is by direct laryngoscopy, done by ENT.

AS-1545.A: Encourage increased free water intake: a 3-month-old should get breast milk or formula only; extra free water risks hyponatremia. If diarrhea develops, oral rehydration solution is used, not plain water.
AS-1545.B: Administer the rotavirus vaccine: she is already up to date, and rotavirus vaccine is given on schedule, not as post-exposure prophylaxis. It would be right only for a missed scheduled dose within the age window.
AS-1545.C: Discontinue fruit juice at dinner: a 3-month-old should not be taking juice at all, and stopping juice does not prevent infection. Juice restriction matters for toddler's diarrhea, not exposure.

AS-1546.A: Check C1 inhibitor levels: tests for hereditary angioedema (recurrent non-itchy swelling, abdominal attacks), not recurrent infections.
AS-1546.B: Hemolytic complement (CH50): screens for complement deficiency, classically recurrent Neisseria (meningococcal) infections or lupus-like disease. It is a second-line test once immunoglobulins are normal, not the first screen for sinopulmonary infections with diarrhea.
AS-1546.C: Thrombocytopenia: a finding, not an investigation. Low platelets with eczema and infections would point to Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, which is not described here.

AS-1550.B: US Abdomen: suits a structural or surgical cause (mass, intussusception, obstruction), but there is no pain, mass or vomiting here. Irritability with diarrhea points to a systemic, endocrine cause.

AS-1553.A: Colonoscopy is for synchronous colonic pathology, e.g. after an appendiceal mass or abscess treated conservatively in an older patient; a small tip carcinoid does not require it.
AS-1553.C: Right hemicolectomy is reserved for carcinoid >2 cm, at the base of the appendix, or with mesoappendix or lymph node invasion (and for appendiceal adenocarcinoma).
AS-1553.D: Staging CT is used for larger or invasive tumours or adenocarcinoma; a 0.5 cm tip lesion does not need staging.

AS-1555.B: The anterior midline is not where this tract goes; anterior external openings (in front of the 3 to 9 line) track radially in a straight line to the nearest crypt, not to 12 o'clock specifically.
AS-1555.C: A lateral internal opening is not predicted by Goodsall's rule; anterior openings drain straight radially and posterior openings curve to the posterior midline.
AS-1555.D: A tract with no internal opening is a sinus, not a fistula; the stem states anal fistula, which by definition connects the anal canal to the skin.

AS-1557.A: X ray: usually done first as a baseline to exclude fracture or foreign body, but early osteomyelitis looks normal on X-ray; bone changes appear only after 1 to 2 weeks. It is the answer if the question asks for the initial study.
AS-1557.C: CT scan: shows cortical bone and sequestrum in chronic osteomyelitis but is poor for early marrow changes and exposes the child to radiation.
AS-1557.D: Nuclear scan: sensitive bone scan useful when the site is unclear or multifocal, or when MRI is unavailable; less specific than MRI and gives no anatomy of abscesses.

AS-1559.A: Systemic chemotherapy: the backbone treatment for the leukemia overall, but standard IV drugs reach the CSF poorly, so on its own it does not control CNS disease.
AS-1559.C: Anticonvulsant: controls the seizures symptomatically but does not treat the leukemic infiltration that is causing them.
AS-1559.D: Ventriculopleural shunt: a CSF diversion for hydrocephalus; it does not treat CNS leukemia and is not part of its management.

AS-1561.A: Fundoplication alone is an anti-reflux operation for GERD; in achalasia it is only added to a Heller myotomy, and on its own it would worsen the outflow obstruction.
AS-1561.C: Oral nitrates (isosorbide dinitrate) give weak, short-lived LES relaxation and are reserved for patients unfit for dilatation or surgery.
AS-1561.D: Botulinum toxin gives temporary relief and is reserved for elderly or high-risk patients unfit for definitive treatment, not a fit 34-year-old.

AS-1563.A: Cardiac catheterization: TOF is diagnosed by echocardiography; catheterization is not needed for diagnosis and is not the urgent step in a cyanotic neonate. It has a role in selected anatomy or interventions later.
AS-1563.C: Elective surgical repair: this is the definitive treatment, usually at 3 to 6 months of age, but it is not the immediate step for a cyanotic 6-day-old whose ductus is closing.

AS-1574.A: Pneumonia: usually brings fever, focal crackles or reduced breath sounds and focal consolidation, not diffuse wheeze in all lung zones.
AS-1574.C: Bronchial asthma: needs recurrent episodes and is not diagnosed in a 4-month-old with a first wheezy illness after a cold; it suits an older child with recurrent wheeze and atopy.
AS-1574.D: Viral croup: an upper airway illness of 6 months to 3 years with barking cough and inspiratory stridor, not expiratory wheeze.

AS-1575.B: Second dose of hepatitis B vaccine: the series continues on schedule at 1 to 2 months, not immediately. It does not replace HBIG, which gives the immediate passive protection the vaccine alone cannot.

AS-1576.A: Karyotyping & ultrasound: needed to confirm genetic sex and internal anatomy in ambiguous genitalia, but they do not treat a life-threatening salt-wasting crisis. They are the answer for a stable baby with ambiguous genitalia and normal electrolytes.

AS-1599.C: Angiodysplasia is the other main cause of painless bleeding in the elderly, typically recurrent and slower, and linked to aortic stenosis or CKD; when diverticulosis is also listed, diverticulosis is the more common cause of a massive bleed.

AS-1600.D: Unrecalled option: no content to judge; the distribution and dry, weepy skin already point to atopic dermatitis.

AS-1601.B: The diaper area is typically spared in atopic eczema because the skin stays moist; a diaper rash suggests irritant or candidal dermatitis.
AS-1601.C: The dorsum of the feet is not the typical infant site; the face, scalp and extensor surfaces are.

AS-1602.A: The upper back is not a characteristic eczema site in childhood.
AS-1602.B: The dorsal feet are not the typical childhood site; dorsal foot dermatitis in a child raises shoe contact dermatitis.
AS-1602.D: Scalp, cheeks and forehead are the infant pattern, not that of a school-age child.

AS-1603.D: Scalp and forehead are the infantile pattern.

AS-1627.C: Hypopituitarism is not a characteristic association of trisomy 21; it goes with midline defects such as septo-optic dysplasia.
AS-1627.D: Hyperthyroidism (Graves) is more frequent in Down syndrome than in the general population but far less common than hypothyroidism.

AS-1649.C: Croup gives a barking cough with inspiratory stridor, hoarseness and often fever and distress after a coryzal prodrome; here the noise is expiratory and the child is stable.

AS-1662.B: Laparotomy: right for positive FAST in an UNSTABLE patient (persistent hypotension or non-responder to fluids), or for peritonitis or evisceration; this card frames the patient as stable.

AS-1663.B: Homocystinuria gives a marfanoid habitus with lens dislocation too, but adds intellectual disability and thrombosis; this child has no mental retardation.
AS-1663.C: Loeys-Dietz causes aortic aneurysms with hypertelorism, bifid uvula or cleft palate and arterial tortuosity; lens dislocation is not a feature, so the eye clue does not fit.
AS-1663.D: Ehlers-Danlos gives skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility and easy bruising; it is not defined by tall stature, long arm span or lens problems.

AS-1668.A: Observation: acceptable only for minor, asymptomatic haemorrhoids; recurrent bleeding with anaemia needs treatment.
AS-1668.B: Band ligation: right for grade I to III internal haemorrhoids bleeding without anaemia, as an outpatient first procedure; here the anaemic, recurrent bleeding is treated as an indication for surgery.
AS-1668.D: Conservative: fibre, stool softeners and sitz baths fit grade I to II haemorrhoids with mild symptoms; it will not reliably control bleeding that has already caused anaemia.

AS-1672.A: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy starts in adolescence with morning myoclonic jerks of the arms and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, normal development and generalized polyspike-wave EEG; it does not occur at 7 months.
AS-1672.C: Lennox-Gastaut presents later (usually 1 to 8 years) with multiple seizure types (tonic, atonic, atypical absence), intellectual disability and slow spike-wave EEG; West syndrome often evolves into it.

AS-1673.A: Skin rash: suggests allergy, which is rare with amide anaesthetics like lidocaine (more often due to preservatives or ester agents); it is not part of the toxicity sequence.
AS-1673.B: Bradycardia: a cardiovascular sign that appears late, at higher plasma levels, after the CNS features.
AS-1673.C: Seizures: occur after the early prodromal symptoms as levels rise further; they are a sign of established, not early, toxicity.

AS-1674.A: AML is the second most common childhood leukemia; favour it when the stem gives myeloid clues such as Auer rods, gum infiltration or DIC.
AS-1674.B: CML is rare in children and presents with marked leukocytosis and splenomegaly in the chronic phase, not pancytopenia.
AS-1674.D: Acute non-lymphoblastic leukemia is another name for AML, which is less common than ALL in children.

AS-1908.D: A 24 month old walks up and down stairs, stacks about 6 blocks and puts 2 words together; this child shows none of these, so 24 months is too old.

AS-1909.B: At 9 months the child pulls to stand and says mama/dada nonspecifically; walking backwards, spoon use and 5 to 6 words are well beyond 9 months.
AS-1909.D: At 24 months the child climbs stairs, uses about 50 words and joins 2 words into phrases; 5 to 6 single words is too few for 24 months.

AS-1911.A: At 3 months the infant only holds the head up and follows objects; crawling, sitting and transferring are not possible yet.
AS-1911.B: At 5 months the infant reaches and rolls front to back, but hand to hand transfer, sitting and crawling are 6 month or later skills.
AS-1911.D: At 9 months a pincer grasp is present; its absence here means the infant is younger than 9 months.

AS-1912.A: At 4 weeks (1 month) social smiling and tracking through 180 degrees are not yet expected.
AS-1912.C: By 12 weeks (3 months) a prone infant lifts the head about 45 degrees with steadier control; here the head is raised only slightly, and every finding is already explained by the 8 week (2 month) milestones.
AS-1912.D: At 16 weeks (4 months) head lag has gone and the infant reaches for objects, both absent here.

AS-1913.A: Read as 4 weeks (1 month), a social smile and 180 degree tracking are not yet expected, and head lag is still marked; 4 years is plainly far too old.
AS-1913.B: 8 weeks (2 months) fits the social smile and tracking, but head lag is still present at 2 months; here it has resolved.
AS-1913.C: At 12 weeks head control is improving, but full disappearance of head lag on pull to sit is the 4 month (16 week) marker.

AS-1925.A: AML is the second most common childhood leukemia; favour it when the stem gives myeloid clues such as Auer rods, gum infiltration or DIC.
AS-1925.B: CML is rare in children and presents with marked leukocytosis and splenomegaly in the chronic phase, not pancytopenia.
AS-1925.D: Acute non-lymphoblastic leukemia is another name for AML, which is less common than ALL in children.

AS-1927.A: 6 months is too early for routine screening in a healthy term infant; earlier testing is only for risk factors such as prematurity or low birth weight.
AS-1927.C: 15 to 18 months is the repeat screen for children with an underlying condition causing anemia, not the initial universal screen.
AS-1927.D: 24 months is too late for the initial screen; iron deficiency could already have affected development.

AS-1929.A: Observation: acceptable only for a small, clearly non-toxic ingestion in a child who stays well with a normal serum iron; a large ingestion in a sick child needs active treatment, and the quiet latent phase can falsely reassure.
AS-1929.B: Gastric lavage: removes iron tablets poorly and does not treat the absorbed iron; it is not the definitive treatment once the child is symptomatic. Chelation is.

AS-1930.A: Haemodialysis: does not effectively remove iron itself; it is used to clear the iron deferoxamine complex if renal failure develops.
AS-1930.B: Gastric lavage: poor at removing iron tablets and not useful several hours later in a symptomatic child; it does not treat absorbed iron.
AS-1930.C: Oral activated charcoal: does not bind iron (nor lithium, alcohols or other metals), so it is ineffective here. Right for many other recent toxic ingestions.

AS-1933.C: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.
AS-1933.D: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-1934.A: Penicillin and rifampin for 1 week: penicillin does not clear nasopharyngeal carriage, and rifampicin prophylaxis is a short 2-day course, not a week. Right when only rifampicin for 2 days is offered for a child contact.
AS-1934.C: Penicillin for 1 week: penicillin treats invasive disease but does not eradicate carriage, so it is not used for prophylaxis. It is not right for any contact prophylaxis scenario.
AS-1934.D: IM ceftriaxone 4 doses: ceftriaxone is a valid prophylactic agent (preferred in pregnancy) but as a single IM dose; multiple doses is a treatment-type regimen, not prophylaxis.

AS-1935.A: Cefdinir 5 days BID: an oral cephalosporin for otitis, sinusitis or pharyngitis; it does not reliably eradicate nasopharyngeal meningococcal carriage and is not a prophylaxis regimen.
AS-1935.C: Ciprofloxacin 3 days BID: ciprofloxacin prophylaxis is a single oral dose, not a 3 day course, and exam keys favour rifampicin for a young child.
AS-1935.D: Ceftriaxone 5 days OD: ceftriaxone prophylaxis is a single IM dose (useful in pregnancy); a 5 day course is a treatment regimen, not prophylaxis.

AS-1936.A: Oesophageal atresia alone: would also coil the NG tube, but with no fistula the abdomen is gasless; gas in the stomach rules it out.
AS-1936.B: Tracheoesophageal fistula alone (H-type): the oesophagus is patent so the NG tube passes into the stomach; it presents later with recurrent chest infections and choking with feeds.
AS-1936.D: Omphalocele: a midline abdominal wall defect with bowel covered by a membrane at the umbilicus, visible at birth; it does not stop an NG tube.

AS-1936B.B: Choanal atresia: causes cyanosis at rest that improves with crying and a catheter cannot pass through the nose; the oesophagus is normal, so an NG tube passed by mouth would not coil.
AS-1936B.C: Tracheomalacia: a floppy trachea causes expiratory stridor and noisy breathing that worsens with crying or feeds; it does not block an NG tube.

AS-1937.A: Hiatus hernia: stomach herniating through the diaphragm causes reflux and vomiting, but the NG tube still passes into the stomach.
AS-1937.C: Tracheoesophageal fistula: an isolated (H-type) fistula leaves the oesophagus patent so the tube passes; it presents with choking and recurrent chest infections. A fistula would be added only if gas is seen in the stomach.
AS-1937.D: Choanal atresia: blocked posterior nasal passages cause cyanosis that improves with crying and failure to pass a catheter through the nose into the pharynx, not a tube coiled in the oesophagus.

AS-1938.B: Choanal atresia: causes cyanosis at rest that improves with crying and a catheter cannot pass through the nose; the oesophagus is normal, so an NG tube passed by mouth would not coil.
AS-1938.C: Tracheomalacia: a floppy trachea causes expiratory stridor and noisy breathing that worsens with crying or feeds; it does not block an NG tube.

AS-1939.B: Adenovirus: causes pharyngoconjunctival fever (fever, sore throat, conjunctivitis); a rash is non-specific and the occipital/postauricular node pattern is not typical.
AS-1939.C: Measles: high fever with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots before a rash that starts behind the ears/hairline; it is a much sicker child and nodes are generalized rather than postauricular-predominant.
AS-1939.D: Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19): "slapped cheek" facial redness then a lacy reticular rash on the limbs, with no prominent lymphadenopathy.

AS-1940.A: Measles: shares the face-to-body spread and coryza/conjunctivitis, but presents with a HIGH fever, a sick child and Koplik spots before a darker, confluent rash; none of that is described here.
AS-1940.C: Epstein-Barr virus: infectious mononucleosis gives exudative pharyngitis, fatigue, generalized nodes and splenomegaly; a rash mainly appears after amoxicillin, not as a face-to-trunk pink exanthem.

AS-1941.A: Toxic shock syndrome: high fever with hypotension and a diffuse sunburn-like erythroderma that later desquamates, often linked to tampons or wounds; no Koplik spots or 3Cs.
AS-1941.B: Gonococcal bacteremia: a few acral pustules with arthritis/tenosynovitis in a sexually active patient, not a viral prodrome with a face-to-limb rash.
AS-1941.D: Rubella: similar face-to-body rash but with only low-grade fever, a mild illness, postauricular nodes and no Koplik spots.

AS-1942.A: Chickenpox gives itchy vesicles in crops at different stages (macule, papule, vesicle, crust), centred on the trunk; this rash is maculopapular and blotchy, not vesicular.
AS-1942.C: Mumps causes fever with parotid (or submandibular) gland swelling and no rash; think of it when the swelling is in front of the ear, not a rash behind it.
AS-1942.D: Rubella also spreads face to body, but it is a mild illness with low-grade fever, discrete pink macules that fade quickly and posterior auricular/suboccipital nodes; a prominent cough with a confluent blotchy rash points to measles.

AS-1942B.B: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.
AS-1942B.C: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.
AS-1942B.D: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-1943.B: Rubella is a milder illness with discrete pink macules and posterior auricular/suboccipital nodes; it does not produce Koplik spots (any palatal petechiae are on the soft palate).
AS-1943.C: Parainfluenza causes croup: barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor; it has no buccal mucosal spots.
AS-1943.D: RSV causes bronchiolitis in infants: coryza followed by wheeze, crackles and respiratory distress; no Koplik spots or conjunctivitis-rash picture.

AS-1959.A: 1200 mL comes from applying 100 mL/kg to all 12 kg; the kilograms above 10 kg are counted at only 50 mL/kg.
AS-1959.C: 1500 mL would be maintenance for a 20 kg child (1000 + 500); it overestimates for 12 kg and would only fit if a deficit were being added.
AS-1959.D: 1000 mL is the maintenance for exactly 10 kg; it ignores the extra 2 kg (another 100 mL).

AS-1960.A: 1000 mL is maintenance only; it ignores the 5% deficit the stem tells you to replace.
AS-1960.B: 1250 mL adds only half the deficit (250 mL); the full 500 mL deficit belongs in the 24-hour total.
AS-1960.D: 1750 mL corresponds to a larger deficit (about 7.5%); the stem fixes the deficit at 5%.

AS-1968.A: This option is garbled in the recall and is not a recognized MSUD therapy; if it refers to nitisinone (NTBC), that drug is used for tyrosinemia type 1, not MSUD.
AS-1968.B: A phenylalanine-restricted diet treats phenylketonuria; MSUD needs restriction of the branched-chain amino acids, not phenylalanine.
AS-1968.C: Sodium benzoate and sodium phenylacetate are ammonia scavengers for hyperammonemia in urea cycle disorders, not the core treatment of MSUD.

AS-1970.A: Alzheimer disease is right when progressive memory loss for recent events interferes with daily activities (getting lost, repeating questions, failing to manage finances); none of that is described.
AS-1970.B: Lewy body dementia is right with fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, parkinsonism or REM sleep behavior disorder; none is present here.
AS-1970.D: Hypertensive encephalopathy is an acute emergency with severe hypertension, headache, confusion, seizures or visual changes; it is not a chronic mild memory complaint with a normal exam.

AS-1971.A: Vascular dementia: stepwise decline with focal deficits, stroke history and early executive dysfunction. Diabetes is a risk factor, but nothing focal or stepwise is described.
AS-1971.B: Alzheimer's dementia: starts with recent (episodic) memory loss; language problems come later. Here memory is explicitly normal.
AS-1971.D: B12 deficiency with cognitive features: metformin can lower B12, but deficiency gives global cognitive slowing or memory problems with neuropathy, ataxia or anemia, not an isolated loss of word meaning.

AS-1974.A: A lateral neck X-ray helps for croup (steeple sign), epiglottitis (thumb sign) or a radiopaque upper airway object; the foreign body here is bronchial, already shown on CXR, and seeds are radiolucent anyway.
AS-1974.B: Laryngoscopy visualizes only the larynx (used for laryngomalacia or laryngeal foreign bodies); it cannot reach or remove an object in the right main bronchus.
AS-1974.D: A tracheal procedure (for example tracheostomy) is reserved for an airway that cannot be secured otherwise; a stable child with a bronchial foreign body needs removal by rigid bronchoscopy.

AS-1974B.A: Subcutaneous epinephrine treats anaphylaxis (urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension); there is no allergic picture here, and adrenaline does not remove an obstructing object.
AS-1974B.C: Sending home with antipyretics fits a simple URTI; a choking history plus unilateral reduced air entry is a foreign body until proven otherwise, and missing it leads to recurrent pneumonia or bronchiectasis.

AS-1979.B: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.
AS-1979.C: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-1983.A: Nodule excision (enucleation) is not an oncological thyroid operation; it leaves uncertain margins and makes later completion surgery harder. Lobectomy is the minimum for a Bethesda 4 lesion.
AS-1983.C: Ultrasound surveillance suits a benign (Bethesda 2) nodule or a nodule below the FNA threshold; it is unsafe for an indeterminate lesion that may be follicular carcinoma.
AS-1983.D: Radiofrequency ablation is for cytologically benign, symptomatic nodules; it destroys tissue and gives no histology, so it is not used for possibly malignant lesions.

AS-1984.B: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.
AS-1984.C: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.
AS-1984.D: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-1985.A: A wound swab needs discharge; a dry wound gives nothing to culture. It is right when the wound is red, tender or discharging pus.
AS-1985.B: A throat swab has no role in postoperative fever without sore throat or pharyngitis symptoms.
AS-1985.C: Re-opening the wound treats a wound abscess or infected collection (pain, redness, swelling, pus); with a dry, quiet wound there is no indication.

AS-1985B.A: CBC and blood cultures are right when the patient looks septic (rigors, tachycardia, hypotension) or has a line or clear source; in a well, asymptomatic patient they are not the first step in this recall.
AS-1985B.B: Urinalysis and culture is right for fever with urinary symptoms or a catheter, typically on days 2 to 3; here the patient has no complaints.
AS-1985B.C: A chest X-ray is right for cough, dyspnoea, crackles or reduced breath sounds, mostly in the first days after surgery (atelectasis, pneumonia); there are no chest findings here.

AS-1986.A: A chest X-ray targets atelectasis or pneumonia, which cause fever on day 1 and days 2 to 3, or a patient with chest signs.
AS-1986.B: Blood cultures are right in a septic, unstable patient or with a central line; they come after clinical examination identifies the likely source.
AS-1986.D: Medication review fits a well patient with a clean wound and no source found; it is considered after the wound and abdomen are assessed.

AS-1987.B: Throat culture is the back-up test when the rapid strep test is negative in a child with a suggestive picture; after a positive rapid test it only delays treatment.
AS-1987.C: Reassurance fits viral pharyngitis (mild hyperemia, coryza, cough, negative rapid test); confirmed GAS needs antibiotics to prevent rheumatic fever and suppurative complications.
AS-1987.D: This option was not recalled, so it cannot be judged; with a confirmed positive rapid test, antibiotic treatment remains the next step.

AS-1989.B: Hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcaemia is the classic endocrine feature of DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome, not Down syndrome.
AS-1989.C: Hypopituitarism is not a characteristic association of trisomy 21; it goes with midline defects such as septo-optic dysplasia.
AS-1989.D: Hyperthyroidism (Graves) is more frequent in Down syndrome than in the general population but far less common than hypothyroidism.

AS-1998.A: Coarctation gives upper limb hypertension with weak or delayed femoral pulses and is linked to Turner syndrome; it does not cause fixed split S2, plethoric lungs or a superior axis.
AS-1998.B: PDA gives a continuous machinery murmur with bounding pulses; S2 is not fixed split and the axis is not superior. Think PDA in prematurity or congenital rubella.
AS-1998.C: An isolated VSD gives a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border without fixed S2 splitting or a superior axis. It is the second most common lesion in Down syndrome.

AS-1999.A: Hypothyroidism: thyroid hormone is needed for skeletal maturation, so bone age is markedly delayed.
AS-1999.B: Chronic renal failure: chronic illness slows growth and delays bone age.
AS-1999.C: Familial short stature: bone age equals chronological age; the child is simply following short parents.

AS-2000.A: Down syndrome is associated with AVSD (endocardial cushion defect), then VSD; coarctation is not its signature lesion.
AS-2000.C: Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) is mainly associated with VSD and PDA, with overlapping fingers and rocker bottom feet.
AS-2000.D: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) is mainly associated with VSD, ASD and PDA, with midline defects such as cleft lip and palate.

AS-2001.A: SLE is rare at age 4, usually affects adolescent girls, and tends to cause malar rash and cytopenias, not dependent purpura with normal platelets.
AS-2001.B: HUS follows bloody diarrhea and causes hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury; here there is no diarrhea and platelets are normal.
AS-2001.D: Kawasaki disease needs fever for 5 days or more with conjunctivitis, mucosal and extremity changes and lymphadenopathy; this child is afebrile.

AS-2002.B: Discharge is safe only for a well infant feeding adequately with normal saturation; hypoxia and tachypnea make it unsafe here.
AS-2002.C: Bronchiolitis is viral (mostly RSV); antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of secondary bacterial infection. Crackles are expected in bronchiolitis and do not mean pneumonia.
AS-2002.D: Bronchodilators and steroids are not routinely recommended in bronchiolitis because they do not improve outcomes; they belong to asthma management.

AS-2006.A: Mixed dementia: needs evidence of both Alzheimer and cerebrovascular disease (strokes, stepwise decline, imaging changes); nothing vascular is given.
AS-2006.C: Multi-infarct dementia: stepwise deterioration with focal neurological signs and vascular risk factors; here the course is smooth and slow.
AS-2006.D: Major depressive disorder: can mimic dementia (pseudodementia) but has prominent low mood, anhedonia and subacute onset; it does not cause a steady 2-year memory decline with aggression.

AS-2010.A: Trans-abdominal ultrasound is the initial imaging in acute pancreatitis to look for gallstones; the key rejects it here because the question targets biochemical confirmation of a late presentation with normal serum amylase.
AS-2010.C: CT is reserved for an unclear diagnosis or for severity and complications, ideally after 48 to 72 hours; it is not the initial investigation.
AS-2010.D: Analysis of aspirated gastrointestinal fluid has no diagnostic role in acute pancreatitis.

AS-2018.A: IV antibiotics alone do not clear an established abscess; they are an adjunct to drainage and suit only small collections (under about 4 cm).
AS-2018.B: IV paracetamol only lowers the temperature and does nothing for the pelvic abscess.
AS-2018.C: Abdominal washout (relaparotomy) is for generalised peritonitis, multiple collections, an unstable patient or failed percutaneous drainage; this is a localised collection.

AS-2019.A: Tracheostomy does not remove the compressing clot and is slow through a swollen, distorted neck; evacuation of the haematoma comes first.
AS-2019.B: Close observation is dangerous with stridor; a tense haematoma can obstruct the airway within minutes.
AS-2019.C: Percutaneous drainage fails because a haematoma is clotted blood, and it delays decompression.

AS-2020.A: Caecal volvulus occurs in younger patients with a congenitally mobile caecum, without the long laxative history; the dilated caecum often moves toward the epigastrium or left upper abdomen with small bowel dilatation, so the chronic constipation is the decisive clue against it.
AS-2020.B: The rectum is fixed in the pelvis without a mobile mesentery, so it does not twist.
AS-2020.D: Transverse colon volvulus is very rare and would give a central or upper abdominal mass rather than a left-sided mass with chronic constipation.

AS-2021.A: Platelets: the count of 90 is low but well above the level usually needed for major surgery (around 50); platelets are given when the count is below that or there is platelet dysfunction.
AS-2021.B: Cryoprecipitate: mainly supplies fibrinogen (plus factor VIII and vWF); it is right for low fibrinogen or DIC, not for a raised INR from global factor deficiency.
AS-2021.D: Packed red blood cells: Hb 90 is above the usual restrictive threshold of 70 in a stable patient and does not correct bleeding risk; give RBCs for active major bleeding or Hb below threshold.

AS-2022.A: Klatskin tumour: obstructs at the hilum above the cystic duct, so the gallbladder is collapsed and not palpable; right when US shows only intrahepatic dilatation with a shrunken gallbladder.
AS-2022.C: Common bile duct stone: the gallbladder is usually chronically inflamed and fibrosed so it does not distend, and jaundice tends to fluctuate with pain; right in fluctuating jaundice with biliary colic or cholangitis.
AS-2022.D: Hepatocellular carcinoma: causes a hepatocellular or mixed picture in a cirrhotic liver, not a distended gallbladder; think of it with cirrhosis, hepatomegaly and raised AFP.

AS-2023.A: Klatskin tumour: a hilar block gives intrahepatic dilatation only with a collapsed gallbladder; here the extrahepatic ducts and gallbladder are distended.
AS-2023.C: Mirizzi's syndrome: a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck compresses the common hepatic duct, usually with a contracted, inflamed gallbladder and pain; right in a gallstone patient with dilatation above the cystic duct level only.
AS-2023.D: Common bile duct stone: can dilate both duct systems, but the scarred stone-bearing gallbladder rarely distends and jaundice is usually painful and fluctuating.

AS-2024.A: Klatskin tumour: a hilar block gives intrahepatic dilatation only with a collapsed gallbladder; here the extrahepatic ducts and gallbladder are distended.
AS-2024.C: Mirizzi's syndrome: a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck compresses the common hepatic duct, usually with a contracted, inflamed gallbladder and pain; right in a gallstone patient with dilatation above the cystic duct level only.
AS-2024.D: Common bile duct stone: can dilate both duct systems, but the scarred stone-bearing gallbladder rarely distends and jaundice is usually painful and fluctuating.

AS-2025.B: Mirizzi's syndrome: due to a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck, so the gallbladder contains stones and is inflamed with RUQ pain; right in a gallstone patient with CHD compression.
AS-2025.C: Gallbladder cancer: shows a gallbladder mass or wall thickening, often with gallstones, rather than a simply collapsed empty gallbladder.
AS-2025.D: Periampullary tumour: a distal block dilates both intra- and extrahepatic ducts and distends the gallbladder (Courvoisier).

AS-2026.A: Do on table angiogram: takes time and needs a stable patient; angiography and embolisation are for persistent arterial bleeding after temporary control.
AS-2026.C: Infra renal aortic clamp: does not control venous plexus bleeding and is not the first step; aortic clamping is reserved for failure of packing with ongoing haemorrhage.
AS-2026.D: Supra celiac aortic clamp: a rescue step when the patient becomes profoundly hypotensive despite packing (the follow-up scenario), not the initial manoeuvre.

AS-2027.A: Do on table angiogram: too slow for a patient at 60/40; angiography and embolisation suit a patient stable enough to wait.
AS-2027.B: Infra renal aortic clamp: needs dissection close to the retroperitoneal and pelvic haematoma and gives less proximal control; it is used for elective aortic work or bleeding with time to expose the infrarenal aorta.
AS-2027.D: Remove the packs and repair the injury: removing packs in a hypotensive patient restarts uncontrolled bleeding; repair comes after inflow control and resuscitation.

AS-2028.A: MRI breast: a problem-solving or high-risk screening tool (e.g. known BRCA, dense breasts, occult primary), not the first test for a palpable lump.
AS-2028.B: Core needle biopsy: the definitive tissue diagnosis and the step after imaging; it becomes the answer once mammography or US shows a suspicious (BI-RADS 4 or 5) lesion.
AS-2028.D: Fine needle aspiration cytology: gives cytology only, cannot distinguish invasive from in situ disease or give receptor status; core biopsy has replaced it for solid lumps.

AS-2029.A: Oxygen mask: adequate for a hypoxic trauma patient with a protected airway, but here the airway is threatened by the neck wound and saturation is already below 88%.
AS-2029.B: Tracheostomy: a formal, slower surgical airway for elective or semi-elective settings, not the emergency step.
AS-2029.C: Cricothyroidotomy: the emergency surgical airway when intubation fails or is impossible (severe maxillofacial trauma, cannot intubate cannot oxygenate).

AS-2030.A: US abdomen (FAST): the bedside test for the unstable patient to look for free fluid; it misses many solid organ, bowel and retroperitoneal injuries.
AS-2030.C: Diagnostic laparoscopy: used mainly for suspected diaphragmatic injury or equivocal penetrating trauma in a stable patient, not as first evaluation.
AS-2030.D: Exploratory laparotomy: for unstable patients with positive FAST, peritonitis, evisceration or gunshot wounds, none of which is present.

AS-2031.A: Checking and correcting glucose is part of care in an IUGR neonate, but IV dextrose treats hypoglycemia, not the cause of refractory hypothermia; it is right when the glucose is documented low.
AS-2031.C: Simply turning up the warmer and reassuring ignores the warning sign; adjusting the environment is right only when the baby is cold because of an inadequate thermal environment.
AS-2031.D: Skin-to-skin contact is a good first measure for routine thermal care of a stable newborn, but it does not address hypothermia that persists despite active warming.

AS-2033.A: ECG is a reasonable screening test and helps for arrhythmic causes (long QT, WPW), but it cannot define a structural lesion behind a murmur; it would be the key if the scenario pointed to an arrhythmia, for example palpitations with a normal exam.
AS-2033.C: Chest X-ray is nonspecific for heart size and lungs and cannot diagnose HCM or valve stenosis.
AS-2033.D: Reassurance fits a typical vasovagal faint at rest with an innocent murmur; exertional syncope with a murmur is never innocent.

AS-2034.B: CT: avoided in children because of radiation; when imaging is needed in a child, ultrasound is first line, and CT is kept for equivocal cases or complications such as abscess.
AS-2034.C: Discharge patient with given instructions: reasonable only for a very low-risk patient with reliable follow-up, but the question asks how to avoid missing the diagnosis, which needs in-hospital serial assessment.

AS-2036.A: Epiglottitis is now rare and presents abruptly with high fever, a toxic look, drooling and tripod position, not a mild low grade prodrome.
AS-2036.B: Acute tonsillitis causes sore throat, fever and dysphagia but does not usually cause stridor unless complicated by a large abscess.

AS-2039.A: Accepting a confined lifestyle is unnecessary because equal asthma control is possible with a portable inhaler and spacer.
AS-2039.B: Arranging a caregiver does not fix the real problem (the device) and isolates the child from family life.
AS-2039.D: A portable nebulizer adds cost and still is not needed, since an inhaler with spacer is equally effective and already portable.

AS-2043C.A: Parenteral iron is reserved for failure of oral iron: malabsorption (e.g. celiac or IBD), true intolerance or persistent nonadherence. Nothing here suggests oral therapy has failed.
AS-2043C.C: Folic acid deficiency gives a megaloblastic <i>macrocytic</i> anemia; this smear is microcytic and hypochromic.
AS-2043C.D: B12 deficiency is also macrocytic and may bring neurological signs; it does not cause spoon nails or a microcytic picture.

AS-2044B.A: Pneumothorax is suggested by sudden deterioration, asymmetric breath sounds or ventilation; here distress is present from birth with no air leak clue.
AS-2044B.B: Apnea of prematurity means pauses in breathing, usually starting after the first day or two, not continuous tachypnea with recession at 30 minutes.
AS-2044B.D: TTN is a <i>term</i> cesarean baby with milder distress and fluid in the fissures on CXR that resolves on its own; severe hypoxia in a 27 week infant points to RDS.

AS-2045.B: Folate deficiency is uncommon in breastfed infants and routine folate supplementation is not recommended; folate is a pregnancy supplement for the mother.
AS-2045.C: Vitamin D is recommended for breastfed infants from birth as routine prophylaxis, but the specific risk this stem highlights (late, slow weaning at 9 months) is iron depletion.
AS-2045.D: Solids should be introduced gradually, one new food a few days apart to watch for reactions; rushing the pace does not reliably fix iron intake and is not the recommended advice.

AS-2048.A: Renal artery stenting treats renovascular hypertension (renal artery stenosis: resistant hypertension, abdominal bruit, asymmetrical kidneys, rise in creatinine on ACE inhibitor). It does not explain episodic adrenergic symptoms like sweating and palpitations.

AS-2049.A: BCG mainly reduces severe childhood forms of TB and does not prevent infection after close household exposure, so reassurance alone is unsafe.
AS-2049.B: Waiting for PPD results delays protection in a child under 5; the early test can be negative during the window period, so prophylaxis is started now and the test repeated later.
AS-2049.C: Multidrug therapy is for <i>active</i> TB, which has not been shown here (asymptomatic contact, CXR not yet done); this would be right if the CXR or symptoms showed active disease.

AS-2050.A: Reduced appetite for solids is common in any sick child; only inability to take <i>fluids</i> or persistent vomiting would push toward admission.
AS-2050.B: Fever is a nonspecific feature of the infection and alone does not indicate severity or need for admission.

AS-2052.A: Abdominal X-ray is the <i>initial</i> test (dilated loops, air-fluid levels) but it cannot show the cause or ischemia; it is the answer when the question says "best initial".
AS-2052.B: Ultrasound is limited by gas-filled bowel in adults; it is the first choice in young children (intussusception) or pregnancy.
AS-2052.D: Colonoscopy is not used to diagnose acute obstruction (insufflation risks perforation); it is used later, e.g. to evaluate a suspected colonic tumour or to decompress sigmoid volvulus.

AS-2053.B: CT abdomen is the confirmatory, most informative test; it is the answer when the question asks "most appropriate" or "confirm", not "initial".
AS-2053.C: Ultrasound is poor in adults because bowel gas blocks the view; it is the initial test in toddlers (intussusception) or pregnancy.

AS-2054.A: Colonoscopy is avoided in acute diverticulitis (perforation risk); it is done 6 to 8 weeks after recovery to exclude colon cancer.
AS-2054.C: Plain X-ray only shows free air or obstruction; it cannot diagnose diverticulitis or its abscess.
AS-2054.D: Ultrasound is operator dependent and less accurate for diverticulitis; it is preferred for gynecologic causes, pregnancy or children.

AS-2057.A: Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer overall and is also linked to Hashimoto, but it is the second association taught; it is the answer when the stem gives radiation exposure, a solitary nodule with lymph node spread, or psammoma bodies.
AS-2057.B: Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, is linked to MEN 2/RET mutation and raised calcitonin, not to autoimmune thyroiditis.
AS-2057.C: Anaplastic carcinoma is a rapidly growing tumour of elderly patients, often arising from long-standing goiter or differentiated cancer; it has no specific link to Hashimoto.

AS-2058.A: Follicular carcinoma presents as a solitary nodule in a normal-sized gland and spreads hematogenously (bone, lung); it does not cause rapid diffuse enlargement in a Hashimoto gland.
AS-2058.B: Medullary carcinoma is a C-cell tumour with raised calcitonin and MEN 2 links, usually a nodule rather than a diffuse goiter.
AS-2058.C: Anaplastic carcinoma also grows fast with compressive symptoms, but it typically affects elderly patients with a long-standing goiter and is a hard, fixed mass; the Hashimoto background points to lymphoma instead.

AS-2059.A: Hemorrhagic goiter (bleed into a nodule or cyst) causes sudden, often painful enlargement over hours to days, without weight loss or a link to Hashimoto.
AS-2059.C: Papillary carcinoma is usually a slow-growing nodule ± cervical nodes; rapid diffuse growth with B symptoms is not its typical course.
AS-2059.D: Subacute thyroiditis presents with a painful, tender gland after a viral illness, fever, transient hyperthyroidism and raised ESR; it is not linked to long-standing Hashimoto or weight loss from malignancy.

AS-2066.A: Surgical resection of the aganglionic segment is the <i>definitive</i> treatment, done electively after decompression and biopsy confirmation, not as an immediate first step; a total colectomy is not the standard operation.
