AS-2068.A: Kawasaki disease needs fever for 5 days or more with <i>non exudative</i> conjunctivitis, lip and tongue changes, extremity changes, rash or a cervical node; exudative tonsillitis and a sibling cluster point to infection instead.
AS-2068.B: Group A strep causes exudative tonsillitis with tender anterior nodes but not conjunctivitis; the conjunctivitis and rapid spread to a 2 year old favor a virus.
AS-2068.D: Infectious mononucleosis gives exudative tonsillitis with prominent lymphadenopathy, fatigue and often hepatosplenomegaly, mostly in adolescents; none of these are present and conjunctivitis is not typical.

AS-2069.A: Neisseria meningitidis is a gram negative <i>diplococcus</i> (kidney bean pairs), often with a petechial or purpuric rash; it is not a pleomorphic coccobacillus.
AS-2069.C: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a gram <i>positive</i> lancet shaped diplococcus; it is the commonest cause in vaccinated children and adults but does not match this Gram stain.

AS-2070.A: ANA is the sensitive <i>screening</i> test for SLE; it stays positive regardless of activity and its titer does not track flares.
AS-2070.B: Rheumatoid factor is linked to rheumatoid arthritis and is nonspecific; it is neither diagnostic of nor a monitor for SLE.

AS-2072.A: Antibiotics have no role in acute pancreatitis unless an infection is confirmed (e.g. infected necrosis), and ERCP is reserved for confirmed gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction; neither is described here.

AS-2076.A: Immediate appendectomy is right for uncomplicated appendicitis or for free perforation with generalized peritonitis; with a contained abscess it risks a difficult, morbid operation.
AS-2076.C: Antibiotics and observation alone fit an appendiceal phlegmon (inflammatory mass without pus). A localized abscess needs the pus drained, and the classic plan then removes the appendix later because the abscess can recur and, in older patients, an underlying appendiceal or cecal tumour must be excluded.

AS-2078.A: Conservative care (sitz baths, analgesia, stool softeners, topical agents) is the usual choice when a thrombosed external hemorrhoid presents after about 72 hours, when the pain is already settling.
AS-2078.B: Rubber band ligation is for grade I to III <i>internal</i> hemorrhoids above the dentate line; banding the somatically innervated external tissue causes severe pain.
AS-2078.D: Needle aspiration does not evacuate the clotted thrombus and is not a standard option; when early intervention is chosen it is excision (or incision and evacuation) of the clot.

AS-2080B.A: Azithromycin (a macrolide) does not reliably cover Gram negative uropathogens such as E. coli and is not used for UTI.
AS-2080B.C: IV ceftriaxone is for infants younger than about 2 months, toxic appearance, vomiting or inability to tolerate oral intake; this infant is alert and feeding well.
AS-2080B.D: IV cefepime is a broad spectrum antipseudomonal agent reserved for severe or resistant infection; a mild febrile UTI does not need it.

AS-2084.A: Aortic injury: deceleration injury that shows a widened mediastinum and hypotension, not free air in the chest and neck.
AS-2084.C: Pulmonary embolism: a clot in the pulmonary arteries causing sudden dyspnea and hypoxia, usually days after trauma or immobility; it never produces air in the tissues.
AS-2084.D: Cardiac contusion: blunt injury to the myocardium presenting with arrhythmias or ECG changes and troponin rise, not with air leak.

AS-2085.A: Tension pneumothorax: explains the pneumothorax but not the pneumomediastinum and cervical emphysema; it would show tracheal shift, raised JVP and hypotension.
AS-2085.B: Open pneumothorax: requires an open chest wall wound (sucking chest wound), which is absent after this blunt injury.
AS-2085.D: Esophageal injury: can also cause pneumomediastinum, but it is rare in blunt trauma and presents with chest pain, dysphagia and sepsis (or follows vomiting in Boerhaave), not immediate respiratory distress with pneumothorax.

AS-2086.A: Reassurance fits mild asymptomatic hypermetropia in young children; this child is symptomatic, so correction is needed.
AS-2086.B: Concave (minus) lenses diverge light and correct myopia, where the image focuses in front of the retina.
AS-2086.D: Patching treats amblyopia (after refractive correction), contact lenses are not first line in a young child, and artificial tears treat dry eye.

AS-2087.A: ABG: may support the assessment of shock but does nothing to stop the bleeding and delays definitive control.
AS-2087.B: Diagnostic laparoscopy: reserved for stable patients with an unclear diagnosis; pneumoperitoneum worsens hemodynamics in shock and the view is poor with massive bleeding.

AS-2088.B: Rotavirus causes acute watery diarrhea with vomiting and fever, mainly under 2 years, lasting days rather than a month.
AS-2088.C: Salmonella causes acute febrile diarrhea, often with blood or mucus and systemic upset, not a month of daytime-only stools in a well child.

AS-2089.A: Croup gives barking cough and stridor in a usually well looking child after a URTI; cyanosis, drooling and tripod position are not expected and would signal failure.
AS-2089.B: Epiglottitis classically gives drooling, tripod position and toxicity, but it starts abruptly in a previously well child without a viral prodrome and is now rare after Hib vaccination.

AS-2091.B: Postponing is for a moderate or severe acute illness (e.g. high fever, ill child); a simple cold does not justify delay.
AS-2091.C: Withholding live vaccines is for immunosuppression or pregnancy (and timing after blood products), not for a minor URTI.

AS-2093.A: Anal fissure: also bleeds bright red blood, but the key feature is sharp, severe pain during and after defecation, usually with constipation.
AS-2093.B: Perianal abscess: a painful, tender perianal swelling with fever and leukocytosis, not bleeding with stool.
AS-2093.D: Fistula: presents with persistent perianal discharge from an external opening, often after a previous abscess, not bleeding with defecation.

AS-2097.A: Papillary carcinoma: arises from follicular cells, spreads by lymphatics to cervical nodes, and is followed with thyroglobulin, not calcitonin.
AS-2097.B: Follicular carcinoma: also a follicular cell tumor followed with thyroglobulin; it spreads hematogenously to bone, lung and liver.
AS-2097.D: Anaplastic carcinoma: a rapidly growing hard mass in an elderly patient with compressive symptoms; it is not a calcitonin secreting tumor.

AS-2098.B: HSV-1 in children causes gingivostomatitis: painful vesicles and ulcers on the lips, gums and mouth with cervical nodes, not crops of truncal vesicles.
AS-2098.C: Smallpox is eradicated; its lesions were all at the same stage and concentrated on the face and limbs (centrifugal).
AS-2098.D: Measles gives a maculopapular (not vesicular) rash starting on the face with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots.

AS-2099.A: Bronchoscopy is not used to diagnose complications of meconium aspiration; it has a role mainly for suspected airway foreign body or structural airway lesions.
AS-2099.C: Lung ultrasound can show parenchymal changes or pneumothorax but cannot assess pulmonary artery pressure or ductal shunting.
AS-2099.D: ECG may show right ventricular strain but is neither sensitive nor specific for PPHN.

AS-2100.B: Fistulogram: an outdated contrast study that poorly shows tracts in relation to the sphincters; it has been replaced by MRI.
AS-2100.C: Rectal US: endoanal ultrasound is an acceptable alternative where MRI is unavailable, but it is operator dependent and less accurate for complex or high tracts.
AS-2100.D: Colonoscopy: used to look for underlying Crohn's disease when complex fistulas occur without a known diagnosis; it does not map the fistula tracts themselves.

AS-2100B.B: MRI: the gold-standard imaging to map fistula tracts and find abscesses; it is the answer when Crohn's is already known and the question asks for fistula anatomy or a suspected abscess.
AS-2100B.C: Fistulogram: an older, less accurate way to outline a tract, largely replaced by MRI and endoanal ultrasound.
AS-2100B.D: US: endoanal ultrasound can assess simple tracts and sphincters, but transabdominal US does not diagnose Crohn's or map complex perianal disease.

AS-2103.A: Infantile spasms (West syndrome) occur in infants with clusters of flexor or extensor spasms, developmental regression and hypsarrhythmia on EEG.
AS-2103.B: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy starts in adolescence with morning myoclonic jerks after waking, and generalized polyspike and wave on EEG.

AS-2105.A: Apgar score reflects transition and asphyxia at birth; it does not explain hemolysis recurring across siblings.
AS-2105.B: Birth weight does not explain a familial hemolytic anemia with jaundice.
AS-2105.C: Type of delivery may relate to bruising or cephalohematoma, but not to recurrent hemolysis requiring exchange transfusion in siblings.

AS-2107.A: Immediate surgical drainage: reserved for collections not reachable percutaneously or failed drainage; excessive for a 1 cm collection in a stable patient.
AS-2107.C: CT-guided drainage: indicated for collections about 4 × 4 cm or larger, or a small one that fails antibiotics.
AS-2107.D: Conservative: observation alone without treatment is inadequate when fever suggests infection; this patient needs antibiotics.

AS-2108.A: Take medications that help with weight loss: a valid adjunct (for example at BMI 30, or 27 with comorbidities), but loss is modest; once BMI is 35 or more with diabetes after failed lifestyle therapy, surgery is the recommended option.
AS-2108.C: Diet: she has already tried diet without success; repeating it does not address her eligibility for more effective treatment.

AS-2111.B: tTG-IgA (with total IgA) is the right first test when there are celiac symptoms (diarrhea, distension, failure to thrive), or as screening of an at-risk relative once older (about 2 to 3 years); this toddler is well and young, so testing can wait.
AS-2111.C: Starting a gluten free diet without serology and biopsy is wrong: it is unnecessary in a healthy child and causes false negative results if testing is later needed.

AS-2112.A: Reassurance misses a high-risk child; normal growth does not exclude celiac disease, which can be silent in relatives.
AS-2112.C: Starting a gluten-free diet before testing is wrong: gluten withdrawal makes serology and biopsy falsely negative, and diet is only started after the diagnosis is confirmed.

AS-2117.A: Blood transfusion: kept for a symptomatic infant (poor feeding, tachycardia, heart failure) or a severe acute hemolytic crisis; this baby is well with a normal exam. It is the main competing option because Hb 70 is lower than the usual nadir.
AS-2117.B: Iron supplement: a term baby has enough iron stores for the first 4 to 6 months, so iron deficiency is not the cause at 53 days; iron is right for an older infant on cow's milk with microcytosis.
AS-2117.D: Folic acid: there is no clue to megaloblastic anemia or folate deficiency; folate is given in chronic hemolytic states with high red cell turnover, not physiological anemia.

AS-2118.A: Hemolytic: right if there is a trigger (fava beans, infection, oxidant drugs) with jaundice, pallor and dark urine or hemoglobinuria; the known G6PD deficiency alone is the trap.
AS-2118.B: Inflammatory: needs an active infection or inflammatory illness, which is not described in this newborn.
AS-2118.C: Of chronic disease: needs a long-standing chronic illness (renal, inflammatory, malignancy); it does not fit a newborn.

AS-2118B.A: Haemolysis: right with a trigger plus jaundice, pallor and dark urine or hemoglobinuria; here the urine is clear and the exam normal, so the known G6PD deficiency is a distractor.
AS-2118B.B: Iron deficiency: term infants have adequate iron stores until about 4 to 6 months; it fits an older infant on cow's milk with low MCV.
AS-2118B.D: Anaemia of chronic disease: needs a chronic inflammatory, renal or malignant illness, which this well infant does not have.

AS-2120.B: Give Desmopressin: oral desmopressin is used when the alarm fails or is unsuitable, or for quick short-term dryness (sleepovers, camps); relapse after stopping is common, and the intranasal form is avoided because of hyponatremia.

AS-2124.A: Give him racemic epinephrine: nebulized epinephrine treats moderate to severe croup (barking cough, stridor in a child who looks well); in epiglottitis it does not fix the obstruction and the procedure can upset the child and precipitate complete obstruction.
AS-2124.B: dexamethasone: the mainstay of croup, which presents with a barking cough after URTI symptoms in a non-toxic child; it does not secure the airway in a toxic child with epiglottitis.

AS-2127.A: Echo: done later to look for structural heart disease or tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (for example in recurrent or prolonged SVT); it does not diagnose the rhythm and is not the first test.

AS-2132.B: Study at home: again an avoidance strategy that removes the child from peers and school and entrenches the problem.
AS-2132.C: Give anxiety medication: drugs (SSRIs) are reserved for severe or refractory anxiety after behavioral therapy fails, not first line in a young child.

AS-2135.A: Amoxicillin: Shigella resistance to ampicillin and amoxicillin is widespread and amoxicillin is poorly effective even for sensitive strains; not recommended.
AS-2135.C: Azithromycin: a recognised oral option for Shigella in children and the drug of choice for Campylobacter dysentery; it is the strongest competitor here (see note).
AS-2135.D: Metronidazole: covers anaerobes and protozoa (Giardia, Entamoeba, C. difficile), not Shigella.

AS-2136.A: Repeating blind catheterization against a known stricture risks a false passage and urethral trauma. A repeat attempt suits a simple technical failure, not a fixed narrowing.
AS-2136.C: The gonorrhea was in the past and the urinalysis is normal; the problem is the scar it left. Antibiotics are right for active urethritis with discharge.
AS-2136.D: Alpha blockers relax prostatic smooth muscle and help BPH in older men; they cannot open a fibrotic urethral stricture in a 38-year-old.

AS-2140.B: EBV: causes infectious mononucleosis with exudative tonsillitis, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes; parotid swelling is uncommon.
AS-2140.C: CMV: usually a mild mononucleosis-like illness or congenital infection (deafness, periventricular calcifications); parotitis is rare, mainly in immunocompromised patients.

AS-2140B.A: Skin: mumps does not typically cause a rash; think measles, rubella or varicella for viral rashes.
AS-2140B.B: Lungs: pneumonia is not a feature of mumps; measles is the viral exanthem with pneumonia as a leading complication.
AS-2140B.C: Testes: orchitis is the commonest complication in post-pubertal males (it can affect fertility), but it is rare before puberty, so it is the answer only if the stem asks about an adolescent or adult male's complication.

AS-2141.A: 40 would need an ICP of 25 with this MAP; it comes from an arithmetic slip, not from MAP minus ICP.
AS-2141.C: 60 is the lower CPP target in severe head injury, a tempting number to recall, but it is not what these values give.
AS-2141.D: 70 would need a MAP of 85; it is the upper end of the usual CPP target range, not the calculated value.

AS-2143.A: Ductography is a second-line test for pathological discharge when mammogram and ultrasound show no lesion; it is not the first investigation.
AS-2143.C: Ultrasound is first-line under 30 (dense breasts) and in pregnancy, and complements mammogram at this age; at 45 it is not the lead test.
AS-2143.D: CT is used to stage distant metastasis, not to evaluate the breast itself.

AS-2145.B: Negative-pressure therapy is for large, deep or heavily exuding wounds, or slow or stalled healing (e.g. after debriding a necrotic wound); a wound already granulating well does not need it.
AS-2145.C: Primary closure is done at the end of the operation; a wound deliberately left open is closed later only by planned delayed primary or secondary closure. This one is healing well by secondary intention, so simple dressings continue.
AS-2145.D: No redness, purulence or fever means no infection; antibiotics would treat nothing.

AS-2146.A: Obesity is a GERD risk factor in older children and adults, not the recognized high-risk group in infancy.
AS-2146.C: Pertussis causes paroxysmal cough with post-tussive vomiting and apnea, but a past pertussis infection is not a recognized risk factor for infant reflux or Sandifer syndrome.
AS-2146.D: Hernia repair is not linked to GERD; post-anesthesia apnea risk after hernia repair relates to prematurity itself, not reflux.

AS-2147.A: Wound infection shows pain, redness, warmth, swelling, purulent discharge and fever, usually from postoperative day 4 to 5; none of these are present.
AS-2147.B: Abnormal healing would show gaping or dehiscence, non-healing, or excess scar (hypertrophic scar or keloid); this wound has closed edges and healthy tissue.

AS-2151.A: Inferior dislocation (luxatio erecta) holds the arm abducted overhead, not adducted at the side.
AS-2151.B: Anterior dislocations hold the arm slightly abducted and externally rotated, usually after a fall on an outstretched arm.
AS-2151.C: Subcoracoid is the most common anterior type overall, but it also holds the arm in abduction and external rotation and is not the seizure-associated type.

AS-2152.A: At 12 months imitation and 1 to 3 words fit, but naming a body part and a 6 to 10 word vocabulary come later.
AS-2152.B: At 15 months a child points to body parts and has a few words, but this many single words with pretend play fits 18 months.
AS-2152.D: At 24 months expect 2-word phrases ("me milk") and about 50 words; this child uses single words only.

AS-2153.A: Surgery comes after staging, and a "10×12 cm" tumour is too large for wide local excision; phyllodes larger than 8 cm needs mastectomy.
AS-2153.B: Whole body PET is not the standard staging test for phyllodes; contrast CT is used.
AS-2153.D: Phyllodes is a stromal tumour that does not respond to hormonal therapy, so receptor testing does not guide management.

AS-2154.B: Option not recalled by the source. Plausible distractors would be ongoing GI losses or inadequate dosing, but the stem stresses maximum replacement, which points to a magnesium deficit.
AS-2154.C: Option not recalled by the source. Alternatives such as hyperaldosteronism or diuretic use would need a supporting history; a postoperative patient refractory to K replacement is classic hypomagnesaemia.
AS-2154.D: Option not recalled by the source. Mechanical obstruction or anastomotic leak would explain distension but not potassium that refuses to rise with full replacement.

AS-2155.A: Loop diuretics increase urinary calcium and magnesium loss and would worsen the hypocalcaemia. Thiazides are used in chronic hypoparathyroidism to reduce hypercalciuria, not acutely here.
AS-2155.B: Recombinant PTH is reserved for chronic hypoparathyroidism not controlled by calcium and active vitamin D; a reversible cause such as low magnesium must be excluded first.
AS-2155.D: An IV bolus of potassium chloride is never given (risk of cardiac arrest), and potassium is not the problem in this scenario.

AS-2156.A: Citrate in stored blood can cause hypocalcaemia after massive transfusion, but it presents with perioral tingling, tetany, arrhythmia and hypotension rather than diffuse oozing; it is the answer when the question asks for the commonest metabolic complication of massive transfusion.
AS-2156.C: An acute haemolytic reaction gives fever, hypotension, back pain and haemoglobinuria soon after starting a unit; nothing here suggests it, while the volume transfused points to dilution.
AS-2156.D: Von Willebrand disease is congenital with a lifelong bleeding history; new bleeding after 15 units in ICU is acquired.

AS-2159.B: Staining using iodine: Lugol iodine (Schiller test) is used on the cervix and vagina to outline abnormal epithelium; it does not diagnose psoriasis.
AS-2159.C: Clinical diagnosis is sufficient: true for typical psoriasis in everyday practice, but the question asks for a definitive diagnosis, which needs histology; right when the lead in is 'how is it usually diagnosed'.
AS-2159.D: Potassium hydroxide skin scraping: confirms fungal infection (hyphae or yeast) such as tinea cruris or candidiasis; useful to exclude a mimic, not to prove psoriasis.

AS-2165.A: A ventral hernia usually has a positive cough impulse and is reducible; here the cough impulse is negative and the onset is acute and painful after strain.
AS-2165.B: An appendicular mass follows days of appendicitis with fever and leukocytosis, is not linked to lifting, and is intra-abdominal so it becomes impalpable when the wall is tensed.
AS-2165.C: An extraperitoneal lipoma is a slowly growing, soft, non-tender lump, not an acutely painful swelling after strain.

AS-2168.B: Clinical clearance (NEXUS or Canadian C-spine rules) needs an alert, sober, examinable patient without distracting injury; it is the answer only in a conscious low-risk patient.
AS-2168.C: MRI is for suspected ligamentous or cord injury, neurological deficit with normal CT, or persistent concern after CT; it is not the first study to clear the spine.
AS-2168.D: AP and lateral X-rays miss a significant proportion of injuries and are inferior to CT; they are used only where CT is unavailable.

AS-2170.A: Multi-infarct dementia: stepwise cognitive decline with focal deficits; memory loss would not wax and wane with mood.
AS-2170.B: Alzheimer's disease: insidious, progressive memory loss over years, with mood change appearing later; not a 4-week mood syndrome with mood-linked forgetfulness.
AS-2170.C: Hypothyroidism: can cause low mood and slowing, but typically with weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation; here he is losing weight.

AS-2174.B: Proteus is a urease producer (alkaline urine, struvite stones), more typical in uncircumcised boys or stone disease; it is a less common cause than E. coli.
AS-2174.C: Klebsiella is a Gram negative cause of UTI but much less common, seen more in hospital acquired or complicated infections.
AS-2174.D: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a Gram positive coccus causing pneumonia, otitis and meningitis, not a urinary pathogen with Gram negative bacilli.

AS-2176.B: Auditory hallucinations: hearing voices without a stimulus; he describes seeing her, not hearing her.
AS-2176.C: Episode of disorganized thoughts: a disorder of thought form (derailment, loose associations, incoherent speech); his answer is clear and goal directed.
AS-2176.D: Delusion: a fixed false belief (a thought problem), not a sensory perception; it would be a delusion if he believed she was alive without perceiving her.

AS-2177.A: Delusional thinking: a fixed false belief. Believing the food is poisoned could be a secondary delusion, but the question describes the voices themselves, which are a perceptual disturbance.
AS-2177.B: Visual hallucination: would require seeing things that are not there; he hears, not sees.
AS-2177.C: Disorganized thinking: loose associations or incoherent speech; nothing about his thought form is described.

AS-2178.A: IV antibiotics alone do not penetrate necrotic tissue; they are added for cellulitis, sepsis or osteomyelitis, but never replace debridement.
AS-2178.B: Primary closure of a contaminated, necrotic pressure wound under tension in an immobile patient will break down; closure suits a clean, fresh wound.
AS-2178.C: A graft will not take on a necrotic or exudative bed; grafting is done later once healthy granulation tissue is present.

AS-2179.A: Primary repair without debridement leaves necrotic tissue in the wound and will fail; it suits only a clean, fresh wound.
AS-2179.B: Primary closure of a discharging, contaminated pressure wound will break down; debridement must be followed by open management first.
AS-2179.C: A primary skin graft will not take on an exudative, poorly vascularised bed; grafting comes later once granulation tissue forms.

AS-2184.B: Rolling prone to supine appears around 4 months, so it is present at 6 months but is an earlier milestone, not the one that characterizes this age.
AS-2184.C: Mature (pincer) grasp is a fine motor skill appearing around 9 to 12 months; at 6 months the grasp is a palmar (raking) grasp.

AS-2186.A: CT abdomen is for the haemodynamically stable trauma patient; an unstable patient should not go to the scanner and instead gets resuscitation and FAST.
AS-2186.B: Brain MRI has no role in acute trauma resuscitation; head injury is imaged with CT once the patient is stabilised.
AS-2186.C: Observation is unsafe in a hypotensive trauma patient; it suits a stable patient with a normal assessment.

AS-2189.A: Immediate repair (however the closure is reinforced) with uncontrolled ascites risks ascitic leak, wound breakdown and recurrence; immediate surgery is right only for a strangulated, incarcerated or ruptured hernia.
AS-2189.B: Laparoscopic mesh repair is not the priority while ascites is uncontrolled; mesh in a patient with ascites carries risk of leak and infection, and the timing problem remains.
AS-2189.D: A single paracentesis followed directly by open repair does not control the ascites, which reaccumulates quickly and leaks through the wound; repair should follow sustained ascites control.

AS-2191.A: Blood tests (smear for schistocytes, LDH, haptoglobin, Coombs) confirm microangiopathic hemolysis and are part of the workup, but they do not identify the triggering infection.
AS-2191.B: Urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria reflecting the renal injury, but it is nonspecific and does not establish the etiology.

AS-2192.A: Pneumonia usually presents with fever, tachypnea and focal crackles or bronchial breathing; diffuse wheeze without fever points away from it.

AS-2203.A: Insert a Foley catheter: contraindicated when urethral injury is suspected, because blind passage can convert a partial tear into a complete one. Right only after a normal retrograde urethrogram.
AS-2203.B: Obtain a KUB CT: CT assesses kidneys, bladder and pelvic organs but does not reliably show the urethra. A CT cystogram is used for suspected bladder injury once the urethra is cleared.
AS-2203.D: Proceed to exploratory laparotomy: indicated for an unstable patient with positive FAST, peritonitis or evisceration. Nothing here points to an intraperitoneal injury needing surgery.

AS-2204.B: US abdomen: FAST looks for free fluid and is the tool for the unstable patient; it misses pancreatic, duodenal and hollow viscus injuries, which are exactly what a handlebar blow causes.
AS-2204.C: Reassure: worsening pain with abdominal wall bruising days after trauma is a red flag for a missed internal injury, so discharge without imaging is unsafe. Right only for a well child with a normal exam and no bruising.

AS-2205.A: Antibiotics alone: enough for mastitis without a collection (no fluctuation). Once pus is seen on ultrasound it must be drained; antibiotics are an adjunct.
AS-2205.C: Incision and drainage: reserved for an abscess of about 5 cm or larger, multiple abscesses, thinned, ischemic or necrotic overlying skin, or failure of repeated aspiration.

AS-2208.B: Acute cholecystitis: fever, prolonged RUQ pain and Murphy sign, but bilirubin is usually normal or only mildly raised because the common bile duct is patent. Marked conjugated jaundice points to the duct.
AS-2208.C: Biliary colic: transient postprandial pain with no fever, no leukocytosis and normal liver tests. Five days of pain with fever excludes it.
AS-2208.D: Hepatic (gallbladder) mucocele: cystic duct obstruction with a distended, often non-tender palpable gallbladder filled with mucus; it does not cause fever with leukocytosis and conjugated jaundice.

AS-2209.B: Homocystinuria causes lens dislocation (downward), marfanoid habitus, intellectual disability and thrombosis, not cataract with liver failure and E. coli sepsis.
AS-2209.C: Methylmalonic acidemia causes severe anion gap metabolic acidosis with ketosis and hyperammonemia, but not cataract, Fanconi syndrome or E. coli sepsis.
AS-2209.D: Maple syrup urine disease presents with poor feeding, encephalopathy and burnt sugar smelling urine; it lacks cataract and hepatomegaly.

AS-2214.A: Antibiotic alone: right for uncomplicated diverticulitis or a small abscess (roughly under 3 to 4 cm). A 6.8 cm collection needs drainage.
AS-2214.B: Exploration: right for purulent or feculent peritonitis (Hinchey III/IV), hemodynamic instability, or failure of percutaneous drainage. None of these is present.

AS-2218.B: Repeat CT: suitable for a small EDH in a fully alert child with no focal deficit, managed with close neuro observation. A dilated pupil removes the option of waiting.
AS-2218.C: Mannitol: a temporizing measure to lower intracranial pressure while theatre is arranged; it does not treat the bleed and is not the definitive answer.

AS-2220.A: Central precocious puberty is driven by early activation of the HPG axis, so LH and FSH are raised into the pubertal range (especially after GnRH stimulation); non-raised gonadotropins with high estradiol argue against it.

AS-2223.A: Ct chest: shows bronchiectasis or structural lung damage once CF is known, but it cannot diagnose CF and does not explain the steatorrhea.
AS-2223.B: Brocho lavage: used to obtain airway cultures (for example Pseudomonas) or to evaluate infection in established lung disease; it is invasive and not a diagnostic test for CF.

AS-2224.B: Oral contraceptive pills: not used to start puberty; induction uses low-dose estrogen increased gradually, and combined pills come later only for maintenance.
AS-2224.C: Estrogen therapy: needed in Turner syndrome to induce breasts and menses, so it is part of her care; the key ranks it after GH because early full-dose estrogen closes the growth plates and limits final height.
AS-2224.D: Gonadotropin replacement therapy: useless here because the problem is primary ovarian failure (streak gonads) with high FSH and LH; gonadotropins are for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

AS-2225.B: give VZIG: right for high-risk contacts (immunocompromised child, newborn whose mother has varicella from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery, preterm infants in hospital); a healthy term 2-month-old is not in these groups.
AS-2225.C: give chicken box vaccine: live varicella vaccine is not licensed under 12 months, so it cannot be used for post-exposure prophylaxis in a 2-month-old.
AS-2225.D: give prophylaxis antibiotics: varicella is viral; antibiotics are only for secondary bacterial skin infection of established lesions.

AS-2225B.A: Observe for a few days: lets the post-exposure window close; observation alone fits a healthy infant too young for the vaccine, not a 6-year-old who can be vaccinated.
AS-2225B.B: give IVIG: passive immunisation is for high-risk contacts (immunocompromised, pregnant, at-risk newborns) when VZIG is unavailable; a healthy child gets the vaccine instead.
AS-2225B.D: I don't remember but irrelevant: a placeholder from the recall, not a management option.

AS-2228.B: Inadequate dietary intake: being nil by mouth contributes little over a short postoperative period because the kidney conserves potassium; it is a cause in prolonged starvation or malnutrition.
AS-2228.C: Renal potassium wasting due to aldosterone: this is the mechanism through which NG suction lowers potassium (volume loss and alkalosis activate aldosterone), but it is secondary; primary aldosteronism would show hypertension with no GI loss.
AS-2228.D: Intraoperative fluid shift: transcellular shifts (insulin, beta agonists, alkalosis) are transient and would not explain persistent hypokalemia during ongoing high-volume suction.

AS-2230.C: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-2234.A: Fluid restriction and diuretics: supportive measures that may accompany treatment, but they do not close the ductus and so do not address the cause of the congestion.
AS-2234.C: Urgent surgical ligation of the ductus: reserved for a significant PDA that fails medical closure or when NSAIDs are contraindicated (for example renal failure, active bleeding, NEC).
AS-2234.D: Prostaglandin E1 infusion: keeps the ductus OPEN; it is right for duct-dependent lesions such as TGA or critical coarctation, and here it would worsen the shunt.

AS-2235.A: Chromosomal analysis: the karyotype confirms a suspected chromosomal syndrome such as trisomy 21; it is the keyed answer for the duplicate of this question, but not for this recall.
AS-2235.B: Metabolic screening: routine newborn screening for inborn errors and congenital hypothyroidism; it is not targeted at a dysmorphic face or growth restriction.
AS-2235.D: Skeletal survey: right when skeletal dysplasia (short limbs, abnormal bones) or non-accidental injury is suspected; facial dysmorphism alone does not call for it.

AS-2236.A: Fine needle aspiration cytology: gives cells only, cannot distinguish invasive from in situ cancer and has a higher non-diagnostic rate; useful for aspirating cysts or sampling axillary nodes.
AS-2236.C: Excisional biopsy: right when core biopsy is non-diagnostic or discordant with imaging, or for lesions such as suspected phyllodes; not the first tissue test.
AS-2236.D: Short-interval follow-up imaging: the plan for BI-RADS 3 (probably benign). Using it for BI-RADS 4 would delay a possible cancer diagnosis.

AS-2238.A: 4: would require one component to score 0 (for example no heart rate, apnea or a limp baby); none is absent here.
AS-2238.C: 7: would need two components at the maximum of 2 (for example heart rate above 100 or a vigorous cry); every sign here is only partial.
AS-2238.D: 9: describes a nearly normal vigorous newborn with only acrocyanosis; this baby is bradycardic, weak and poorly flexed.

AS-2239.A: Simple mastectomy treats large phyllodes tumors or selected cancers; removing one breast for a bilateral risk marker makes no sense. Bilateral risk-reducing mastectomy is only a patient choice in very high-risk women (e.g. BRCA carriers).
AS-2239.B: Adjuvant radiotherapy follows breast-conserving surgery for DCIS or invasive cancer; classic LCIS is not irradiated.
AS-2239.C: Adjuvant chemotherapy is for invasive cancer with systemic risk; LCIS is non-invasive and has no metastatic potential.

AS-2240.B: Emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy treats acute cholecystitis; done alone it leaves the obstructing CBD stone, so the duct must be cleared first.
AS-2240.C: MRCP only diagnoses; it is chosen when the chance of a CBD stone is intermediate (e.g. abnormal LFTs with a normal-calibre duct). Here a dilated duct plus jaundice already makes a stone highly likely and therapy is needed.
AS-2240.D: Percutaneous cholecystostomy drains the gallbladder in acute cholecystitis when the patient is too sick for surgery; it does not relieve a blocked CBD.

AS-2241.A: Give ivig: passive immunisation is for high-risk, non-immune contacts after exposure; this child is well and already immune.
AS-2241.B: Give vaccine now: right for a non-immune child at 12 to 15 months or a child with an uncertain history; a provider-verified episode makes vaccination unnecessary.
AS-2241.C: Give vaccine at 2 years: there is no reason to delay or schedule a varicella dose in a child who is already immune.

AS-2243.B: Penicillin allergy: vaccines do not contain penicillin, so it is not a contraindication; only anaphylaxis to a vaccine component or a prior dose is.
AS-2243.C: Pharmacological therapy: current antibiotics or most other drugs do not stop vaccination; the exceptions are immunosuppressive therapy (avoid live vaccines) and recent blood products (delay MMR and varicella).

AS-2246.A: 2 months is too early for rooting; the asymmetrical tonic neck (fencing) reflex is the one that fades around 2 to 3 months.
AS-2246.C: 6 months is when the Moro and palmar grasp reflexes disappear, not rooting.
AS-2246.D: Rooting should be long gone by 8 months; this is around when the parachute reflex appears (a protective reflex that persists for life).

AS-2248.A: Initiate low-dose haloperidol therapy: reserved for severe agitation that endangers the patient or staff after non-drug measures fail; not routine supportive care.
AS-2248.C: Apply physical restraints to prevent accidental falls: restraints increase agitation, injury and delirium duration; use only as a last resort for immediate danger.
AS-2248.D: Place the patient in a dark, completely isolated room: sensory deprivation and isolation worsen disorientation; the room should be well lit by day with familiar people present.

AS-2249.A: Failure to thrive is weight faltering from poor intake or illness; it would show weight dropping across centiles first, not an isolated low IGF-1 with a delayed bone age.
AS-2249.B: Constitutional delay also has a delayed bone age, but IGF-1 is appropriate for bone age and growth velocity is normal, with a family history of late puberty; it would be right if labs were normal and a parent was a late bloomer.

AS-2250.A: Ulcerative colitis gives continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum upward with no skip areas, and usually bloody diarrhea with urgency; it would be right with bloody stools and diffuse friable mucosa.
AS-2250.C: Celiac disease is a small bowel disease seen on duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy) with positive tTG antibodies; it does not produce colonic ulceration.
AS-2250.D: Pseudomembranous colitis follows antibiotic use and shows yellow-white plaques (pseudomembranes) from C. difficile, with an acute course rather than 3 months of weight loss.

AS-2254.B: Abdominal X-ray is less sensitive for small amounts of free air; it is the first film when bowel obstruction (distension, vomiting, colicky pain) is the main concern.
AS-2254.C: Abdominal CT is the confirmatory test when plain films are inconclusive or to assess pancreatitis severity, but it is not the initial step.
AS-2254.D: Abdominal US is first for biliary pain or gallstone pancreatitis; gas limits it and it is poor for detecting free air.

AS-2257.B: Familial short stature has a bone age equal to chronological age and normal IGF-1; it would be right if bone age were 9 with normal labs and short parents.
AS-2257.C: Nutritional failure to thrive affects weight before height and the child is usually thin with abnormal exam; here weight and height track together and the exam is normal.
AS-2257.D: Constitutional delay also shows a delayed bone age, but IGF-1 is normal for bone age and there is a family history of late puberty; the low IGF-1 points away from it.

AS-2258.A: IV acyclovir treats HSV and serious varicella infections; it has no activity against measles virus. It would be right for neonatal HSV or varicella in an immunocompromised child.
AS-2258.C: Antibiotics do not treat a viral illness; they are used only when a secondary bacterial complication such as pneumonia or otitis media develops.

AS-2260.B: A HIDA scan assesses biliary excretion (for example biliary atresia or acute cholecystitis); it does not address chronic liver disease with encephalopathy.
AS-2260.C: 24-hour urinary copper is a supportive diagnostic test for Wilson disease (with low ceruloplasmin and Kayser-Fleischer rings), but the question asks for management, not diagnosis.

AS-2263.A: MRI pelvis is too slow for acute trauma and is used later to plan delayed urethral reconstruction, not for the initial diagnosis.
AS-2263.B: CT with contrast is used in a stable patient to assess pelvic and visceral injuries (and CT cystography for bladder injury), but it does not reliably show the urethra; the urethrogram answers the question raised by meatal blood.
AS-2263.C: Pelvic angiography (with embolisation) is for an unstable patient with ongoing pelvic arterial bleeding; this patient is stable.

AS-2265.A: ASA 1 is a normal healthy patient with no systemic disease; this patient has several.
AS-2265.B: ASA 2 is mild, well-controlled systemic disease (e.g. controlled DM or HTN alone); his poorly controlled HTN and prior MI push him higher.
AS-2265.D: ASA 4 is severe disease that is a constant threat to life, such as an MI within the last 3 months, ongoing ischaemia or decompensated heart failure; his MI was 2 years ago and he is stable.

AS-2266.B: Surgical rib fixation is reserved for selected flail chest (failure to wean from the ventilator, severe chest wall instability or deformity), not as the next step in a patient breathing on his own.
AS-2266.C: A chest tube treats a pneumothorax or haemothorax; preserved breath sounds give no reason to place one.
AS-2266.D: Needle decompression is for tension pneumothorax (absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, hypotension, tracheal shift), none of which is described.

AS-2267.A: Angiography (or CT angiography) is for soft signs only, such as a diminished pulse or small stable hematoma with a viable limb; with an ischaemic, paralysed foot it wastes time.
AS-2267.C: Fasciotomy is often added at the time of revascularisation to prevent reperfusion compartment syndrome, but on its own it does not fix the arterial injury causing the ischaemia.
AS-2267.D: Observation for spasm is never acceptable after penetrating trauma with ischaemic signs; a pulse deficit must be assumed to be an arterial injury.

AS-2269.A: Colon cancer usually causes slow, occult or low-volume bleeding with anaemia, weight loss or a change in bowel habit; a sudden clot-forming bleed without these features is less typical, though colonoscopy is still needed at this age.
AS-2269.C: IBD presents with bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain, urgency and often weight loss, usually in younger patients; isolated painless bleeding does not fit.

AS-2271.B: Pharyngeal erythema is a common, nonspecific finding in viral respiratory infections and by itself does not change management; it would matter only with features of bacterial pharyngitis (exudate, tender nodes, no cough).

AS-2274.B: Thyroidectomy is planned only after cytology: lobectomy for Bethesda IV (and some V), total or near-total thyroidectomy for Bethesda VI. Operating on imaging alone skips the diagnosis.
AS-2274.C: This option was not recalled; other plausible distractors are a TSH level (the first test in any nodule workup, scan if TSH is low) or ultrasound follow-up, which suits nodules without suspicious features.

AS-2276.A: L3-L4 roots supply the anterior thigh, knee and medial leg (knee extension, knee reflex); they do not reach the lateral calf or lateral foot.
AS-2276.B: L4-L5 roots cover the medial leg (L4) and the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot (L5); the lateral foot (S1) would be spared.
AS-2276.D: S1-S2 roots cover the lateral foot (S1) and the posterior thigh and calf (S2); the lateral calf is L5, so this pair misses it.

AS-2276B.B: L4-L5: compresses the L5 root, giving numbness of the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot / big toe with weak big toe extension; the deficit here is medial, not dorsal.
AS-2276B.C: L5-S1: compresses S1, giving numbness of the lateral foot, little toe and sole with a reduced ankle reflex; that is the lateral version of this question.
AS-2276B.D: S1-S2: sacral roots supply the posterior calf, heel and lateral border of the foot (sural territory), not the medial leg.

AS-2285.A: At 2 months term infants still have iron stores from birth, so routine screening is not useful; physiological anemia of infancy is expected around this age.
AS-2285.B: At 4 months, stores are usually still adequate; 4 to 6 months is when iron supplementation or iron-rich complementary foods are started, especially in breastfed infants, not when screening is done.
AS-2285.D: 18 months is the optional repeat screen for at-risk children, not the universal first screen.

AS-2289.A: FFP corrects clotting factor deficiency and may be added if a coagulopathy is found, but it does not replace lost red cells; it is not the primary treatment for hemorrhagic shock with Hb 7.5.
AS-2289.B: "Immediate resuscitation" is too vague; option C states the specific resuscitation this baby needs (volume plus red cells for blood-loss shock).

AS-2290.B: ERCP and sphincterotomy: treats choledocholithiasis or cholangitis, signalled by jaundice, raised bilirubin and ALP and a dilated CBD; here the stones and inflammation are in the gallbladder itself.

AS-2294.A: Amoxicillin to prevent endocarditis: reserved for high-risk patients (prosthetic valve, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease) undergoing high-risk procedures such as dental work with gingival manipulation; MVP does not qualify.
AS-2294.B: Cefazolin to prevent wound infection: right for clean-contaminated surgery or clean surgery with an implanted prosthesis/mesh; a thyroidectomy is clean and implant-free.
AS-2294.D: Both cefazolin and amoxicillin: neither indication is present, so combining them only adds side effects and resistance.

AS-2298.A: Albumin: may be added when very large crystalloid volumes are needed, but it does not reverse vasodilatory hypotension; the priority at a MAP in the 50s is a vasopressor.
AS-2298.B: 2 L crystalloid: fluid is right in early hypotension or oliguria with normal BP (fluid challenge); after 6 L and a CVP of 10, more fluid adds edema and lung injury without restoring pressure.
AS-2298.D: Furosemide: the low urine output is from renal hypoperfusion, not overload; a diuretic would worsen hypotension. Right only for confirmed fluid overload in a perfused patient.

AS-2306.A: Immediate intubation: indicated for SpO2 below 88%, GCS 8 or less, or aspiration risk, or a high cervical injury with failing breathing; a T6 lesion spares the diaphragm and he is breathing well.
AS-2306.C: CT: the best imaging to clear spinal and abdominal injuries, but only after the patient is hemodynamically stabilised; a BP of 70/40 belongs in resuscitation, not the scanner.

AS-2316.A: IV vasodilators: the ischemia is mechanical compression by eschar, not vasospasm; dilators cannot overcome an external constriction and may drop systemic BP.
AS-2316.C: IV fluids, burn dressing, limb elevation: routine care for every burn and enough for a non-circumferential burn with good perfusion; once pulses fade it does not relieve the eschar.
AS-2316.D: Measure intracompartmental pressure: useful when deep muscle compartment syndrome is suspected but equivocal, e.g. after escharotomy fails or in electrical/crush injury; here perfusion is clearly compromised and measuring only delays release.

AS-2324.A: Tracheostomy: a planned procedure for prolonged ventilation (common later in high cord injury), not an emergency airway.
AS-2324.B: Cricothyroidotomy: the emergency surgical airway when orotracheal intubation fails or is impossible, e.g. severe maxillofacial injury or profuse oral bleeding; not first line here.
AS-2324.D: Nasotracheal tube: less reliable, needs spontaneous breathing, and is contraindicated with midface or basal skull fractures; it is not the preferred trauma airway.

AS-2325.A: The medication is safe to take during pregnancy: false; isotretinoin causes severe craniofacial, cardiac and CNS malformations and is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.
AS-2325.B: She can try to get pregnant after she finishes the treatment: omits the required drug free interval after the last dose, so conception could occur while the drug is still present.
AS-2325.C: Stop and try to get pregnant immediately: no washout period at all; conception must wait after the last dose.

AS-2326.A: She can conceive as soon as she stops the isotretinoin: no washout; conception must wait 1 month after the last dose.
AS-2326.B: She can conceive while taking isotretinoin: absolutely contraindicated; isotretinoin causes severe craniofacial, cardiac and CNS malformations.
AS-2326.C: She can conceive after 3 months off isotretinoin: overly long for isotretinoin; long post treatment intervals apply to acitretin, not isotretinoin.

AS-2328.A: Ex lap does not reach a retroperitoneal pelvic bleed and opening the abdomen can release the tamponade and worsen the bleeding. It is right when the unstable trauma patient has intraperitoneal bleeding (positive FAST / free intraperitoneal blood).

AS-2334.A: 3 to 6 months is for a large polyp removed piecemeal or incompletely, to check the resection site; here it was removed completely.
AS-2334.C: 10 years is the interval after a normal colonoscopy (average-risk screening) or for small hyperplastic polyps, not after an advanced adenoma.
AS-2334.D: An adenoma is a premalignant lesion, so surveillance is always needed; stopping screening is never right after an adenoma in a man of this age.

AS-2338.A: Cellulitis gives redness, warmth and pain after minor trauma but no crepitus and no rapidly spreading dusky discoloration; pain out of proportion plus crepitus means necrotizing infection.
AS-2338.B: Testicular torsion presents with sudden testicular pain, a high-riding horizontal testis and absent cremasteric reflex, usually in an adolescent; it does not cause perineal crepitus or spreading skin necrosis.

AS-2347.A: Cystic hygroma is a lateral (posterior triangle) soft, transilluminating lymphatic mass, usually seen in infancy; it is not midline and does not move with swallowing.
AS-2347.C: A midline dermoid cyst is also midline but is not attached to the hyoid, so it does not move with swallowing or tongue protrusion; it is often more superficial or submental.
AS-2347.D: Submental lymph nodes lie above the hyoid, are often tender when reactive and do not move with swallowing.

AS-2380.A: Melasma: the same pigmentary process (chloasma is melasma occurring in pregnancy); the recall prefers the pregnancy specific term, while melasma fits a non pregnant woman, for example on oral contraceptives.
AS-2380.C: Tinea nigra: a painless brown to black macule, usually single, on the palms or soles; it does not cause symmetric facial patches.
AS-2380.D: Lichen planus: itchy, purple, polygonal, flat topped papules with Wickham striae on wrists, shins and oral mucosa; not brown facial patches.

AS-2386.A: Angiography with embolectomy is the definitive treatment for embolic mesenteric ischemia, but it follows resuscitation and heparin; it is not the initial step.
AS-2386.B: Thrombolysis is contraindicated here because of an ischemic stroke within the last 3 months, and it is not the first step anyway; catheter-directed lysis is reserved for selected early cases without peritonitis.
AS-2386.D: Abdominal ultrasound is limited by bowel gas and does not show the mesenteric vessels adequately; CT angiography is the diagnostic test of choice.

AS-2397.A: 8 would require motor 4 (withdrawal from pain) instead of localizing, or one point less elsewhere; localizing to pain is motor 5.
AS-2397.C: 10 would need inappropriate words (V3) or eye opening to speech (E3); groaning is V2 and opening to pain is E2.
AS-2397.D: 11 overscores by two points, e.g. it would need both eyes to speech and words rather than sounds.

AS-2414.A: Physiotherapy is for mechanical back pain or rehabilitation after decompression; it delays treatment of a cord compression.
AS-2414.B: MRI is the right test but it must be urgent (same day), not outpatient; outpatient imaging is for back pain without red flags or neurological deficit.
AS-2414.D: Analgesia and reassessing after 24 hours wastes the window to save neurological function; that approach suits simple back pain without red flags.

AS-2415.B: Start him on trial of amphetamines: stimulants are started only after the diagnosis is confirmed; a therapeutic trial is not a diagnostic test.
AS-2415.C: Reassure the mother that these are normal behaviors at his age: premature; dismissing her report without school information can miss true ADHD. Reassurance fits only after collateral history is normal.
AS-2415.D: Do neurological exam: part of a general assessment to exclude other causes, but it does not establish or refute ADHD, which is a clinical diagnosis based on history across settings.

AS-2417.A: Preschool examinations are screening visits, not a treatment; this child is 7 and already of school age, so they do nothing to change his behavior.
AS-2417.B: Cutting screen time is reasonable general advice but has no proven effect as a treatment for ADHD symptoms or aggression; it would only be a supportive add on.
AS-2417.D: Special education resources are for a child with a learning disability or academic failure; nothing in the stem describes school performance problems, and they do not address outbursts at home.

AS-2420.B: Screening bloods are chosen when growth velocity is slow, the child crosses centiles downward, or there are symptoms of systemic disease (malabsorption, renal, chronic illness). None are present here.
AS-2420.C: Sunlight is advice for vitamin D deficiency or rickets (bowed legs, widened wrists, bone pain), which is not suggested in a healthy child growing at a normal rate.
AS-2420.D: Avoiding dairy has no role; it would reduce calcium and protein intake. Dairy restriction is only for proven cow's milk protein allergy.

AS-2421.B: Adenovirus gives cough with fever, conjunctivitis and often diarrhea; choose it when those extra-respiratory features appear, which are absent here.
AS-2421.C: Mycoplasma pneumonia mainly affects school-age children and young adults, with a gradual dry cough and malaise; it is uncommon at 3 months and does not cause a whoop.
AS-2421.D: Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia has a staccato (not whooping) cough, preceding conjunctivitis, crackles, no fever and eosinophilia; the preceding illness here was a runny nose, not conjunctivitis.

AS-2422.A: Pertussis gives a whooping cough without conjunctivitis or crackles, usually after a runny nose rather than an eye infection; typical labs show lymphocytosis, not isolated eosinophilia.
AS-2422.B: Adenovirus also causes conjunctivitis and cough, but it brings fever and diarrhea; choose it when diarrhea is present.
AS-2422.C: Mycoplasma is a pneumonia of school-age children and adolescents and is not associated with neonatal conjunctivitis or eosinophilia.

AS-2423.A: Pertussis causes isolated whooping paroxysms without fever, conjunctivitis or diarrhea, typically in an unvaccinated infant; a whoop alone is not enough when these extra features are present.
AS-2423.C: Mycoplasma pneumonia is a disease of older children and young adults and does not cause conjunctivitis with diarrhea in a 3-month-old.
AS-2423.D: Chlamydia also follows conjunctivitis, but it is afebrile, has a staccato cough and does not cause diarrhea.

AS-2425.B: Acute pancreatitis gives epigastric pain radiating to the back with clear epigastric tenderness and a risk factor such as gallstones or alcohol; it is chosen when amylase/lipase is ≥3 times the upper limit with characteristic pain. Here the cardiac history and pain out of proportion favour ischemia.

AS-2429.A: Egg allergy is not a contraindication to MMR or other routine childhood vaccines; it matters mainly for yellow fever vaccine, and current guidance gives influenza vaccine to egg-allergic children without special precautions.
AS-2429.C: Mild illness with or without fever is not a contraindication; only moderate to severe acute illness is a precaution that delays vaccination, so a fever check alone is less decisive.
AS-2429.D: Inspecting the previous vaccine site has no bearing on whether the next dose is safe or effective; a past mild local reaction is not a contraindication.

AS-2431.A: 6 months is a short-interval follow-up for a probably benign finding (BI-RADS 3), not for a completely normal screening mammogram.
AS-2431.C: 2 years is the interval taught for average-risk women aged 50 to 74 (and some guidelines apply it from 40); in this card's 40 to 50 rule the answer is yearly.
AS-2431.D: 3 years is not a mammography interval; it is the Pap smear (cytology) interval for cervical screening.

AS-2433.A: Antibiotics alone do not remove the injected material; they are an adjunct given alongside surgery. Antibiotics alone fit simple cellulitis without a retained injected substance.
AS-2433.B: Antibiotics and steroids are sometimes used as adjuncts after surgical debridement, but neither removes the oil, so they cannot replace surgery.
AS-2433.D: Elevation and ice is for a minor soft tissue contusion or sprain; it gives false reassurance and lets necrosis progress in an injection injury.

AS-2434.A: Physical restraint worsens agitation, prolongs delirium and causes injury; it is a last resort only for immediate danger when other measures fail.
AS-2434.B: A quiet room alone is part of the environmental care but isolation without orientation cues can worsen confusion; orientation is the active intervention asked for.
AS-2434.C: Antipsychotics (e.g. low dose haloperidol) are used only when non-drug measures fail and agitation is severe or dangerous; they are not the first step in an elderly patient.

AS-2436.A: Neglect requires evidence such as missed feeds, poor hygiene, unexplained injuries or a disengaged caregiver; here the mother feeds regularly and the error is technical.
AS-2436.B: Celiac disease needs gluten exposure, which starts with weaning to cereals after about 6 months; it presents later with diarrhea, distension and buttock wasting, not in an exclusively formula-fed 4-month-old.
AS-2436.D: Feeding every 3 hours (about 8 feeds a day) is normal for this age, so frequency is not the problem.

AS-2437.B: خيار غير صحيح بناءً على معطيات السؤال.

AS-2438.A: Pancreatitis: causes epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting, but nephrotic syndrome itself does not specifically predispose to it; consider it only if lipase is raised or the child is on drugs that cause it.
AS-2438.B: Hepatitis: presents with jaundice, RUQ tenderness and raised transaminases; nephrotic syndrome does not increase hepatitis risk and it would not explain acute distension with persistent vomiting.
AS-2438.D: Heart failure: gives edema, hepatomegaly and tachycardia with breathlessness, not an acute painful distended abdomen; the edema here is explained by hypoalbuminemia.

AS-2442.B: Observation is not appropriate for a large 10 cm lesion, which risks airway compression, infection and hemorrhage into the cyst; spontaneous regression is uncommon.
AS-2442.C: Chemotherapy is for malignancy (e.g. lymphoma, rhabdomyosarcoma); clear lymphatic fluid indicates a benign malformation.
AS-2442.D: Radiotherapy has no role in a benign lymphatic malformation in a child and carries growth and malignancy risks.

AS-2445.A: Urine oxalic level: used to look for hyperoxaluria in recurrent kidney stones or nephrocalcinosis, not a tumour marker.
AS-2445.C: PSA: a marker of prostate disease in adult men; it has no role in a 12-week-old infant or in liver tumours.
AS-2445.D: Urine HVA and VMA: catecholamine metabolites used for neuroblastoma (adrenal or paraspinal mass), not for a liver lesion.

AS-2446.A: MRI with contrast is slower, harder in a sick patient with hydrocephalus and less sensitive for acute blood; MR angiography is an alternative mainly when CT contrast is not possible, not the standard first vessel study.
AS-2446.B: Lumbar puncture only confirms SAH (xanthochromia, persistent RBCs) when CT is negative and more than 6 hours from onset; here CT is already positive and LP gives no information about the artery.
AS-2446.D: Transcranial Doppler is used after SAH to monitor for vasospasm, not to locate the ruptured aneurysm.

AS-2452.A: 500 ml initially is far below the threshold; the immediate output that mandates thoracotomy is more than 1500 ml.
AS-2452.C: Hemopneumothorax is managed with the same chest tube; the presence of air plus blood is not itself an indication for surgery.
AS-2452.D: Some drop in Hb and hematocrit is expected with any hemothorax and resuscitation; the trigger is chest tube output or hemodynamic decompensation, not a lab change alone.

AS-2453.B: An initial 500 ml is a moderate hemothorax that the chest tube alone usually manages; the immediate criterion is more than 1500 ml.

AS-2454.A: Crepitation: crackles come from alveolar or small airway fluid, as in pneumonia or bronchiolitis; croup is an upper airway disease.
AS-2454.B: Wheezing: an expiratory sound of lower airway narrowing (asthma, bronchiolitis), not the inspiratory upper airway noise of croup.
AS-2454.D: Gasp: gasping is an agonal pattern of impending arrest, not the typical finding in a child with mild retractions and stable vitals.

AS-2456.A: Urine culture: right when dysuria, frequency or a febrile child without another focus suggest UTI; here the fever fits the throat infection and the dark urine is glomerular hematuria, not infection.
AS-2456.B: Renal ultrasound: helpful for stones, obstruction or structural anomalies, but adds little in suspected acute glomerulonephritis.
AS-2456.C: Renal biopsy: reserved for atypical or non-resolving cases (persistent low C3, rapidly rising creatinine, nephrotic-range proteinuria), never the first step.

AS-2457.A: Blood culture: a useful adjunct, but it is positive in only a minority and cannot confirm joint infection on its own.
AS-2457.C: IV antibiotics: essential and given promptly, right after joint fluid is obtained; giving them first can sterilise the aspirate and hide the organism. Right first only if aspiration would be delayed in an unstable or septic child.

AS-2458.B: Bacterial: gives a low CSF glucose, raised protein and neutrophil predominance with turbid fluid.
AS-2458.C: Tuberculous: also lymphocytic, but with low glucose and markedly raised protein, usually after weeks of fever and headache in an endemic setting.

AS-2462.A: Bicuspid aortic valve: usually gives an ejection click or murmur and is not a typical familial cause of sudden death in youth.
AS-2462.B: Patent ductus arteriosus: produces a continuous machinery murmur (absent here) and is not a hereditary cause of sudden cardiac death.
AS-2462.C: Ventricular septal defect: produces a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border (absent here) and does not cause familial sudden death.

AS-2464.A: Antibiotics do not help a sterile granuloma; they are reserved for a secondarily infected lesion or associated preseptal cellulitis.

AS-2465.A: Hypovolemic shock causes vasoconstriction with cold, clammy extremities and tachycardia; it would be the answer if the patient were cold and tachycardic after trauma.
AS-2465.C: Cardiogenic or obstructive shock gives cold peripheries, tachycardia and cardiac signs such as raised JVP or muffled heart sounds, none of which are present.
AS-2465.D: Septic shock is also warm, but needs an infective source and produces tachycardia; it does not appear immediately after an accident.

AS-2471.A: NPO: withholding oral feeds while the baby is tachypneic reduces aspiration risk, but on its own it does not maintain hydration; this recall keys fluid support as the most important step.
AS-2471.B: Empirical antibiotics: right when sepsis or congenital pneumonia is suspected (maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, worsening course); TTN itself is not infective.

AS-2529.A: Sertraline treats depression or anxiety in dementia; there is no mention of mood symptoms and it does not slow cognitive decline.
AS-2529.B: Adding memantine to donepezil is used in moderate to severe disease when the patient is benefiting from or tolerating the cholinesterase inhibitor; the stem stresses complete lack of response, which the key treats as a reason to switch rather than combine.
AS-2529.D: Rivastigmine is another cholinesterase inhibitor with the same mechanism; switching within the class is mainly for intolerance of donepezil rather than lack of effect, and the decline is now moderate.

AS-2532.A: Urgent referral to ENT for tonsillectomy: tonsillectomy is elective treatment for recurrent tonsillitis or obstructive sleep apnea, not an emergency airway measure.
AS-2532.B: Complete sepsis work up, followed by antibiotics for 7 days: cultures and antibiotics are needed, but only after the airway is secured; doing them first can provoke obstruction.
AS-2532.C: Send home on oral antibiotics for 7 days and referral to ENT: suits a well child with simple bacterial pharyngitis; a toxic, drooling child must never be discharged.

AS-2534.A: Urgent colonoscopy is the diagnostic and therapeutic test for lower GI bleeding (polyp is a likely source), but only after resuscitation and bowel preparation; it is never the first step in a tachycardic patient.
AS-2534.B: CT (angiography) is used to localise active bleeding in a patient who keeps bleeding, after resuscitation has started; it does not replace volume and blood replacement.
AS-2534.C: Oral iron treats chronic iron deficiency anaemia in a stable outpatient; it does nothing for acute haemorrhage with tachycardia.

AS-2535.A: Unfractionated heparin is preferred when LMWH is unsuitable: severe renal impairment, very high bleeding risk needing rapid reversal, or acute arterial limb ischaemia. None of these is stated.
AS-2535.C: IVC filter is reserved for proximal DVT/PE when anticoagulation is contraindicated (e.g. active bleeding) or for clot progression despite adequate anticoagulation.
AS-2535.D: Thrombolysis is contraindicated soon after major surgery and is kept for massive PE with shock or limb-threatening iliofemoral DVT, not routine DVT.

AS-2536.A: IV ceftriaxone: afebrile with a clear chest and normal radiograph; mild leukocytosis is common in DKA. Antibiotics are right only when an infective trigger is found.
AS-2536.C: IV potassium chloride: K 4.4 is normal; potassium is added to the fluids once insulin starts and K falls. Replacing potassium before insulin is needed only when K is below 3.3.
AS-2536.D: IV sodium bicarbonate: reserved for very severe acidosis (pH below 6.9); pH 7.10 corrects with fluids and insulin.

AS-2536B.A: IV bicarbonate is reserved for very severe acidosis (pH below 6.9); at pH 7.15 it adds no benefit and risks hypokalemia and paradoxical CNS acidosis.
AS-2536B.B: Subcutaneous insulin is used once DKA has resolved (overlapping with the infusion before stopping it); absorption is unreliable in a dehydrated acidotic patient, so it is not the initial treatment here.

AS-2536C.A: IV bicarbonate is not routine and in children is linked to cerebral edema and hypokalemia. It is considered only in extreme acidosis (pH below about 6.9) or life-threatening hyperkalemia.
AS-2536C.C: Subcutaneous insulin with oral hydration suits only mild DKA in an alert child who tolerates fluids. With pH 7.0 and vomiting, absorption and oral intake are unreliable.
AS-2536C.D: Raising bicarbonate does not stop ketosis; only insulin switches off ketone production. This option misunderstands the pathophysiology.

AS-2536D.B: Uncontrolled hyperglycemia: describes a glucose number, not the cause of the acidosis and fruity breath; and RBS 8.9 mmol/L is not markedly high.
AS-2536D.C: Hyponatremia: sodium 131 is a mild consequence of vomiting and diarrhea, not the cause of drowsiness and ketotic breath.
AS-2536D.D: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state: needs very high glucose and high osmolality with little or no ketosis; here glucose is near normal and the breath is ketotic.

AS-2538.A: Methotrexate: the correct anchor DMARD, but alone it gives no rapid control of active synovitis while it takes effect; in this recall the bridge is the missing piece.
AS-2538.B: Methotrexate and sulfasalazine: an acceptable DMARD combination, but it still lacks the steroid bridge for active arthritis.
AS-2538.C: Methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine: good maintenance DMARDs, but no bridging glucocorticoid for the currently active joints.

AS-2540.A: Chest x ray: useful to confirm each pneumonia episode, but it cannot show dynamic airway collapse or the cause of a fixed central obstruction.
AS-2540.B: CBC and blood culture: assess infection or sepsis in an acute episode, but do not explain why pneumonia keeps recurring with a fixed wheeze.
AS-2540.C: Spirometry: the diagnostic test for asthma or COPD in older children and adults; it needs cooperation and is not feasible at 5 months.
